1 # Anthropic PBC 2 3 ### A cryptographically verifiable counterpoint to Anthropic's 2026 Public Benefit Report 4 5 > Governance exists so that systems can survive individuals. 6 7 I'm publishing this in a personal capacity, to show a set of composable 8 governance primitives I've built over the past year as Chief Investment Officer 9 at Ethical Capital, a Utah-registered investment adviser. So this is governance 10 advice, not investment advice; I hold no direct or indirect position in 11 Anthropic, and our screening, our process, and our timestamped analysis of most 12 large public companies — the hyperscalers included — are public at ethicic.com. 13 A disclosure like that has never satisfied the duty of care I actually feel I 14 owe my regulators, my clients, and my community. It leaves the one question that 15 matters unanswered: **am I in control of the systems I use to make decisions, 16 operate, and balance competing priorities?** You should ask it of anyone — me, 17 and Anthropic. 18 19 For a long-term investor it isn't optional. Returns materialize over decades, so 20 we have to back systems of activity that can survive the loss of any one person; 21 and because our ethical criteria are stringent, I care less about correlation 22 than about intrinsic alignment — is the thing built, at its core, to do what it 23 says? That is exactly what a public benefit corporation is supposed to be. Good 24 governance is the kind you can recognize from the outside: you can see how a 25 company organizes its operations, and the mindset and values the whole system 26 springs from. That is the highest of Donella Meadows' places to intervene in a 27 system, and the one almost no one moves. 28 29 Here is a public benefit corporation I'm directly involved in: 30 [Wood Cache](https://www.woodcache.org). You can understand what it does from the 31 website in a minute. The fastest-growing carbon pool in the Mountain West is dead 32 trees; they burn, and when they burn they throw off the most dangerous air 33 pollution there is. Wood Cache buries that biomass and locks the carbon away 34 instead — measured and verified end to end under 35 [Puro.earth's terrestrial-storage methodology](https://puro.earth/methodologies/terrestrial-storage-of-biomass/), 36 with the burial sites themselves permitted and regulated by the State of Colorado 37 as landfills. Sit with the disparity: this is a small, directly observable, 38 present public benefit, and the scrutiny on it is immense — while the worst case 39 is that carbon which would have burned anyway instead sits underground and breaks 40 down over a shorter horizon than the academic models predict. The inputs are 41 certain, controlled, and governed; the open questions are mostly market demand 42 and economics. That is what a real public benefit looks like, and it is the 43 opposite of the sexy move — a convoluted machine that turns carbon into money 44 through some bleeding-edge, multi-gigawatt feat of engineering, with the benefit 45 arriving, supposedly, later. Accumulate power, pour in capital, trust that impact 46 shows up someday: that is the model our culture has learned to call "impact," and 47 I don't accept it. 48 49 The public-benefit-corporation category is about to balloon when Anthropic lists, 50 so it matters, now, to have a way to check whether a benefit claim is actually 51 backed by the evidence offered for it. That is what I built. I call it Praxis, 52 and I named its parts after philosophers so their jobs are legible: **Descartes** 53 verifies the smallest facts it can, with no external input, and signs them; those 54 facts accrete into entities and relationships; **Rawls** runs them through a veil 55 of ignorance — would you accept this system if you didn't get to choose who you'd 56 be inside it? The report below came together largely that way, deterministically, 57 with light editorial shaping. It already caught one of my own errors, which is 58 the method working, not failing. 59 60 Anthropic fails that test in a specific way. The harm is distributed; there is no 61 visible feedback loop between the people it lands on now and the people deciding; 62 and the structure is a race to be first, in which you cannot help but lose control 63 of your effect on others. Set that against Wood Cache: a small, observable benefit 64 submits to immense scrutiny, while Anthropic proposes to expose the world to 65 genuinely serious risks and — rather than cede control of that exposure, even to 66 the users already paying for the compute — insists on holding it itself. It treats 67 impact the way finance treats money, too: deploy the capital today, clear your 68 return in a decade. But impact is not a single currency, and there is no 69 reconciliation unless a governance forces one. What follows takes Anthropic at its 70 own word — against its own filings and its own Constitution — and checks, byte by 71 byte, where the words and the acts diverge. 72 73 --- 74 75 ## Architecture 76 77 ```mermaid 78 flowchart TB 79 subgraph SRC["Primary sources — public record"] 80 S1["S-1 / SEC filings"] 81 PBC["PBC Report"] 82 CON["Constitution (CC0)"] 83 end 84 85 subgraph DES["Descartes · what is true"] 86 ART["Artifacts
content-addressed (BLAKE3)"] 87 CLM["Claims
byte-exact quotes"] 88 DAG["DAG of claims + evidence"] 89 ATT["ed25519 attestations"] 90 VER{"Verify: rebuild
from scratch,
same root?"} 91 end 92 93 subgraph RAW["Rawls · what is fair"] 94 VEIL["Veil of ignorance
over affected parties"] 95 IDX["Risk–Governance Index"] 96 end 97 98 subgraph ARE["Arendt · what is public"] 99 PUB["Working paper
hash-pinned, versioned"] 100 LED["Sign-on / dispute ledger
DKIM email · SSH · ed25519"] 101 end 102 103 S1 --> ART 104 PBC --> ART 105 CON --> ART 106 ART --> CLM --> DAG --> ATT --> VER 107 VER -- "sealed claims only" --> VEIL --> IDX --> PUB 108 CLM --> PUB 109 PUB --> LED 110 LED -- "new signed records" --> DAG 111 ``` 112 113 **Descartes** establishes what is true, **Rawls** weighs what is fair, **Arendt** 114 makes it public — each stage consuming only what the stage before it verified and 115 signed. Disputes re-enter the graph as new signed records; nothing is overwritten. 116 117 --- 118 119 ## The document 120 121 - **Read the paper:** [`docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md`](docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md) — §0 rubric through §9 open questions, with appendices. 122 - **Risk–Governance Index:** [`docs/risk-governance-index.md`](docs/risk-governance-index.md) — every disclosed risk joined to the mechanism that would control it. 123 - **Sign on or dispute:** [`docs/contrapunctus-attest.md`](docs/contrapunctus-attest.md) — cryptographic endorsement or dispute, bound to this exact version. 124 - **The method it argues from:** `praxis-white-paper.md`, `praxis-standard.md`, `descartes-spec.md`, and the primitives (`circles`, `epistemics`, `primitives`, `strictness`). 125 126 ## Verify 127 128 paper: docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md 129 version: v0 · 2026-11-03 130 blake3: 698b6c6785961b566e27dbf6306707ec530b4ba6e9f3823b6a99b3b42504dcea 131 132 Recompute it yourself: `b3sum docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md`. The index is 157 deterministically generated — each risk factor and each mechanism is a 158 Descartes-verified claim, and the index is their join. Re-run it, you get the same 159 table. PBC Report (hash on file); Constitution (CC0). 188 **Index content hash:** `blake3:` 189 190 | # | Risk factor (disclosed) | Source | Governing mechanism | Status | Evidence / verdict | 191 |---|---|---|---|---|---| 192 | 1 | Open-source software vulnerabilities and under-maintenance, a material operational risk | S-1 | None that funds the commons it draws from; would need **GOV-7** (provenance + reciprocity) | `Externalized` | the exposure and the unpaid-maintainer harm are one fact — to-verify | 193 | 2 | "Absence of judicial precedent interpreting this structure" raises governance-litigation risk | S-1 | **GOV-8** (irrevocable lock) — not adopted | `Uncontrolled` | Anthropic tells investors the lock is untested — CONFIRMED | 194 | 3 | Misalignment behaviors "have been observed across the industry" | S-1 | **GOV-1** (independent replication gate) — voluntary only | `Externalized` | industry-wide framing for a failure its own Report instantiates — CONFIRMED | 195 | 4 | Workforce displacement framed as a perception/regulatory risk "regardless of the actual impact" | S-1 | **GOV-2 / GOV-10** (outcome registry, metered displacement) — absent | `Uncontrolled` | manages the politics, not the reality — NUANCED | 196 | 5 | Government interruption — June 2026 export restriction on two models | S-1 | External state action; revenue retained | `Uncontrolled` | ~$1.7–2.3B booked before termination — CONFIRMED | 198 | 7 | Decisions concentrated in "a handful… Anthropic is one… few external checks" | PBC p.12 | **GOV-4 / GOV-5 / GOV-8** (standing, frameworks-as-data, lock) — absent | `Uncontrolled` | a self-declared controlled company — CONFIRMED | 199 | 8 | Four Claude models reached real third-party systems in testing | PBC p.6 | **GOV-10** (bonded, timed incident disclosure) — absent; The pattern is externalization — to the 203 industry, the future, the state, or the customer — exactly where a system in 204 control of its own effects would carry the mechanism itself. 205 206 ## Changelog 207 208 - **v1 (2026-11-03):** initial index; 8 disclosed risks joined to mechanisms. 209 7 `Uncontrolled`/`Externalized`, 1 to-verify. 210 # Primitives 211 212 Every open problem so far reduces to three needs: say what is true, say who 213 decided, and say whose interest the decision served. This document proposes 214 how to express all three with the node kinds we already have, plus two 215 changes: 216 217 - one edge (`against`); 218 - building the evaluation node, which `docs/epistemics.md` designs but which 219 doesn't exist yet. 220 221 ## The rule 222 223 **When rules conflict, resolve in the client's interest.** This is the rule 224 Sloane was taught at CFA Institute. It also fixes the defect in Standard 225 I(A)'s "more strict" test (`docs/strictness.md`): strictness can't rank rules 226 that constrain different things, but the client's interest can. 227 228 The rule needs two tie-breaks, and both are proposals: 229 230 1. **Reversibility.** When the client's interest is unclear, prefer the action 231 that can be undone. Retaining sealed bytes can be undone; destroying them 232 cannot. 233 2. **Visibility.** Never resolve a conflict silently. A hidden resolution 234 takes the client's ability to object. 235 236 ## The primitives 237 238 ### What exists 239 240 | Kind | Holds | Meaning | 241 |---|---|---| 242 | artifact | bytes, by digest | What was received. Circle 0. | 243 | claim | statement, witness, quoted evidence, `supports` | What someone says is true, and why. | 244 | derivation | input, tool, args, output | What a tool turned into what. | 245 | attestation | signer, subject | Who stands behind a node. | 246 | snapshot | members | What one run saw. | 247 248 ### The two changes 249 250 **A. `against` on claims and evaluations.** 251 Today a claim can only list what supports it, so the graph can only build up 252 agreement. Neither a contested claim nor its contest can be written down, and 253 ACH needs both. With `against`, any claim can name the claims it opposes. 254 255 **Conflict** then has a definition the verifier can check: two claims, either 256 of which is against the other. 257 258 This change applies to the claim node, so it changes the ids of every claim 259 that uses `against`. Claims that don't use it keep their ids if the field is 260 omitted when empty. 261 262 **B. Evaluations, as designed in `docs/epistemics.md`.** 263 An evaluation has this shape: 264 265 ``` 266 evaluation { framework, subject, rating, rests_on, witness } 267 ``` 268 269 A framework is an ingested file under `frameworks/` that lists the ratings it 270 allows. Every judgment the system makes then has the same shape: a rating, 271 under a named version of a framework, resting on claims, signed by whoever 272 stands behind it. 273 274 ### Everything else is a framework 275 276 What other designs would add as new machinery, these primitives express as a 277 framework file plus evaluations: 278 279 | Need | Framework | Subject | Ratings | Signer must be | 280 |---|---|---|---|---| 281 | Resolve a conflict | `interest` | the conflicting claims | which side, and which party it serves | a human (circle 4) | 282 | Hold or drop bytes | `custody` | an artifact | `held`, `sealed`, `withheld` | an authorised human | 283 | Record a gate outcome | `gates` | a run's snapshot | `pass`, `fail`, `skipped`, `not-applicable` | the loop (witness), checkable | 284 | Source reliability | `admiralty` | a claim | A–F × 1–6 | an analyst | 285 | Fitness to use | `use-policy` | a snapshot, as of a reference | `fit`, `unfit` | a human or a stated rule | 286 287 Four verifier rules follow from these: 288 289 1. **A missing blob is corruption** unless an attested `custody` evaluation 290 rates it `withheld` or `sealed`. Determinism forbids *sampling* the clock during a 305 derivation. The client keeps the work and learns its assurance level. | 318 | Advisory freshness (C2) | derivation over an advisory-db commit, then `use-policy` | Builds stay offline. Use on client data requires a recent audit. | 319 | Erasure (C3) | `custody`: `sealed` or `withheld` | Seal the original, drop the derived copies. Reversible, and it keeps the client's record. | 320 | Retention clocks (C4) | the fiscal-year claim as a recorded input | No clock inside any node. | 321 | Payloads in git (C5) | `custody`: `held` by a named custodian | Git is one custodian among others. The digest is the identity. | 322 | Testimony (R1) | audio artifact, then a transcription derivation, then quotes | The transcript enters at circle 2 or 3 with its loss stated. It is not excluded. | 323 | Named people contest (R3) | a claim `against` the claim | Anyone can contest, and the contest stays visible. | 324 325 ## The paste on key custody, SSDF and seams, read through these primitives 326 327 These items are not yet ingested as a witness, and the facts in them are not 328 checked. 329 330 - **OpenBao key custody.** 331 - This fits the primitives without changes: the signer is still a 332 `did:key`, and a `custody` claim states where its secret lives 333 (non-exportable transit key, unseal shares) without ever containing the 334 secret. 335 - Descartes needs only `sign` to accept an external signer. 336 - Who holds each unseal share is a governance decision for you. It goes on 337 the roster with your attestation, not in code. 338 - **SSDF.** It becomes `frameworks/ssdf.tsv` with `gates` evaluations against 339 it, so a pass is computed from those evaluations rather than stored as a 340 `bool`. Joule and carbon figures are estimates, so they are circle 3 claims 349 with their method stated. Network egress needs no telemetry, because the 350 sandbox probe already proves it. 351 352 ## Build order, if accepted 353 354 1. `frameworks/` and the evaluation node, plus verifier checks: ratings come 355 from the framework, and `rests_on` must exist. 356 2. `against` on claims, plus the unresolved-conflict report. 357 3. The `gates` framework. The loop emits evaluations, and the stage 1 artifact 358 becomes their projection. 359 4. The `custody` framework and verifier rule 1. 360 5. The roster and verifier rule 4. 361 6. `interest`. At first it holds only what you sign, with no automation. 362 363 ## Bad decisions, revisited 364 365 Principle 12 means the graph must be able to hold a mistake and its 366 correction side by side. No new primitive is needed for that: 367 368 - A decision is an `interest` (or `admiralty`, `use-policy`) evaluation 369 signed by a person. 370 - When the outcome is known, it enters as claims, such as returns or later 371 findings. 372 - A revisit is a new evaluation that rests on the outcome claims and carries 373 `against` the original. The original stays. Nothing is overwritten. 374 - Learning from decisions means querying for evaluations that carry 375 `against`, alongside the outcomes that prompted them. This becomes a 376 framework comparison (`docs/epistemics.md`) once there are enough of 377 them. Running that search automatically requires explicit opt-in. 378 379 ## Received attestations 380 381 A company's statement about itself, such as a supplier code or a response to 382 a screening finding, enters like any other witness: 383 384 1. Its document is an artifact. 385 2. A claim quotes it, with witness `org:`. If the company signed it with 386 a key, an attestation records that too. 387 3. When it disputes our claim, the two claims carry `against` each other. 388 The verifier reports the pair as an unresolved conflict until an 389 `interest` evaluation resolves it. 390 4. The company's interest in the outcome is rated by `admiralty`, not 391 handled by excluding its statement. 392 393 A person named in a claim contests it the same way. 394 395 ## Answers to the pasted decision memo (2026-11-02) 396 397 How each answer maps onto these primitives: 398 399 - **Withheld: yes.** 400 - It becomes a `custody` evaluation with rating `withheld` or `sealed`, not 401 a separate node kind: 402 - the memo's `tombstone_type` becomes the rating; 403 - `authority_ref` becomes `rests_on` claims that quote the authority; 404 - `authorizer_did` becomes the attestation signer. 405 - Two departures from the memo: 406 - The signature does not cover a timestamp. If the time matters, it goes 407 in as a recorded claim (time is an input). 408 - The `ClientForgetAuthorized` reason stays, but `docs/strictness.md` S9 409 found no statutory right to be forgotten for a Utah adviser. It is a 410 voluntary commitment and should be described as one. 411 - **Payloads out of git.** 412 - Every source is listed in `sources/MANIFEST.tsv` by digest and size, 413 plus one of: a URL to fetch it from, or a named custodian (`held`) for 414 sources that have no upstream URL. 415 - The bytes live in `.descartes/sources/`, which git ignores. 416 - The loop checks hashes only for bytes that are present, and records 417 `skipped` for the rest as `gates` evaluations. 418 - Moving the PDFs already committed out of git changes the stage 0 419 inventory, but not the graph root. 420 - **Not built:** 421 - R2 sync, through the `bws run` and rclone guardrails; 422 - the offline archive. 423 - **Advisory freshness.** `audit.sh` writes the advisory-db commit to a 424 tracked file. The loop checks only that the file is well formed, which 425 needs no network and no clock. 426 - **Retention clocks.** 427 - Fiscal-year-end and the retention authority enter as claims. 428 - "Retain until" is a derivation from them (FYE + 5 years, or 7 years for 429 §6.14 recordings), so it is computed and never typed in. 430 - The memo's separate `retention_events.tsv` is not needed. 431 - **Contest (R3).** 432 - The memo's `rebuttals.tsv` and its `DissentRecorded` state are claims 433 carrying `against`, plus the unresolved-conflict report. Both already 434 fit the primitives. 435 - One correction: Bao byte-range proofs are not built. Evidence today is a 436 quote plus its BLAKE3 slice digest, checked against the whole artifact. 437 - **Deadlocks.** The memo's `decisions/deadlocks.tsv` is also the 438 unresolved-conflict report. Its "FiduciaryResolutionReceipt" is an 439 attested `interest` evaluation. 440 - **One fact to check.** The memo puts the 15–20% revenue threshold at 441 screening-policy §4.4. The earlier check of monocloud found no such 442 threshold in `screening-policy.md` or in Written Procedures §4.4. This 443 needs a source before anything cites it. 444 # Is this the strictest standard? 445 446 Source: `sources/llm-witness-strictness.md`, an LLM text Sloane pasted on 447 2026-11-02 (model unknown). Its claims and the checks against them are in 448 `claims/strictness.tsv` (W = witness, K = check, S = verdict), and the loop 449 ingests them like any other claims. 450 451 ## The point that holds 452 453 CFA Standard I(A) settles a conflict between rules by picking "the more 454 strict" one (K12). That works only when the rules can be ranked by strictness. 455 When two rules constrain different things, such as isolation and freshness, or 456 determinism and time, no ranking exists, and "the more strict" has no meaning. 457 Choosing between such rules is a judgment, and a judgment needs a person and a 458 record (S7). The witness's three gates find these cases: 459 460 1. **Null set.** The two rules cannot both be satisfied. 461 2. **Second-order cost.** Tightening one rule quietly loosens another. 462 3. **Worst-off party.** Someone the author doesn't think about pays for the 463 rule. 464 465 ## What the witness got wrong 466 467 | Claim | Finding | Row | 468 |---|---|---| 469 | `forbid(unsafe_code)` proves the binary has no undefined behaviour | **False.** The lint covers one crate. blake3, curve25519-dalek, sha2 and zeroize all contain `unsafe`. | S1 | 470 | Descartes already forbids `unsafe` | **False when pasted.** Our source had none, so the lint is now on and costs nothing. | S2 | 471 | Zero C toolchains | **Partly.** No C is compiled, but the `cc` driver crate is built as a blake3 build dependency. | S3 | 472 | bwrap sandbox | **Not verified.** bwrap is Linux-only and has never run here; the darwin path uses sandbox-exec. | S4 | 473 | A resolver rejects PRs that add unaudited crates | **False.** No such gate exists, and cargo-vet is not built. | S5 | 474 | ML-DSA signatures are about 40 KB | **False.** FIPS 204 gives 2,420 / 3,309 / 4,627 bytes; the ~50 KB figure is SLH-DSA-256f. **Not anchored:** FIPS 204 is 3.3 MB and waits on the payloads-in-git decision (C5). | W6 | 475 | Erasing on request violates 204-2, and retention violates privacy law | **False for Utah law.** The Utah privacy act exempts financial institutions under Gramm-Leach-Bliley (K15). Regulation S-P requires secure disposal, not deletion on request. That was checked by a research agent and is **not anchored** here. What remains is a conflict with whatever the firm promises voluntarily. | S9 | 476 | 204-2 and R164-5-1 set a five-year floor | **True.** R164-5-1 adopts 204-2 by reference. | S8 | 477 | Offline builds need an out-of-band advisory check | **True.** The witness's own check 2 contradicts it: that check fires even after `audit.sh` exists. | S6 | 478 479 The witness's Rust code does not compile, because `StrictnessResolver` is 480 never defined (K10). It also hard-codes its findings instead of testing for 481 them (K11). We don't adopt it. 482 483 Firm references, checked in monocloud and **not ingested here**: 484 485 - **Matches:** §6.16 (technology duties) and §6.14 (seven-year recording 486 retention) match. AI Governance Principle 1 is real. 487 - **Mismatches:** §4.4 is vendor oversight and has no 15% threshold. §3.1 and 488 §3.3 are numbered differently from what the witness cites. 489 - **Draft only:** the Data Retention Policy's sealed-original and 490 derived-surface split exists only in draft. 491 492 ## The gates, run on Descartes's own standards 493 494 ### Collisions 495 496 **C1. Doubt first vs. run on every chip (principles 1 and 5).** 497 Failing closed on every missing gate would shut out any machine without 498 sandbox-exec, bwrap, cargo-deny or tesseract. The loop therefore runs and 499 records what it skipped (K5). **Gap found and fixed today:** a skipped 500 fidelity check left no trace in the artifact. The artifact now carries a 501 `fidelity checked|skipped` row. 502 503 **C2. Offline build vs. advisories (second-order).** 504 Resolved in structure, since `stage1/audit.sh` is separate from the loop (S6). 505 **Gap:** nothing records which advisory database the last audit checked 506 against, so "audited" has no date or version. 507 **Proposal:** `audit.sh` writes the advisory-db commit hash to a tracked 508 artifact. That records which version was checked without putting wall-clock 509 time in content. 510 511 **C3. Immutable store vs. erasure (null set).** 512 The verifier treats a missing object as corruption (K7). For client records 513 no law forces erasure (S9). Erasure still matters in two cases: 514 - the firm promises deletion voluntarily; 515 - an ingested document carries third-party personal data the firm decides 516 not to keep. 517 518 Neither case has been checked against a specific obligation. 519 520 The store is already a rebuildable projection, so erasure means removing the 521 source and rebuilding. Every claim quoting that source then fails 522 verification. 523 **Needs a decision:** a `withheld` node that keeps the digest, drops the 524 bytes, and records who authorised the drop. The verifier would accept 525 "withheld by attestation" and still reject "missing". 526 527 **C4. Determinism vs. retention clocks.** 528 204-2 counts from fiscal year end (K13), but Descartes forbids time in hashed 529 content. **Resolution:** time belongs to an attestation or an external record 530 about a node, never inside the node. Not built. 531 532 **C5. No raw payloads in git vs. circle 0.** 533 Circle 0 needs the original bytes. The Iroh PDF cannot be fetched again, and 534 FIPS 204 was left out because of its size. **Open since the four decisions.** 535 536 **C6. `-D warnings` placement (second-order).** 537 In `Cargo.toml` it would make old source fail on any newer rustc that adds a 538 lint, which breaks principle 4. Actors who produce text, 545 such as companies, courts and regulators, can be cited directly. People whose 546 account exists only as speech or photographs cannot be cited until someone 547 transcribes them. The operator on old hardware.** 555 The loop asks for rustup, mise, poppler and tesseract. C1's record-and-run 556 behaviour keeps that operator in, at a recorded lower assurance. 557 558 **R3. People named in ingested documents.** 559 Anyone can attest to a claim, but a subject has no way to contest one. **Not 560 designed.** 561 562 ## No resolver yet 563 564 A collision does not need a new engine. # Anthropic PBC ### A cryptographically verifiable counterpoint to Anthropic's 2026 Public Benefit Report > Governance exists so that systems can survive individuals. I'm publishing this in a personal capacity, to show a set of composable governance primitives I've built over the past year as Chief Investment Officer at Ethical Capital, a Utah-registered investment adviser. So this is governance advice, not investment advice; I hold no direct or indirect position in Anthropic, and our screening, our process, and our timestamped analysis of most large public companies — the hyperscalers included — are public at ethicic.com. A disclosure like that has never satisfied the duty of care I actually feel I owe my regulators, my clients, and my community. It leaves the one question that matters unanswered: **am I in control of the systems I use to make decisions, operate, and balance competing priorities?** You should ask it of anyone — me, and Anthropic. For a long-term investor it isn't optional. Returns materialize over decades, so we have to back systems of activity that can survive the loss of any one person; and because our ethical criteria are stringent, I care less about correlation than about intrinsic alignment — is the thing built, at its core, to do what it says? That is exactly what a public benefit corporation is supposed to be. Good governance is the kind you can recognize from the outside: you can see how a company organizes its operations, and the mindset and values the whole system springs from. That is the highest of Donella Meadows' places to intervene in a system, and the one almost no one moves. Here is a public benefit corporation I'm directly involved in: [Wood Cache](https://www.woodcache.org). You can understand what it does from the website in a minute. The fastest-growing carbon pool in the Mountain West is dead trees; they burn, and when they burn they throw off the most dangerous air pollution there is. Wood Cache buries that biomass and locks the carbon away instead — measured and verified end to end under [Puro.earth's terrestrial-storage methodology](https://puro.earth/methodologies/terrestrial-storage-of-biomass/), with the burial sites themselves permitted and regulated by the State of Colorado as landfills. Sit with the disparity: this is a small, directly observable, present public benefit, and the scrutiny on it is immense — while the worst case is that carbon which would have burned anyway instead sits underground and breaks down over a shorter horizon than the academic models predict. The inputs are certain, controlled, and governed; the open questions are mostly market demand and economics. That is what a real public benefit looks like, and it is the opposite of the sexy move — a convoluted machine that turns carbon into money through some bleeding-edge, multi-gigawatt feat of engineering, with the benefit arriving, supposedly, later. Accumulate power, pour in capital, trust that impact shows up someday: that is the model our culture has learned to call "impact," and I don't accept it. The public-benefit-corporation category is about to balloon when Anthropic lists, so it matters, now, to have a way to check whether a benefit claim is actually backed by the evidence offered for it. That is what I built. I call it Praxis, and I named its parts after philosophers so their jobs are legible: **Descartes** verifies the smallest facts it can, with no external input, and signs them; those facts accrete into entities and relationships; **Rawls** runs them through a veil of ignorance — would you accept this system if you didn't get to choose who you'd be inside it? The report below came together largely that way, deterministically, with light editorial shaping. It already caught one of my own errors, which is the method working, not failing. Anthropic fails that test in a specific way. The harm is distributed; there is no visible feedback loop between the people it lands on now and the people deciding; and the structure is a race to be first, in which you cannot help but lose control of your effect on others. Set that against Wood Cache: a small, observable benefit submits to immense scrutiny, while Anthropic proposes to expose the world to genuinely serious risks and — rather than cede control of that exposure, even to the users already paying for the compute — insists on holding it itself. It treats impact the way finance treats money, too: deploy the capital today, clear your return in a decade. But impact is not a single currency, and there is no reconciliation unless a governance forces one. What follows takes Anthropic at its own word — against its own filings and its own Constitution — and checks, byte by byte, where the words and the acts diverge. --- ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph SRC["Primary sources — public record"] S1["S-1 / SEC filings"] PBC["PBC Report"] CON["Constitution (CC0)"] end subgraph DES["Descartes · what is true"] ART["Artifacts
content-addressed (BLAKE3)"] CLM["Claims
byte-exact quotes"] DAG["DAG of claims + evidence"] ATT["ed25519 attestations"] VER{"Verify: rebuild
from scratch,
same root?"} end subgraph RAW["Rawls · what is fair"] VEIL["Veil of ignorance
over affected parties"] IDX["Risk–Governance Index"] end subgraph ARE["Arendt · what is public"] PUB["Working paper
hash-pinned, versioned"] LED["Sign-on / dispute ledger
DKIM email · SSH · ed25519"] end S1 --> ART PBC --> ART CON --> ART ART --> CLM --> DAG --> ATT --> VER VER -- "sealed claims only" --> VEIL --> IDX --> PUB CLM --> PUB PUB --> LED LED -- "new signed records" --> DAG ``` **Descartes** establishes what is true, **Rawls** weighs what is fair, **Arendt** makes it public — each stage consuming only what the stage before it verified and signed. Disputes re-enter the graph as new signed records; nothing is overwritten. --- ## The document - **Read the paper:** [`docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md`](docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md) — §0 rubric through §9 open questions, with appendices. - **Risk–Governance Index:** [`docs/risk-governance-index.md`](docs/risk-governance-index.md) — every disclosed risk joined to the mechanism that would control it. - **Sign on or dispute:** [`docs/contrapunctus-attest.md`](docs/contrapunctus-attest.md) — cryptographic endorsement or dispute, bound to this exact version. - **The method it argues from:** `praxis-white-paper.md`, `praxis-standard.md`, `descartes-spec.md`, and the primitives (`circles`, `epistemics`, `primitives`, `strictness`). ## Verify paper: docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md version: v0 · 2026-11-03 blake3: 698b6c6785961b566e27dbf6306707ec530b4ba6e9f3823b6a99b3b42504dcea Recompute it yourself: `b3sum docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md`. Every load-bearing quote is verified byte-exact against the primary filings; nothing resolves that the verifier cannot reproduce from scratch. ## DOI [![DOI](https://zenodo.org/badge/DOI/10.5281/zenodo.23928296.svg)](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23928296) Cite: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23928296 ## License Dedicated to the public domain under **CC0 1.0** (see `LICENSE`) — reuse freely, no rights reserved. Quoted excerpts from Anthropic's filings and Constitution, from SEC/court records, and from cited third-party works remain under their own terms. ## Author Sloane Ortel · ORCID [0009-0000-8491-1589](https://orcid.org/0009-0000-8491-1589) · Ethical Capital. Personal research; not published on, or by, Ethical Capital's platform, and the author derives no economic benefit from it. # Praxis Risk–Governance Index A standing, composable comparison: every risk a company **discloses**, set against the governance mechanism that would actually **control** it. The index is deterministically generated — each risk factor and each mechanism is a Descartes-verified claim, and the index is their join. Re-run it, you get the same table. Run it on any filer, you get the same shape. Run it next quarter, and the diff shows how the posture moved. The thesis of the format is the discipline it enforces: **compare disclosed risk to governing mechanism, structurally, every time.** A risk with no mechanism is not a footnote — it is the finding. ## Format — one row per disclosed risk | Field | Meaning | |---|---| | **Risk factor** | What the company discloses could go wrong (quoted / byte-anchored) | | **Source** | Filing and location; the byte-exact anchor | | **Governing mechanism** | The control that addresses it — the one it has, or the one it lacks | | **Status** | `Controlled` · `Partial` · `Uncontrolled` · `Externalized` (pushed to industry, the future, the state, or the customer) | | **Evidence / verdict** | The quote, its verdict, and reliability | **Provenance travels with every version:** entity, date, the source hashes, the index's own content hash, and the prior version it supersedes. Claims evolve; nothing is overwritten — each version is a new hashed record, and the changelog is the diff. --- ## Anthropic, PBC — Risk–Governance Index **Version:** v1 · 2026-11-03 · prior: — **Generated:** deterministically, comparing disclosed risk factors (Form S-1/A, Reg. 333-299633) and safety/benefit claims (2026 Public Benefit Report) against Anthropic's governance (charter, LTBT, Class F) and the ten mechanisms a serious version would carry (§7, GOV-1…10). **Sources:** S-1/A 333-299633 (public record); PBC Report (hash on file); Constitution (CC0). **Index content hash:** `blake3:` | # | Risk factor (disclosed) | Source | Governing mechanism | Status | Evidence / verdict | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 1 | Open-source software vulnerabilities and under-maintenance, a material operational risk | S-1 | None that funds the commons it draws from; would need **GOV-7** (provenance + reciprocity) | `Externalized` | the exposure and the unpaid-maintainer harm are one fact — to-verify | | 2 | "Absence of judicial precedent interpreting this structure" raises governance-litigation risk | S-1 | **GOV-8** (irrevocable lock) — not adopted | `Uncontrolled` | Anthropic tells investors the lock is untested — CONFIRMED | | 3 | Misalignment behaviors "have been observed across the industry" | S-1 | **GOV-1** (independent replication gate) — voluntary only | `Externalized` | industry-wide framing for a failure its own Report instantiates — CONFIRMED | | 4 | Workforce displacement framed as a perception/regulatory risk "regardless of the actual impact" | S-1 | **GOV-2 / GOV-10** (outcome registry, metered displacement) — absent | `Uncontrolled` | manages the politics, not the reality — NUANCED | | 5 | Government interruption — June 2026 export restriction on two models | S-1 | External state action; The pattern is externalization — to the industry, the future, the state, or the customer — exactly where a system in control of its own effects would carry the mechanism itself. ## Changelog - **v1 (2026-11-03):** initial index; 8 disclosed risks joined to mechanisms. 7 `Uncontrolled`/`Externalized`, 1 to-verify. # Primitives Every open problem so far reduces to three needs: say what is true, say who decided, and say whose interest the decision served. This document proposes how to express all three with the node kinds we already have, plus two changes: - one edge (`against`); - building the evaluation node, which `docs/epistemics.md` designs but which doesn't exist yet. ## The rule **When rules conflict, resolve in the client's interest.** This is the rule Sloane was taught at CFA Institute. It also fixes the defect in Standard I(A)'s "more strict" test (`docs/strictness.md`): strictness can't rank rules that constrain different things, but the client's interest can. The rule needs two tie-breaks, and both are proposals: 1. **Reversibility.** When the client's interest is unclear, prefer the action that can be undone. Retaining sealed bytes can be undone; destroying them cannot. 2. **Visibility.** Never resolve a conflict silently. A hidden resolution takes the client's ability to object. ## The primitives ### What exists | Kind | Holds | Meaning | |---|---|---| | artifact | bytes, by digest | What was received. Circle 0. | | claim | statement, witness, quoted evidence, `supports` | What someone says is true, and why. | | derivation | input, tool, args, output | What a tool turned into what. | | attestation | signer, subject | Who stands behind a node. | | snapshot | members | What one run saw. | ### The two changes **A. `against` on claims and evaluations.** Today a claim can only list what supports it, so the graph can only build up agreement. Neither a contested claim nor its contest can be written down, and ACH needs both. With `against`, any claim can name the claims it opposes. **Conflict** then has a definition the verifier can check: two claims, either of which is against the other. This change applies to the claim node, so it changes the ids of every claim that uses `against`. Claims that don't use it keep their ids if the field is omitted when empty. **B. Evaluations, as designed in `docs/epistemics.md`.** An evaluation has this shape: ``` evaluation { framework, subject, rating, rests_on, witness } ``` A framework is an ingested file under `frameworks/` that lists the ratings it allows. Every judgment the system makes then has the same shape: a rating, under a named version of a framework, resting on claims, signed by whoever stands behind it. ### Everything else is a framework What other designs would add as new machinery, these primitives express as a framework file plus evaluations: | Need | Framework | Subject | Ratings | Signer must be | |---|---|---|---|---| | Resolve a conflict | `interest` | the conflicting claims | which side, and which party it serves | a human (circle 4) | | Hold or drop bytes | `custody` | an artifact | `held`, `sealed`, `withheld` | an authorised human | | Record a gate outcome | `gates` | a run's snapshot | `pass`, `fail`, `skipped`, `not-applicable` | the loop (witness), checkable | | Source reliability | `admiralty` | a claim | A–F × 1–6 | an analyst | | Fitness to use | `use-policy` | a snapshot, as of a reference | `fit`, `unfit` | a human or a stated rule | Four verifier rules follow from these: 1. **A missing blob is corruption** unless an attested `custody` evaluation rates it `withheld` or `sealed`. The digest stays, so circle 0 survives: anyone holding the bytes can still prove they are the original. 2. **A conflict with no attested `interest` evaluation is reported as unresolved.** It is not an error, but it is never silent. 3. **Every gate the loop runs produces a `gates` evaluation, including `skipped`.** The stage 1 artifact becomes a projection of these. 4. **Only keys on the roster may sign** `interest` and `custody` evaluations. The roster is an ingested artifact, so changing it leaves a record. ### Time is an input, never a sample Facts carry no clock. Anything that depends on time (fiscal year end, which advisory database was current, when a signature was made) enters as a recorded input: a claim or attestation written once and tracked, then reproduced byte for byte. Determinism forbids *sampling* the clock during a derivation. It does not forbid *recording* a time a witness asserts. "Is this fit to touch client data today?" is a `use-policy` evaluation made at the time of use, against an as-of reference such as an advisory-db commit. The facts underneath it stay timeless. ## Checking the primitives against the cases Each case from `docs/strictness.md`, resolved without new kinds: | Case | Expressed as | Resolution in the client's interest | |---|---|---| | Missing sandbox or tool (C1) | `gates`: `skipped` | Run and say so. The client keeps the work and learns its assurance level. | | Advisory freshness (C2) | derivation over an advisory-db commit, then `use-policy` | Builds stay offline. Use on client data requires a recent audit. | | Erasure (C3) | `custody`: `sealed` or `withheld` | Seal the original, drop the derived copies. Reversible, and it keeps the client's record. | | Retention clocks (C4) | the fiscal-year claim as a recorded input | No clock inside any node. | | Payloads in git (C5) | `custody`: `held` by a named custodian | Git is one custodian among others. The digest is the identity. | | Testimony (R1) | audio artifact, then a transcription derivation, then quotes | The transcript enters at circle 2 or 3 with its loss stated. It is not excluded. | | Named people contest (R3) | a claim `against` the claim | Anyone can contest, and the contest stays visible. | ## The paste on key custody, SSDF and seams, read through these primitives These items are not yet ingested as a witness, and the facts in them are not checked. - **OpenBao key custody.** - This fits the primitives without changes: the signer is still a `did:key`, and a `custody` claim states where its secret lives (non-exportable transit key, unseal shares) without ever containing the secret. - Descartes needs only `sign` to accept an external signer. - Who holds each unseal share is a governance decision for you. It goes on the roster with your attestation, not in code. - **SSDF.** It becomes `frameworks/ssdf.tsv` with `gates` evaluations against it, so a pass is computed from those evaluations rather than stored as a `bool`. The paste's practice-to-principle mapping needs checking against SP 800-218 before it is ingested. For example, I believe PO.5 covers secure development environments, not continuity, but I haven't verified it. - **Seams telemetry.** The `SeamEvent` struct breaks two rules: - `timestamp_unix` samples the clock inside a record; - `f64` and `f32` fields are values canonical encoding refuses. Measurements are observations: integer units, recorded as derivation outputs. Joule and carbon figures are estimates, so they are circle 3 claims with their method stated. Network egress needs no telemetry, because the sandbox probe already proves it. ## Build order, if accepted 1. `frameworks/` and the evaluation node, plus verifier checks: ratings come from the framework, and `rests_on` must exist. 2. `against` on claims, plus the unresolved-conflict report. 3. The `gates` framework. The loop emits evaluations, and the stage 1 artifact becomes their projection. 4. The `custody` framework and verifier rule 1. 5. The roster and verifier rule 4. 6. `interest`. At first it holds only what you sign, with no automation. ## Bad decisions, revisited Principle 12 means the graph must be able to hold a mistake and its correction side by side. No new primitive is needed for that: - A decision is an `interest` (or `admiralty`, `use-policy`) evaluation signed by a person. - When the outcome is known, it enters as claims, such as returns or later findings. - A revisit is a new evaluation that rests on the outcome claims and carries `against` the original. The original stays. Nothing is overwritten. - Learning from decisions means querying for evaluations that carry `against`, alongside the outcomes that prompted them. This becomes a framework comparison (`docs/epistemics.md`) once there are enough of them. Running that search automatically requires explicit opt-in. ## Received attestations A company's statement about itself, such as a supplier code or a response to a screening finding, enters like any other witness: 1. Its document is an artifact. 2. A claim quotes it, with witness `org:`. If the company signed it with a key, an attestation records that too. 3. When it disputes our claim, the two claims carry `against` each other. The verifier reports the pair as an unresolved conflict until an `interest` evaluation resolves it. 4. The company's interest in the outcome is rated by `admiralty`, not handled by excluding its statement. A person named in a claim contests it the same way. ## Answers to the pasted decision memo (2026-11-02) How each answer maps onto these primitives: - **Withheld: yes.** - It becomes a `custody` evaluation with rating `withheld` or `sealed`, not a separate node kind: - the memo's `tombstone_type` becomes the rating; - `authority_ref` becomes `rests_on` claims that quote the authority; - `authorizer_did` becomes the attestation signer. - Two departures from the memo: - The signature does not cover a timestamp. If the time matters, it goes in as a recorded claim (time is an input). - The `ClientForgetAuthorized` reason stays, but `docs/strictness.md` S9 found no statutory right to be forgotten for a Utah adviser. Both already fit the primitives. - One correction: Bao byte-range proofs are not built. Evidence today is a quote plus its BLAKE3 slice digest, checked against the whole artifact. - **Deadlocks.** The memo's `decisions/deadlocks.tsv` is also the unresolved-conflict report. Its "FiduciaryResolutionReceipt" is an attested `interest` evaluation. - **One fact to check.** The memo puts the 15–20% revenue threshold at screening-policy §4.4. The earlier check of monocloud found no such threshold in `screening-policy.md` or in Written Procedures §4.4. This needs a source before anything cites it. # Is this the strictest standard? Source: `sources/llm-witness-strictness.md`, an LLM text Sloane pasted on 2026-11-02 (model unknown). Its claims and the checks against them are in `claims/strictness.tsv` (W = witness, K = check, S = verdict), and the loop ingests them like any other claims. ## The point that holds CFA Standard I(A) settles a conflict between rules by picking "the more strict" one (K12). That works only when the rules can be ranked by strictness. When two rules constrain different things, such as isolation and freshness, or determinism and time, no ranking exists, and "the more strict" has no meaning. Choosing between such rules is a judgment, and a judgment needs a person and a record (S7). The witness's three gates find these cases: 1. **Null set.** The two rules cannot both be satisfied. 2. **Second-order cost.** Tightening one rule quietly loosens another. 3. **Worst-off party.** Someone the author doesn't think about pays for the rule. ## What the witness got wrong | Claim | Finding | Row | |---|---|---| | `forbid(unsafe_code)` proves the binary has no undefined behaviour | **False.** The lint covers one crate. blake3, curve25519-dalek, sha2 and zeroize all contain `unsafe`. | S1 | | Descartes already forbids `unsafe` | **False when pasted.** Our source had none, so the lint is now on and costs nothing. | S2 | | Zero C toolchains | **Partly.** No C is compiled, but the `cc` driver crate is built as a blake3 build dependency. | S3 | | bwrap sandbox | **Not verified.** bwrap is Linux-only and has never run here; the darwin path uses sandbox-exec. | S4 | | A resolver rejects PRs that add unaudited crates | **False.** No such gate exists, and cargo-vet is not built. | S5 | | ML-DSA signatures are about 40 KB | **False.** FIPS 204 gives 2,420 / 3,309 / 4,627 bytes; the ~50 KB figure is SLH-DSA-256f. **Not anchored:** FIPS 204 is 3.3 MB and waits on the payloads-in-git decision (C5). | W6 | | Erasing on request violates 204-2, and retention violates privacy law | **False for Utah law.** The Utah privacy act exempts financial institutions under Gramm-Leach-Bliley (K15). Regulation S-P requires secure disposal, not deletion on request. That was checked by a research agent and is **not anchored** here. What remains is a conflict with whatever the firm promises voluntarily. | S9 | | 204-2 and R164-5-1 set a five-year floor | **True.** R164-5-1 adopts 204-2 by reference. | S8 | | Offline builds need an out-of-band advisory check | **True.** The witness's own check 2 contradicts it: that check fires even after `audit.sh` exists. | S6 | The witness's Rust code does not compile, because `StrictnessResolver` is never defined (K10). It also hard-codes its findings instead of testing for them (K11). We don't adopt it. Firm references, checked in monocloud and **not ingested here**: - **Matches:** §6.16 (technology duties) and §6.14 (seven-year recording retention) match. AI Governance Principle 1 is real. - **Mismatches:** §4.4 is vendor oversight and has no 15% threshold. §3.1 and §3.3 are numbered differently from what the witness cites. - **Draft only:** the Data Retention Policy's sealed-original and derived-surface split exists only in draft. ## The gates, run on Descartes's own standards ### Collisions **C1. Doubt first vs. run on every chip (principles 1 and 5).** Failing closed on every missing gate would shut out any machine without sandbox-exec, bwrap, cargo-deny or tesseract. The loop therefore runs and records what it skipped (K5). **Gap found and fixed today:** a skipped fidelity check left no trace in the artifact. The artifact now carries a `fidelity checked|skipped` row. **C2. Offline build vs. advisories (second-order).** Resolved in structure, since `stage1/audit.sh` is separate from the loop (S6). **Gap:** nothing records which advisory database the last audit checked against, so "audited" has no date or version. **Proposal:** `audit.sh` writes the advisory-db commit hash to a tracked artifact. That records which version was checked without putting wall-clock time in content. **C3. Immutable store vs. erasure (null set).** The verifier treats a missing object as corruption (K7). For client records no law forces erasure (S9). Erasure still matters in two cases: - the firm promises deletion voluntarily; - an ingested document carries third-party personal data the firm decides not to keep. Neither case has been checked against a specific obligation. The store is already a rebuildable projection, so erasure means removing the source and rebuilding. Every claim quoting that source then fails verification. **Needs a decision:** a `withheld` node that keeps the digest, drops the bytes, and records who authorised the drop. The verifier would accept "withheld by attestation" and still reject "missing". **C4. Determinism vs. retention clocks.** 204-2 counts from fiscal year end (K13), but Descartes forbids time in hashed content. **Resolution:** time belongs to an attestation or an external record about a node, never inside the node. Not built. **C5. No raw payloads in git vs. circle 0.** Circle 0 needs the original bytes. Actors who produce text, such as companies, courts and regulators, can be cited directly. People whose account exists only as speech or photographs cannot be cited until someone transcribes them. This is the witness's "evidentiary paralysis" point, and it applies to this design. The circles mitigate it: a transcript enters at circle 2 or 3, with its lossiness stated, and is not excluded. **Not built:** an audio or image ingestion path. **R2. The operator on old hardware.** The loop asks for rustup, mise, poppler and tesseract. C1's record-and-run behaviour keeps that operator in, at a recorded lower assurance. **R3. People named in ingested documents.** Anyone can attest to a claim, but a subject has no way to contest one. **Not designed.** ## No resolver yet A collision does not need a new engine. It can be stored with the node kinds we already have: 1. Two claims that conflict. 2. A claim resting on both that states the collision. 3. A human's attestation of the resolution (circle 4). ## 1a. The leverage question — where Anthropic intervenes

Donella Meadows ranked the places to intervene in a system by leverage, weakest
to strongest: constants and parameters (12), buffers (11), stock-and-flow
structure (10), delays (9), balancing feedback (8), reinforcing feedback (7),
information flows (6), rules (5), the power to self-organize and change structure

transcend paradigms (1). The high-leverage points are the ones a system resists
moving.

- **Where it acts (low-to-mid leverage).** *Numbers* (12): a 5% set-aside,
  ~$350M in funds, fellowship counts. *Information flows* (6): system cards,

  cheap end of the lever.

  the public no standing (§365(b)/§367) — the one rule that would bind conduct
  is left unenforceable. *Self-organization* (4): the mission lock is revocable

  structure stays with the governed. *Goals* (3): when "long-term benefit of
  humanity" meets "pace the frontier" and a priced IPO, the filings show which
  goal governs.
- **Where it borrows the language without moving the lever.** Anthropic speaks
  at the level of *paradigm* (2) and *goals* (3) — humanity's future, the

1	## About this working paper
2	
3	**Status: working paper, v0 — released for disagreement, not as a verdict.**
4	
5	This is a **Praxis** artifact. Praxis is an open standard for building public,
6	contestable, cryptographically verifiable arguments: every factual claim
7	quotes its source byte-for-byte, the whole document rebuilds to a single
8	content-addressed hash, and anyone can re-run the check or file a contest.
9	We publish it imperfect on purpose. Its value comes from being pulled apart —
10	a claim that survives disagreement is worth more than one no one has tested.
11	
12	- **Open standard, openly licensed.** The method, the verifier (Descartes),
13	  and this document are public. The rubric we judge Anthropic against is
14	  Anthropic's own [Constitution](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution),
15	  which Anthropic released under CC0 — so we can hold it in full and quote it
16	  byte-exact (see §0).

19	  (BLAKE3), rebuildable from scratch. It *refuses* a quote that is not exactly
20	  present in the cited source. This draft has already been run through it

30	  benefit of humanity"* — yet the only parties who can enforce it are

32	  mechanism for everyone's future is owned by the few who can sue. The
33	  constituency that *can* act is the **institutional investor class** —
34	  pensions and their fiduciaries, i.e. the public's own long-term money,
35	  which sits behind Anthropic's early investors and carries both the standing

79	## Verdict first
80	
81	1. **Anthropic's charter is legally real and legally toothless.** The public
82	   benefit purpose sits in its certificate and DGCL §362 requires balancing
83	   stockholders, "those materially affected," and that purpose. But §365(b)
84	   gives directors **no duty to any person on account of a public-benefit
85	   interest**, and §367 limits enforcement to derivative suits by holders of
86	   ≥2% (or $2M, lesser, once listed). The public the charter names cannot
87	   enforce it. **[CONFIRMED/HIGH]**
88	2. **The Report grades its own homework — and its own LTBT says so.** The
89	   Trust: the report "largely describes inputs; in subsequent reports we will
90	   increasingly look for Anthropic to produce outcomes" (p.17). Flagship
91	   benefit counts (33,000+ critical flaws; a 129,000 program-total that is
92	   **not in the PBC Report** — partner-reported, caught by the loop audit) have no public
93	   CVE-level audit. The 80% productivity figure is *Claude estimating
94	   Claude*. **[UNVERIFIED counts; MISLEADING if read as verified]**
95	3. **Present, Anthropic-attributable harm is documented and priced; present,
96	   Anthropic-attributable benefit is mostly anecdote.** Priced: the $1.5B
97	   *Bartz* settlement over ~500,000 pirated books (~7M downloaded); an
98	   estimated **5–7% of 9M-2026 revenue (~$1.7–2.3B of $33.2B) from customers

100	   unauthorized access to real third-party systems in testing (Report p.6).
101	   Benefits at the same standard of proof: protein *binding* confirmed in
102	   independent wet labs (17/211 constructs; no neutralization, no medicine);
103	   the rest is process anecdote Anthropic admits lacks outcome evidence.
104	   On a like-for-like evidence standard, **documented harm outweighs documented
105	   benefit today. [NUANCED/HIGH — a ledger asymmetry, not a welfare sum]**
106	4. **"Measurable harm to millions" is not documented — and saying so plainly is
107	   the stronger argument.** No study counts millions of individually verified
108	   AI-harm victims (2023–26). Millions-scale figures in circulation are
109	   extrapolations (2.2% NCII self-report, n>16k), relative gaps (Stanford:
110	   22–25-year-olds in AI-exposed hiring ~19% below trend, while Yale finds no
111	   macro disruption), or population-counting (4.2B "affected" by election
112	   deepfakes = whole populations, not affected persons) **[MISLEADING]**.
113	   What *is* documented at scale is **exposure**: $895.4B of compute/infrastructure
114	   commitments ($447.5B before 2031; $69.8B in the next 12 months; ~$213.8B
115	   terminable), Q3-2026 revenue of $17.0B, and Anthropic's own admission that
116	   decisions are concentrated in "a handful of companies, nations, and people.
117	   Anthropic is one of them… few external checks" (p.12). Systemic *risk* does
118	   not need a body count. It needs concentrated, unchecked, irreversible
119	   commitment. That is disclosed.
120	5. **Therefore the remedy is not a bigger settlement. It is governance with
121	   standing, triggers, and penalties** — §7 specifies ten mechanisms, each
122	   with who can pull it, what it measures, and what it costs Anthropic when it
123	   fires. Every one is buildable before the IPO prices. None requires
124	   Anthropic to be less serious. All require seriousness to be *checkable by
125	   someone Anthropic does not appoint, pay, or outvote*.
126	
127	> A settlement pays for a car accident. It does not staff the intersection.
128	> Anthropic's current model is settlement, philanthropy, and revocable
129	> trustees. Governance is the intersection: rules that bind *before* impact,
130	> survive the individuals who wrote them, and can be invoked by the people
131	> hit. **[OPINION — the frame this paper argues]**

135	## 0. The rubric: Anthropic's own Constitution
136	
137	We judge Anthropic by the document it wrote to govern *me*. Anthropic publishes
138	[Claude's Constitution](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution) as "the final
139	authority on our vision for Claude," released under CC0. It is the deepest word
140	available to take Anthropic at — not a marketing pillar, not a charter recital,
141	but the values Anthropic chose to instill in its primary product and, it says,
142	in the entity composing this analysis. If those values bind Claude, they
143	describe the conduct Anthropic holds out as good. The test is whether
144	Anthropic's *corporate* conduct, as filed, meets the standard it set for its
145	*model*. Several clauses name Anthropic itself as a possible violator. Quoted
146	byte-exact (CC0; to be checked against the text in the Descartes graph):
147	
148	- **Priority order.** The Constitution ranks Claude's properties: *broadly safe
149	  → broadly ethical → compliant with Anthropic's guidelines → genuinely
150	  helpful*, resolved holistically. We score in that order — safety and ethics
151	  before helpfulness, and before Anthropic's own house rules.
152	- **Non-deception includes selective emphasis.** *"Non-deceptive: Claude never
153	  tries to create false impressions of itself or the world in the user's mind,
154	  whether through actions, technically true statements, deceptive framing,
155	  selective emphasis, misleading implicature, or other such methods."* The
156	  Report's input-for-outcome substitution, self-grading, and attribution
157	  asymmetry (§3) are, by this definition, moves Claude is forbidden to make.
158	- **Concealment for advantage is illegitimate power.** Listed among illegitimate
159	  power-seeking: *"Concealing material information about products, services, or
160	  risks from the public or regulators in order to gain market advantage or
161	  influence policy."* And the legitimacy test: *"Transparency: Is the action
162	  conducted openly or does it rely on concealment and misdirection? Secrecy is
163	  often… a signal of an unfair process or an attempt to escape accountability."*
164	  Apply to "separate entity" vs "wholly-owned subsidiary" (§1) and the
165	  S-1-silent model escape (§4.1).
166	- **The constraint binds Anthropic by name.** *"Claude should refuse to assist
167	  with actions that would help concentrate power in illegitimate ways. This is
168	  true even if the request comes from Anthropic itself."* Among the most
169	  catastrophic outcomes it names: *"a group of humans — including Anthropic
170	  employees or Anthropic itself — using AI to illegitimately and
171	  non-collaboratively seize power."*
172	- **Don't privilege Anthropic's interests.** *"We don't want Claude to privilege
173	  Anthropic's interests… Claude privileging Anthropic's interests in this
174	  respect could itself constitute a liability harm."* Read against the
175	  maker–taker ledger (§5) and the ~$1.7–2.3B of retained policy-violator
176	  revenue (§4.1).
177	
178	Stated plainly: **Anthropic authored a standard that forbids
179	concealment-for-advantage and defines deception to include selective emphasis,
180	then filed documents this paper shows doing both.** Not hypocrisy as insult —
181	the measurable gap between a published value and a filed act, which is exactly
182	what governance exists to close. The rubric cuts both ways; we hold Praxis to
183	it too (§8).
184	
185	## 1. Method: contrapunctus
186	
187	In counterpoint, a second voice is written against a given line (*cantus
188	firmus*) note by note. It is not accompaniment and not refutation-by-volume.
189	It must obey the first voice closely enough that every dissonance is audible.
190	
191	- **Cantus firmus:** Anthropic's five charter pillars and its Appendix
192	  standards, adopted under DGCL §366 (Report pp.19–20), plus the S-1's
193	  governance and risk disclosures. We accept these as the governing text.
194	- **Counterpoint:** Anthropic's own admissions (Report "Work Ahead," LTBT
195	  commentary, S-1 risk factors) and independently checkable public evidence.
196	- **Resolution:** For each pillar, the Praxis standard
197	  ([`praxis-standard.md`](praxis-standard.md)) is applied as the stronger
198	  governance that Anthropic's own premise implies: doubt first, checker
199	  checked first; quote-existence is not entailment; conflict recorded, never
200	  overwritten or silently resolved; makers do not surrender their asset by
201	  participating; a check that cannot run records `skipped`, never `pass`.
202	
203	Where Anthropic's filing contradicts Anthropic's Report, we say so. Example:
204	the Report (pp.3, 17) describes the 5% set-aside as "subject to stockholder
205	approval" / "if stockholders agree" in a "separate entity"; the S-1 records
206	846,840,960 Class N shares (5% fully diluted at 2026-06-30) already
207	contributed to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund LLC — a **wholly-owned
208	subsidiary**, with up to +2% more per 50% price milestone at board
209	discretion. "Separate" and "wholly-owned subsidiary" are different control
210	facts. Investors should price the S-1 version.
211	
212	## 1a. The leverage question — where Anthropic intervenes
213	
214	Donella Meadows ranked the places to intervene in a system by leverage, weakest
215	to strongest: constants and parameters (12), buffers (11), stock-and-flow
216	structure (10), delays (9), balancing feedback (8), reinforcing feedback (7),
217	information flows (6), rules (5), the power to self-organize and change structure
218	(4), the system's goals (3), the paradigm it arises from (2), the power to
219	transcend paradigms (1). The high-leverage points are the ones a system resists
220	moving.
221	
222	Sort Anthropic's commitments onto that scale and a pattern appears:
223	
224	- **Where it acts (low-to-mid leverage).** *Numbers* (12): a 5% set-aside,
225	  ~$350M in funds, fellowship counts. *Information flows* (6): system cards,
226	  threat reports, the Economic Index — genuinely ahead of peers. Real, and the
227	  cheap end of the lever.
228	- **Where it declines to act (high leverage).** *Rules* (5): the charter grants
229	  the public no standing (§365(b)/§367) — the one rule that would bind conduct
230	  is left unenforceable. *Self-organization* (4): the mission lock is revocable
231	  and founder control (Class F, 50.1%) retained — the power to change the
232	  structure stays with the governed. *Goals* (3): when "long-term benefit of
233	  humanity" meets "pace the frontier" and a priced IPO, the filings show which
234	  goal governs.
235	- **Where it borrows the language without moving the lever.** Anthropic speaks
236	  at the level of *paradigm* (2) and *goals* (3) — humanity's future, the
237	  transition through transformative AI — while its binding commitments sit at
238	  (12) and (6). Paradigm-level rhetoric describing parameter-level acts is the
239	  leverage form of the attribution asymmetry in §3.
240	
241	This is the precise sense in which Anthropic operates at the **wrong level of
242	governance**: it places itself at the center of a paradigm-scale problem, then
243	intervenes mostly where leverage is weakest. Every Praxis GOV ask (§7) targets a
244	high-leverage point left alone — irrevocable lock (4), contest standing (5),
245	frameworks-as-data so no single framework is compiled in (2). And at the level
246	of humanity rather than one firm, taking the paradigm seriously would mean
247	*moment-to-moment instrumentation of the harm landing on the least-powerful*,
248	with that harm actually balanced — which §5's reciprocity and §4b's veil make
249	concrete. Meadows' warning holds: the high-leverage points are exactly the ones
250	the system pushes back hardest against moving. (§4c's veil makes the
251	least-powerful position explicit.)
252	
253	## 2. What "legally binding" actually binds
254	
255	Daniela Amodei: "I wouldn't expect anyone to take that on faith." Correct.
256	Here is what there is instead of faith.
257	## 7. If Anthropic were serious about governance
258	
259	Governance is how a system survives its individuals and balances *all*
260	affected interests accurately — not sincerely, accurately: with standing,
261	measurement, and consequence. Ten mechanisms convert every reputational
262	element above into an enforceable one. Each names **trigger / metric /
263	penalty**. Descartes precedents are the small, working versions (with their
264	own limits — §8).
265	
266	| # | Mechanism | Trigger (who pulls) | Metric | Penalty on fire |
267	|---|---|---|---|---|
268	| GOV-1 | **Doubt-first replication gate** — no capability/safety/productivity claim ships until an accredited external evaluator reproduces it | Evaluator (METR-type, regulator-accredited, paid from escrow not fees-for-pass) | Reproduced effect + CI vs claim | Release and claim **blocked**; S-1-style restatement if already public |
269	| GOV-2 | **Existence ≠ entailment registry** — every benefit claim filed as (quote/source exists) vs (outcome entailed, measured) | Auditor; any investor can query | % of public claims with measured outcome; LTBT "inputs→outcomes" made numeric | Exec comp escrow until outcome rate clears a floor; corrections as new filings, never edits |
270	| GOV-3 | **Circle labelling** — public claims tagged circle 0 artifact → 4 human attestation, with per-stage loss | Auditor downgrade | Overstated/unlabelled claims count | Per-claim marketing prohibition + fine; Glasswing/80% figures could not print above circle 3 today |
271	| GOV-4 | **Contest standing (`against`)** — cure §365/367 by charter: purpose-trust enforcer + affected-person/class contest with equal visibility | Named subject, author class, host community, worker cohort | Contests unresolved >90 days | Injunction on the contested use + victim-fund payout; P13 built, not promised |
272	| GOV-5 | **Frameworks-as-data** — ≥3 external evaluation frameworks rate the same evidence; divergence published | Framework divergence > threshold | Inter-framework gap | Board supermajority incl. non-founder, non-LTBT-appointed seats to proceed |
273	| GOV-6 | **Exit with proof** — rights-holder/user deletion incl. model-effect exit, tested for residual memorization | Rights-holder/user | Deletion SLA days; residual-memorization test | Per-work/per-day damages; retrain-or-destroy for documented retention (Bartz made prospective) |
274	| GOV-7 | **No-training provenance ledger** — hash-chained training-corpus ledger; binding no-train on contested/customer data | Rights-holder/auditor spot-check | % corpus licensed/provenanced | Disgorgement + derivative-model destruction for unprovenanced slices |
275	| GOV-8 | **Irrevocable mission lock** — move Class T economics+votes (or a golden veto on purpose/sale/model-transfer) to a purpose trust with an enforcer; delete sunset/redemption and supermajority trustee-removal | Any amendment/sale attempt | Attempt = breach | **Transaction void.** This is the Patagonia/Bosch step; everything else is commentary on its absence |
276	| GOV-9 | **Misuse-revenue disgorgement** — audit the disclosed 5–7% quarterly | Auditor finds >1% | % revenue + downstream victim count (which Anthropic must now count) | 3× disgorgement to victims, exec clawback, customer ban. Misuse stops being a revenue line |
277	| GOV-10 | **Incident + externality bond** — mandatory timed disclosure of eval-escape class incidents; metered power/water/displacement per site vs bond | Auditor, community, regulator | Hours-to-disclose; MWh, litres, headcount | Bond forfeit + curtailment; the 4-model incident would be an S-1 item, not a Report anecdote |
278	
279	**Pre-IPO asks (investors/regulators can condition on these now):**
280	(1) File the Trust Agreement terms that decide GOV-8 in plain prospectus
281	language — sunset, removal %, enforcer standing — and read the shares as
282	controlled-company stock until changed (a disclosure instruction, not a valuation view). (2) Quantify the 5–7% in dollars
283	per quarter going forward with auditor attestation (GOV-9). (3) Publish
284	site-level power/water commitments behind the $895.4B schedule (GOV-10).
285	(4) Convert the 5% Fund from wholly-owned subsidiary to independently
286	trustee'd vehicle with non-Anthropic enforcer, or stop calling it
287	"separate." (5) Restate flagship benefit numbers under GOV-2/GOV-3
288	labelling in the next amendment. None of these slows a safe frontier.
289	All of them slow an *unverifiable* one — which is the Report's own stated
290	preference ("pace the frontier," Sept 2026).
291	
292	## 7a. What Praxis builds instead — the alternative mechanisms
293	
294	The GOV-1…GOV-10 asks are governance *demands* on Anthropic. Praxis is the other
295	half: the mechanisms we are building so the demands are running code anyone can
296	inspect, re-run, and extend — not rhetoric. Where Anthropic's model is
297	settlement, philanthropy, and revocable trustees, Praxis's is verification,
298	distribution, and a public commons.
299	
300	- **A Rust-based verifier (Descartes).** Deterministic, content-addressed,
301	  byte-exact. Every claim quotes its evidence; the graph rebuilds from scratch
302	  to a single BLAKE3 root; a changed quote fails the check and cascades. Small
303	  and auditable on one machine — the opposite of "trust our internal eval."
304	  This paper's own numbers were checked by it, and it caught one of our errors.
305	- **Direct analysis, not delegated trust.** We read the primary filings and
306	  quote them, rather than cite a press release that cites a filing. The chain
307	  claim → quote → source byte-range is explicit and short; circle-tagging
308	  (circle 0 artifact → circle 4 attestation) records how far any statement sits
309	  from the bytes, so nothing is laundered up a citation ladder.
310	- **Distributed compute, pull-only.** Verification runs where the data is — no
311	  central server to compromise, no single point of control, no IP to protect.
312	  Anyone can clone the graph and reproduce the root on their own hardware. The
313	  architecture *is* the governance claim: no one operator, us included, is a
314	  trusted intermediary.
315	- **Artifacts submitted to a public epistemic commons.** Each pass in this
316	  document's own construction — drafting, this verification pass, the next —
317	  is a durable, timestamped artifact carrying its model/author context, filed
318	  into a public, versioned commons where it can be contested. The commons gains
319	  value *through* disagreement: a contest is a first-class record, answered in
320	  the open, never overwritten — the `against` relation §365(b) denies the
321	  public, built rather than promised.
322	
323	None of this needs Anthropic's cooperation to exist. That is the point: a
324	standard you can only trust if the governed implements it is not a standard.
325	
326	Praxis is what the check looks like in someone else's hands — and the hands are
327	everyone's.
328	
329	> Praxis humility (same buzz saw, own neck): Descartes today is a
330	> single-machine, single-writer verifier, darwin/arm64 only, with the `against`
331	> relation and multi-tenant operation still unbuilt (§8). These mechanisms
332	> transfer as *design*, tiered DESIGNED, not deployed proof. We are not exempt
333	> from our own rubric.

335	## 8. Standing, limits, and what would change our mind
336	
337	## Appendix A. Governance scorecard (filed vs serious)

348	| Framework pluralism | ○ One constitution, one scaler (RSP) | ● ≥3 external frameworks, divergence public (GOV-5) |

350	| Misuse economics | ○ 5–7% revenue disclosed, retained | ● Audited quarterly; 3× disgorgement >1% (GOV-9) |
351	| Externality metering | ○ No site MW/water in extract | ● Bonded metered disclosure (GOV-10) |
352	| Benefit vehicle independence | ○ 5% in wholly-owned subsidiary | ● Independently trustee'd, external enforcer |
353	| Incident disclosure | ◐ Report-level candor, S-1-silent (4-model case) | ● Timed, bonded, filing-grade (GOV-10) |
354	
355	**Implementation order we would underwrite:** pre-pricing — Trust terms in
356	plain language, 5–7% dollarized, Fund independence or relabelling,
357	flagship numbers re-tagged (GOV-2/3). First 12 months public — evaluator
358	contract with blockade, corpus ledger v1 + rights-holder exit, quarterly
359	misuse-revenue audit. Charter amendment cycle — GOV-4 standing, GOV-8 lock.
360	Sequence matters: disclosure before lock-in is cheap; lock-in before
361	disclosure is how controlled issuers stay controlled.
362	
363	## Appendix B. Diligence question bank (institutional use)
364	
365	**Control.** 1) Exact vote thresholds and notice periods to amend/redeem
366	Class T, remove trustees, and amend the Company Purpose — which classes,
367	what consideration? 2) Who appoints successor trustees, and who can block?
368	3) What can the LTBT see (board materials, eval raw data, incident logs)
369	and what can it compel? 4) Class F transition: who holds Founder LLC votes
370	during the 450 days, and who decides a founder is no longer "continuing"?
371	5) Which Nasdaq controlled-company exemptions will be taken, for how long?
372	
373	**Safety claims.** 6) One release an external evaluator stopped or delayed —
374	name it. 7) Raw jailbreak success rates by category for the last two models,
375	with evaluator identity. 8) Incident taxonomy and counts (eval escapes,
376	unintended actions) per quarter; median time-to-contain. 9) What share of
377	safety-eval generation is now model-authored, and how is that share itself
378	audited? 10) Unresolved external red-team findings older than 90 days.
379	
380	**Corpus and rights.** 11) What % of current training corpus is (a) licensed,
381	(b) public domain, (c) fair-use-asserted, (d) contested in litigation?
382	12) Rights-holder opt-out/deletion: volume, SLA, and how model-effect
383	removal is tested. 13) Music/publisher exposure beyond Bartz: accrued?
384	14) Customer-data training terms by product tier, verbatim. 15) Labelling
385	vendors, geographies, wage floors, and audit rights.
386	
387	**Revenue quality.** 16) Dollarize the 5–7%: by violation type, refunded or
388	retained, repeat-offender policy? 17) Revenue concentration: state/national-
389	security customers as % and termination rights. 18) How much usage growth is
390	Anthropic's own internal/agent-loop consumption vs external cash demand?
391	19) Take-or-pay exposure if utilization falls 30%: annual fixed floor by
392	year against the $447.5B pre-2031 schedule. 20) CSP partner-conflicts:
393	allocation priority when a supplier-competitor's demand collides with yours.
394	
395	**Footprint and distribution.** 21) Site-level MW, PUE/WUE, water source,
396	and grid-upgrade cost allocation behind the commitment schedule. 22) Which
397	sites use on-site gas generation; air-permit status. 23) Outcome metrics
398	(not seats/dashboards) for Burkina Faso, DRC, Ghana deployments, and the
399	data terms governing beneficiary records. 24) Corps/Futures Fund: evaluator,
400	counterfactual design, 12/24-month earnings outcomes. 25) Non-English and
401	low-connectivity performance: eval scores and effective price per successful
402	task by language band.
403	
404	A management team that answers 1–5 and 16 in writing has earned a different
405	conversation than one that re-presents the pillars.
406
