1. **GDELT phrase timelines.**
   - Sources: the GDELT TV 2.0 API (https://api.gdeltproject.org/api/v2/tv/tv, mode=timelinevol, and the TV GKG described at https://blog.gdeltproject.org/announcing-the-american-television-global-knowledge-graph-tv-gkg/) and the GDELT DOC 2.0 API for online news (https://api.gdeltproject.org/api/v2/doc/doc, mode=timelinevol / timelinevolraw).
   - Queries:
     - "health of democracy" as an exact phrase;
     - Anthropic and the phrase together (and Claude together with democracy, if the query syntax allows proximity or co-occurrence; document what it does);
     - a control set: "democracy" alone and "Anthropic" alone.
   - Use the longest timespan each API allows; record the actual coverage.
   - Raw volume is not comparable over time, so prefer the normalized share where the API gives it (percent of monitored airtime or articles) and keep raw counts beside it.
   - Save every raw API response verbatim into a gitignored `.democorpus/`, and record request URL, response SHA-256 and BLAKE3, and as-of in `corpus/democracy/MANIFEST.tsv`. API responses are not reproducible later, so the saved bytes are the pin.
   - Write `corpus/democracy/gdelt-timelines.tsv` (source, query, date, value, unit).
   - Respect GDELT rate limits (sleep between calls; send a descriptive User-Agent).
2. **Rooney Institute Health of Democracy Survey** (https://rooneyinstitute.nd.edu/research/health-of-democracy-survey/rooney-reports/).
   - List every report and its PDF; pin the PDFs as above in `.democorpus/`.
   - Extract topline series that recur across waves (e.g. satisfaction with democracy, trust in institutions, views of tech companies or AI if asked) into `corpus/democracy/rooney-toplines.tsv`. Each row needs the report, wave/year, question wording verbatim, response option, percent, and the page number.
   - Hand-transcribe only numbers you can see in the PDF text, with page anchors. If a figure is only in an image, record it as not extracted.
   - Note whether microdata is available and on what terms.
3. **Feasibility notes only (no build):**
   - The Trust Project (https://thetrustproject.org): what it is (a news-credibility standard and set of trust indicators, not a survey of trust levels, if that is what you find) and whether it yields any time series.
   - The BCG Trust Index (https://www.bcg.com/publications/2022/trust-index-analyzing-companies-trustworthiness): its method (dimensions, data sources, scoring) as BCG describes it; whether it was updated after 2022; and concretely how the method could be extended to Anthropic and peers (OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, Meta) with this repo's tools: the two NLI witnesses, the earnings-call and Hacker News corpora, and GDELT. Include which parts need proprietary data.
   - Other free proxies worth considering, such as V-Dem, Freedom House, the Pew trust series, the Gallup confidence-in-institutions series and the Edelman Trust Barometer. For each give the license, the cadence and whether it covers AI or tech.

Deliverables: `scripts/democracy_proxies.py` (subcommands per source: pin/fetch/build/verify as fits), `corpus/democracy/` (MANIFEST.tsv, the TSVs, README.md with attribution and terms per source), and `docs/democracy-proxies.md` (method, what each proxy measures, what none of them answers, and the feasibility notes). Check determinism: two builds from the saved bytes must be byte-identical.

Constraints: no LLM-generated labels or numbers; every number traces to saved source bytes. Do not edit docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md, index.html, README.md, frameworks/, sources/, enrich_*.py, seal.py, or the spec. Do not commit. Report back with the GDELT series highlights (coverage, peaks, Anthropic co-mention counts), the Rooney toplines found, the BCG extension plan, every judgment call, and anything that failed.

I have results for Hacker News and Wikipedia. The CVE series and the health-of-democracy proxies are still being built by the two background agents.

## Hacker News (comment IDs only, January 2021 to August 2026)
- **Size:** 111,662 comments in two sets: one on Anthropic or Claude, one on AI security incidents (CVEs, breaches, prompt injection, jailbreaks, leaked weights or keys).
- **Rebuilds and checks:** the extraction rebuilds byte-identical, and re-checking every comment's hash found 0 mismatches.
- **Nothing personal is committed:** no comment text and no usernames are stored. Example comments are listed as `news.ycombinator.com/item?id=…` links.
- **Scored on Modal:** both models ran on both sets.

Anthropic comments rose from about 1,000 a month in early 2025 to 8,500–9,800 a month from February to July 2026. Over the same period, the share the models flag as AI risk rose from about 3.6% to 7–12%.

**Risk mix over the last 12 months:** share of AI-risk passages naming each type.

| Type | Earnings calls | HN: Anthropic | HN: AI security |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cybersecurity | 36% | 23% | 85% |
| Safety, ethics, misuse | 12% | 40% | 24% |
| Regulation | 2% | 12% | 4% |
| Overspending / capex | 8% | 10% | 1% |
| Accuracy / hallucination | 0% | 3% | 3% |

The chart is at `proposals/hacker-news/report/risk-ranking-ttm.svg`.

The models are less reliable on HN than on calls, because comments are sarcastic and quote each other. The two models agree at κ 0.54 on AI risk, against 0.61 on calls. Worse, "safety/ethics" and "regulation" pick up general complaints about outages, terms of service and spending: in a spot check, about half the "regulation" hits were off-topic. So the HN shares only show the rough order of risk types, not levels you could compare with calls.

## Wikipedia
The corpus is 151 articles pinned to their last revision on or before 2026-11-04, cut into 3,749 passages. The section headings give 110 candidate risk dimensions.

Scoring Wikipedia with our current codebook answers your "dialogue space" question:

- **Half the public discussion of AI risk has no category in our codebook.** The models flag 833 Wikipedia passages as AI risk. Of those, 426 (51%) fit none of our specific risk types, only the catch-all "safety/ethics". The gaps concentrate in:
  - existential risk (84% of its AI-risk passages are untyped)
  - alignment (86%)
  - AI safety (63%)
  - ethics of AI
  - misinformation
- **The risks executives talk about barely appear on Wikipedia.** Across all 3,749 passages, overspending/capex appears once, disruption of the business once and chip supply never.

Put plainly: the codebook was written for company speech, and the public discussion is about different risks. The missing dimensions, read straight off Wikipedia's headings, are:
- loss of control / alignment
- existential risk
- power concentration ("dominance by tech giants")
- misinformation and deepfakes
- weapons
- biosecurity
- manipulation
- transparency and accountability

## Decision for you: a v0.2 codebook
I can draft v0.2 hypotheses for those dimensions, worded from the Wikipedia headings, for you to edit and approve. Then I'd rescore all four sources: executive remarks, analyst questions, HN and Wikipedia. That gives one map of the whole dialogue space, showing who talks about which risks and who stays silent. Rescoring costs a few dollars on Modal. Go ahead?

## Not committed yet
The HN corpus, the Wikipedia corpus, the `--out` option in the classifier, the report scripts and the new spec §10 entry are all uncommitted. Should I commit them now or wait for the CVE and democracy work?

content.text:
The CVE series is in the main tree, and its verify step passes: the pins re-hash and all four outputs rebuild identical.

**It reproduces Epoch exactly.** Epoch's chart code turned out to contain its monthly data, so the agent compared it with our rebuild from the official CVE list, pinned to the 2026-11-04 snapshot. All 82 months match on the total, on every reporting organization, and on every severity level. The one difference is filing: Epoch counts 112 CVEs scored 0.0 under "low", and we keep them as "none".

**CVE volume has quadrupled since Mythos.** The jump starts around the 2026-04-07 Claude Mythos announcement.

| Month | Published | Excluding Linux |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-03 | 5,923 | 5,745 |
| 2026-06 | 7,815 | 7,302 |
| 2026-08 | 12,253 | 10,610 |
| 2026-10 | 17,013 | 15,962 |

We exclude Linux because it began issuing CVEs in bulk for routine bug fixes in 2024, which inflates the totals.

**CVEs that credit an AI system as finder.** We read this from each CVE's credits field. It rose from 11 in January to 258 in October, and Claude is the most credited system:

| Month (2026) | Credit an AI system | Credit Claude |
|---|---|---|
| June | 59 | 16 |
| August | 123 | 44 |
| September | 166 | 112 |
| October | 258 | 134 |

- "Mythos" by name appears only once, so the jump after the announcement shows up as credits to Claude or Anthropic, not to Mythos.
- OpenAI and Codex credits rise from July.
- Credits are entered by whoever files the CVE and are incomplete, so these are lower bounds.

**What it can't show:** a CVE count measures reporting, not risk. Both new organizations joining and AI-assisted bug finding raise it, and the series can't tell those apart. That caveat is in `docs/cve-series.md`.

The agent didn't run your required editing passes (buzz-saw-editor and brand-voice) on that doc. I'll run them on all the new method docs together before they go anywhere public.

The health-of-democracy agent is still working on the GDELT timelines, the Rooney toplines and the BCG notes.

I still need two answers from you: should I draft the v0.2 codebook from the Wikipedia dimensions, and should I commit the HN, Wikipedia and CVE work now?

---
name: corpus-source-policy
description: Which data sources to add to the anthropic-pbc corpora — broad and verifiable, never sensationalist
metadata:
  type: project
---

When adding sources to the anthropic-pbc corpora, take as much broad, verifiable, normalisable data as possible. Do not hand-pick the most sensationalist sources ("no shrill bullshit").

- Hacker News is enough as the social-forum voice; don't add other social media.
- Prefer structured research datasets, such as Epoch AI (epoch.ai/data/*, CC BY).
- Also in scope: the effect of AI agents and scraping on the open web (Sloane pointed to voidly.ai as an example, 2026-11-04).

**Why:** sensationalist sources are hard to normalise and weaken a verifiable corpus.

**How to apply:** pin each source like the others (MANIFEST plus hashes), and report coverage and denominators beside every finding. Related: [[commit-as-verified]].

toolUseResult.originalFile:
# AGENTS.md

Public research repository: a hash-sealed working paper on Anthropic PBC, plus
public-data corpora that test its method across the S&P 500. Everything here is
published, so proprietary Ethical Capital work belongs in monocloud, never here.
Repo content is CC0 except `corpus/*/`, which carries its own attribution README.

## Where to look

- **Editing the paper** (`docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md`): every hash pin moves
  with it. Run `uv run scripts/seal.py check --allow-unsealed`; README "Maintaining the seal".
- **Any model output** (BERT, NLI, embeddings, topics): read
  `docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md` §5 and §9 first. Models are *witnesses* whose
  output is a proposal in `proposals/`, never a verdict. Results are appended to
  that spec's §10 log, never edited into §§1–9.
- **Earnings-call AI corpus**: `docs/earnings-call-ai-corpus.md` (method, unit,
  rebuild order). Data is in `corpus/earnings-calls/`.
- **10-K Item 1A risk-factor corpus**: `docs/risk-factor-corpus.md`.

## Compute

GPU work goes to **Modal**. It is authenticated through the local `modal`
profile via `uvx`, with no venv and no BWS secret:

    uvx --with duckdb==2.0.0 --with blake3 modal run scripts/ec_classify_modal.py --model deberta

Measured speeds, costs and alternatives (Mac MPS, RunPod via BWS
`RUNPOD_API_KEY`, CPU-only k3s on the Proxmox cluster) are in
`docs/earnings-call-ai-corpus.md` §9. Copy the `ec_classify_modal.py` pattern
for new GPU jobs: shared scoring functions in the local script, imported by the
Modal class.

## Conventions

- **Deterministic.** No clock, host or random id enters any output; time is a
  recorded argument. A rebuild must be byte-identical, so check that by
  re-hashing.
- **Verbatim and anchored.** Stored text carries BLAKE3 and character offsets,
  and a `verify` command re-slices and re-hashes everything.
- **Pinned.** Scripts are `uv run` PEP 723 scripts with exact versions. Sources
  are pinned by revision and hash in a `MANIFEST.tsv`, and bulk bytes live in a
  gitignored dot-directory (`.eccorpus/`, `.rfcorpus/`) that the manifest can
  re-fetch.
- **Denominators.** Report a rate against every unit attempted (for example
  `calls.tsv`), and report coverage beside every finding.

## Gotchas

- `scripts/ec_classify_modal.py` must not use `from __future__ import annotations`:
  Modal reads `modal.parameter()` types at runtime.
- Modal methods return only plain Python types: the local side has no torch,
  so a torch object or exception (even `torch.__version__`) fails to unpickle
  after the GPU work is done. Shards are saved as they arrive, so rerunning
  only merges.
- Shards are tagged by model, dtype and backend, so runs on different hardware
  never merge, by design. To combine workers, pass the same `--backend`.

## About AI data centers

## What is an AI data center?

We define an AI data center as a collection of one or more buildings which are located near each other, have a shared hardware owner or facility operator, and which run hardware specialized for AI. This hardware includes GPUs or custom chips like Google's TPUs. These data centers may be used to experiment on, train, and deploy AI models.

We don't use a hard limit for how close together the data center buildings have to be, but a rule of thumb is less than 10 km apart. The buildings may or may not be networked together.

We do not distinguish between campuses of multiple buildings and individual buildings in what we classify as a data center.

## What are the largest AI data centers?

The largest known AI data center by IT power is Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle, owned by Amazon in New Carlisle, IN, drawing 1,037 MW. It is followed by Colossus 2 (SpaceXAI, 946 MW), OpenAI Stargate Abilene (Oracle, 824 MW), Microsoft Fairwater Atlanta (Microsoft, 636 MW), and DayOne Nusajaya (473 MW).

The largest AI data center by compute is Colossus 2, owned by SpaceXAI in Memphis, TN, with 1,112k H100e. It is followed by OpenAI Stargate Abilene (Oracle, 1,019k H100e), Anthropic-Amazon New Carlisle (Amazon, 818k H100e), Microsoft Fairwater Atlanta (Microsoft, 769k H100e), and Google Pryor (North) (Google, 637k H100e).

### Frequently asked questions

## How do you choose what data centers to cover?

We mostly prioritize AI data centers by computing capacity. However, we have a lower bar for capacity internationally compared to the US, to achieve more globally balanced coverage. We also limit coverage to data centers that become operational in 2024 or later, with some exceptions. This includes planned data centers, but only if those data centers are under construction and have a significant chance of being completed. In practice, this limits most of the future coverage to 2–3 years from now.

## Why are most of the data centers in this database located in the United States?

Based on our prior work we believe most, but not all, of the largest data centers are in the United States. Additionally, focusing on the US first allowed us to become familiar with permitting standards, providing an additional source for us to validate our methodology. We continue to expand coverage in other countries.

## What information do you collect about AI data centers?

We collect general information about each data center, such as the location, owner and users. We also collect satellite, aerial and drone images, and estimate key metrics over time as each data center evolves. Every data center we cover has a timeline of total IT power capacity, compute capacity, and capital cost.

## How do you estimate IT power, compute, and cost?

IT power is estimated for each data center based on the available evidence, which may include cooling equipment observed in satellite imagery, permitting documents, and statements from companies. Compute is usually calculated from IT power, based on the energy efficiency of chips that we believe are most likely to be used (which is mostly informed by the chip owners dataset). In the uncommon case where the specific type and quantity of chips is reported, then compute estimates are based on that. Capital costs are entirely calculated from IT power, based on a general cost-per-watt model. We estimate construction start dates, operation dates and expansion dates primarily from commercial satellite imagery, but also publicly available imagery and commercial drone imagery. For details, see the methodology.

## How comprehensive is the data?

The database is the result of a continuous effort since mid-2025 to cover the largest AI data centers globally, most of which are in the US. Based on the total amount of AI compute reported in the chip sales database, we estimate this database’s coverage of global deployed AI computing capacity to be 45% as of November 4, 2026 (90% CI: 30% to 78%).

These percentages are based on a model that accounts for our uncertainty in each data center’s capacity and operational dates (see FAQ: “How confident are you in the data?”), and the lag between chip sales and deployment. More recent dates have higher coverage, improving steadily since Q1 2024 where coverage is 22% (90% CI: 11% to 49%). We continue to expand coverage globally, including Asia, Europe and the Middle East.

The coverage is strongest for the largest AI data centers between 2024 and 2028, because we have prioritized finding those. We believe the database captures the majority of record-holding facilities (in terms of compute capacity) during that period.

## How is this database different from the GPU clusters database?

The deprecated GPU clusters database covers computing clusters used for AI and other applications. These clusters may make up just part of the total compute present in one data center building or campus. GPU clusters has broad coverage across time and space, but only covers an estimated 10–20% of global compute as of March 2025. In contrast, this database looks at AI data centers at a project level, and focuses on the largest current and upcoming data centers to achieve higher compute coverage. It also uses primary sources much more, including permitting and satellite imagery, to get greater detail and accuracy on individual data centers.

## How confident are you in the data?

We model our uncertainty both in terms of quantities and construction timelines. We expect that 80% of the time, a given IT power capacity estimate is accurate within a factor of 1.4x. For compute capacity, this factor increases to 1.5x, and for cost, the factor is 1.6x. As for the timelines, we expect that 80% of the time, our estimated date is within 6 months of the actual date.

These confidence levels are informed by data on how our estimates differ from the most credible reference values, and modeling on top of that data. We expect our estimates to become more accurate as we find more data centers and do more research on how they work.

## What do “Speculative” and “Likely” mean next to data center users?

By default, if we list a user, owner, or other affiliate of a data center, we have strong evidence for it. However, sometimes we are uncertain about these affiliations, especially the data center users. We indicate this uncertainty with “Speculative” and “Likely” tags.

“Speculative” means that we have no record of an affiliation, but we have some reason to believe it. For example, we speculate that Anthropic will use two Amazon data centers in Mississippi because the New York Times reported that at least one of the Anthropic-Amazon Project Rainier data centers is located there, but they didn’t specify which ones.

“Likely” means we have some record of an affiliation, but we aren’t confident. For example, OpenAI is a “Likely” user for Microsoft Fairwater because a Microsoft spokesperson stated it “initially will be used to train OpenAI models”, but Microsoft’s partnership with OpenAI has been weakening since 2023.

## Can an entire data center be used to train one AI model?

This is possible, but does not happen often in practice. The total capacity of a data center is more like a cap on the size of a training run in that data center. Data centers often run multiple jobs in parallel and/or get partitioned for multiple users. Even if the entire data center is deployed on a single job, hardware failures will slightly reduce the capacity. Relatedly, when we report the total compute capacity of a data center in 8-bit OP/s, this is the theoretical peak capacity for number formats of 8 bits or above. In practice, the computational performance is typically 20–50% of the peak value, due to inefficiencies.

## Can any of these data centers be networked together to do bigger training runs?

A previous analysis concluded that distributed training runs across distant data centers is technically feasible. AI companies have also proposed distributed training runs. Our database will document which data centers are networked together as we learn more.

GPU clusters has broad coverage across time and space, but only covers an estimated 10–20% of global compute as of March 2025. In contrast, this database looks at AI data centers at a project level, and focuses on the largest current and upcoming data centers to achieve higher compute coverage. It also uses primary sources much more, including permitting and satellite imagery, to get greater detail and accuracy on individual data centers.

## How confident are you in the data?

We model our uncertainty both in terms of quantities and construction timelines. We expect that 80% of the time, a given IT power capacity estimate is accurate within a factor of 1.4x. For compute capacity, this factor increases to 1.5x, and for cost, the factor is 1.6x. As for the timelines, we expect that 80% of the time, our estimated date is within 6 months of the actual date.

These confidence levels are informed by data on how our estimates differ from the most credible reference values, and modeling on top of that data. We expect our estimates to become more accurate as we find more data centers and do more research on how they work.

## What do “Speculative” and “Likely” mean next to data center users?

By default, if we list a user, owner, or other affiliate of a data center, we have strong evidence for it. However, sometimes we are uncertain about these affiliations, especially the data center users. We indicate this uncertainty with “Speculative” and “Likely” tags.

“Speculative” means that we have no record of an affiliation, but we have some reason to believe it. For example, we speculate that Anthropic will use two Amazon data centers in Mississippi because the New York Times reported that at least one of the Anthropic-Amazon Project Rainier data centers is located there, but they didn’t specify which ones.

“Likely” means we have some record of an affiliation, but we aren’t confident. For example, OpenAI is a “Likely” user for Microsoft Fairwater because a Microsoft spokesperson stated it “initially will be used to train OpenAI models”, but Microsoft’s partnership with OpenAI has been weakening since 2023.

## Can an entire data center be used to train one AI model?

This is possible, but does not happen often in practice. The total capacity of a data center is more like a cap on the size of a training run in that data center. Data centers often run multiple jobs in parallel and/or get partitioned for multiple users. Even if the entire data center is deployed on a single job, hardware failures will slightly reduce the capacity. Relatedly, when we report the total compute capacity of a data center in 8-bit OP/s, this is the theoretical peak capacity for number formats of 8 bits or above. In practice, the computational performance is typically 20–50% of the peak value, due to inefficiencies.

## Can any of these data centers be networked together to do bigger training runs?

A previous analysis concluded that distributed training runs across distant data centers is technically feasible. AI companies have also proposed distributed training runs. Our database will document which data centers are networked together as we learn more.

- Do not commit.

Report back:
- each dataset's bytes and table count
- any download that failed
- what you committed verbatim and what you kept local
- the Anthropic row counts
- two inventory hashes, showing the rebuild is identical
- every judgment call you made

- Rate-limit politely and send a descriptive User-Agent.
- No analysis or charts.
- Do not edit docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md, index.html, README.md, frameworks/, sources/, enrich_*.py, seal.py, or docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md.
- Do not commit.

- each dataset's bytes and table count
- any download that failed

- the Anthropic row counts

input.content:
# Corpus roadmap

Planned sources and open questions for the public-data corpora. Nothing here is
built yet unless it links to a method doc.

## Source policy (Sloane, 2026-11-04)

- **Take everything, not the loudest.** Grab as much verifiable data as
  possible so the corpus is broad and normalisable. Do not index the most
  sensationalist sources: they are hard to normalise and invite cherry-picking.
- **One social forum.** Hacker News
  ([`hacker-news-corpus.md`](hacker-news-corpus.md)) is the social voice. No
  other social media.
- **Prefer structured research datasets.** Epoch AI (epoch.ai/data, CC BY) is
  the model; its CVE series is already rebuilt in [`cve-series.md`](cve-series.md).
  A snapshot of every Epoch dataset is in progress in `corpus/epoch/`.
- Every source is pinned (MANIFEST plus hashes), with coverage and
  denominators reported beside any finding.

## Codebook

`corpus/codebooks/codebook-v0.2-draft.tsv` keeps the 16 v0.1 hypotheses
unchanged and adds 14. Each new one cites the Wikipedia heading and revision
it came from (`corpus/wikipedia-ai-risk/dimensions-candidate.tsv`). It is a
draft until Sloane approves the wording. Motive: scoring Wikipedia with v0.1
left 51% of its AI-risk passages with no specific type
([`wikipedia-ai-risk-corpus.md`](wikipedia-ai-risk-corpus.md)).

## Open question: what have AI agents and scraping done to the open web?

Wikipedia names this dimension ("Ethics of artificial intelligence",
Challenges > Strain on open knowledge platforms; v0.2 hypothesis `open_web`).
These candidate sources are broad and measurable, and each must be checked for
license and pinnability before use:

- **Wikimedia**: pageview and bandwidth statistics by agent type (user,
  spider, automated), and Wikimedia's own reports on crawler load.
- **Stack Exchange**: question and answer volume by month, from the data dump
  or the Data Explorer. It is the standard proxy for Q&A sites displaced by
  chat assistants.
- **robots.txt and terms of service restricting AI crawlers**: the Data
  Provenance Initiative's longitudinal audit of web-domain consent, and
  Common Crawl's robots.txt captures.
- **Crawler-to-referral ratios by AI operator**, from Cloudflare Radar
  (check its license terms).
- **Voidly** (voidly.ai): CC BY 4.0 incident records of internet censorship

### What this corpus is, and what it refuses to be

Status: METHOD. Binds nothing. The corpus is an input to analysis, not a finding.
Nothing here is scored, summarized, or judged. Every downstream claim must cite a
`text_blake3` value and re-slice it, per [`descartes-spec.md`](descartes-spec.md).

Sources: SEC EDGAR primary documents, addressed through the

`defeatbeta/yahoo-finance-data` publishes `data/US/stock_sec_filing.parquet`:
7,913,275 rows across 10,818 symbols, filing dates 1993-08-13 → 2026-11-02. Its
columns are metadata only — `symbol, cik, accession_number, company_name,
form_type, form_type_description, filing_date, report_date, acceptance_date_time,
filing_url`. There is no filing text in it.

So the dataset supplies the two things that make an EDGAR crawl addressable — CIK
and accession number — and nothing else. Every word in this corpus was fetched

input.content: #!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script # /// script # requires-python = ">=3.10" # dependencies = ["blake3==1.0.11"] # /// """Write DATASETS.md, the central catalog of every corpus, as a Marp deck. One registry, corpus/datasets.tsv, holds what cannot be read from files: title, source, license, pin date, how often the source changes, and the refresh commands. Everything else is read from the repository: each corpus's MANIFEST.tsv (row count and BLAKE3), its committed files, and the witness runs under proposals//. No clock: the deck changes only when the inputs change. uv run scripts/datasets_md.py # write DATASETS.md uv run scripts/datasets_md.py check # exit 1 if DATASETS.md is stale Render: npx @marp-team/marp-cli DATASETS.md (or the Marp VS Code extension) """ from __future__ import annotations import csv import json import sys from pathlib import Path import blake3 ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent REGISTRY = ROOT / "corpus" / "datasets.tsv" OUT = ROOT / "DATASETS.md" HEAD = """--- marp: true paginate: true size: 16:9 title: Datasets style: | section { font-size: 22px; } table { font-size: 16px; } code { font-size: 15px; } --- # Datasets Every corpus in this repository: where it comes from, when it was pinned, how often the source changes, and how to rebuild it. Model output is a witness proposal in `proposals/`, never a finding (`docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md` §5). """ def b3(p: Path) -> str: return blake3.blake3(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest() def cell(s: str) -> str: return s.replace("|", "\\|").replace("\n", " ") def manifest_info(d: Path) -> tuple[str, str]: m = d / "MANIFEST.tsv" if not m.exists(): return "—", "—" n = sum(1 for _ in m.open()) - 1 return str(n), b3(m)[:16] def committed_files(d: Path) -> tuple[int, int]: files = [p for p in d.rglob("*") if p.is_file()] return len(files), sum(p.stat().st_size for p in files) def runs(ds: str) -> list[tuple[str, str, str, str]]: """(output dir, model, scores, backend) for every witness run under proposals//.""" base = ROOT / "proposals" / ds out = [] for r in sorted(base.rglob("run-*.json")) if base.exists() else []: j = json.loads(r.read_text()) n = j.get("n_scores") or j.get("scores") or "" out.append((str(r.parent.relative_to(ROOT)), j.get("model_key") or r.stem[4:], str(n), j.get("backend") or j.get("runtime", {}).get("backend", ""))) return out def epoch_table() -> list[str]: m = ROOT / "corpus" / "epoch" / "MANIFEST.tsv" rows = list(csv.DictReader(m.open(), delimiter="\t")) seen: dict[str, list[str]] = {} for r in rows: seen.setdefault(r["dataset"], []).append(r["updated"]) lines = ["| Epoch dataset | Files | Source last updated |", "|---|---:|---|"] for k in sorted(seen): lines.append(f"| {k} | {len(seen[k])} | {', '.join(sorted(set(seen[k])))} |") return lines def render() -> str: reg = list(csv.DictReader(REGISTRY.open(), delimiter="\t")) o = [HEAD, "---", "", "## Overview", "", "| Dataset | Pinned as of | Source cadence | Manifest rows |", "|---|---|---|---:|"] for r in reg: d = ROOT / r["corpus_dir"] if r["corpus_dir"] != "—" else None n, _ = manifest_info(d) if d else ("—", "—") o.append(f"| [{cell(r['title'])}](#{r['id']}) | {r['pinned_as_of']} | {cell(r['source_cadence'])} | {n} |") for r in reg: d = ROOT / r["corpus_dir"] if r["corpus_dir"] != "—" else None n, h = manifest_info(d) if d else ("—", "—") nf, nb = committed_files(d) if d else (0, 0) o += ["", "---", "", f"", "", f"## {r['title']}", "", "| | |", "|---|---|", f"| Source | {cell(r['source'])} |", f"| License | {cell(r['license'])} |", f"| Pinned as of | {r['pinned_as_of']} |", f"| Source cadence | {cell(r['source_cadence'])} |", f"| Committed | {cell(r['committed'])} |", f"| Folder | `{r['corpus_dir']}` · {nf} files · {nb / 1e6:.1f} MB |" if d else "| Folder | — |", f"| Manifest | {n} rows · BLAKE3 `{h}` |", f"| Method | [`{r['doc']}`]({r['doc']}) |", "", "Refresh:", "", f" {r['refresh']}"] rs = runs(r["id"]) if rs: o += ["", "| Witness output | Model | Scores |", "|---|---|---:|"] o += [f"| `{a}` | {b} | {c} |" for a, b, c, _ in rs] if r["id"] == "epoch": o += ["", "---", "", "## Epoch AI: per-dataset update dates", ""] + epoch_table() return "\n".join(o) + "\n" def main() -> int: text = render() if len(sys.argv) > 1 and sys.argv[1] == "check": ok = OUT.exists() and OUT.read_text() == text print("DATASETS.md is current" if ok else "DATASETS.md is stale: run uv run scripts/datasets_md.py") return 0 if ok else 1 OUT.write_text(text) print(f"wrote {OUT.relative_to(ROOT)} ({len(text)} bytes)") return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": sys.exit(main())

# AGENTS.md

Public research repository: a hash-sealed working paper on Anthropic PBC, plus
public-data corpora that test its method. **It exists to be worked on by
others.** A researcher or agent who has never seen it should be able to clone
it, rebuild every dataset, check every number, and add to it, with no access
to anything private. Every convention below serves that.

Everything here is published, so proprietary Ethical Capital work belongs in
monocloud, never here. Repo content is CC0 except `corpus/*/`, which carries
its own attribution README.

## Start here

- **`DATASETS.md`** is the catalog of every corpus: source, license, pin date,
  how often the source changes, refresh commands, and witness runs. It is a
  Marp deck generated from `corpus/datasets.tsv` and each corpus's
  `MANIFEST.tsv` by `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py`. Never edit it by hand.
- **`docs/corpus-roadmap.md`** lists what is planned and what is open. Pick up
  work there.

## Collaborating

- **Leave the work rebuildable by a stranger.** Every result traces to a
  committed script, a pinned source and a hash. A step that only works on one
  machine or with one person's credentials is unfinished.
- **Commit each piece as soon as it is complete and verified**: rebuild
  byte-identical, `verify` passes. Small commits, one corpus or one result each.
- **Keep to your own files.** Others work in this tree at the same time. Stage
  only your own paths and hunks; never stage `__pycache__/` or `.claude/`.
- **Disagree in the open.** A finding is changed by appending to the spec's
  §10 log, never by rewriting earlier entries. Codebooks change only by human
  review: a draft is marked `DRAFT` until approved.
- **Gold labels come from people.** `scripts/ec_gold.py code --coder NAME`
  records one coder per file, so several people can code the same sample and
  agreement can be measured. No LLM labels (spec §9).
- **Write for the next reader.** The method doc for each corpus says what it
  does *not* answer, as plainly as what it does.

## Adding a dataset

1. Choose broad, verifiable, normalisable data, such as Epoch AI datasets, over
   hand-picked sensational sources. Hacker News is the only social forum.
2. Write `scripts/<name>.py` with `pin` (or `fetch`), `build` and `verify`, and
   pin the source in `corpus/<name>/MANIFEST.tsv` (URL, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3).
3. Write `corpus/<name>/README.md` (files and attribution) and
   `docs/<name>.md` (method and limits).
4. Respect source terms. A dataset whose terms bar AI ingestion is not
   fetched. Private individuals' text is stored as ids and hashes only (see the
   Hacker News corpus).
5. Add a row to `corpus/datasets.tsv`, run `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py`, and
   commit the deck with the data. `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py check` fails
   if the deck is stale.

## Where to look

- **Editing the paper** (`docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md`): every hash pin moves
  with it. Run `uv run scripts/seal.py check --allow-unsealed`; README "Maintaining the seal".
- **Any model output** (BERT, NLI, embeddings, topics): read
  `docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md` §5 and §9 first. Models are *witnesses* whose
  output is a proposal in `proposals/`, never a verdict. Results are appended to
  that spec's §10 log, never edited into §§1–9.
- **Per-corpus method**: one doc per corpus in `docs/`, linked from `DATASETS.md`.

## Compute

GPU scoring runs on **Modal** in the maintainer's setup (the local `modal`
profile via `uvx`, no BWS secret):

    uvx --with duckdb==2.0.0 --with blake3 modal run scripts/ec_classify_modal.py --model deberta

Without Modal, `scripts/ec_classify.py` runs the same scoring locally (MPS or
CPU) and can split shards across machines. Measured speeds and costs are in
`docs/earnings-call-ai-corpus.md` §9. For another corpus or codebook, pass
`--units`, `--codebook`, `--id-col` and `--out`. Copy the `ec_classify_modal.py`
pattern for new GPU jobs: shared scoring functions in the local script,
imported by the Modal class.

## Conventions

- **Deterministic.** No clock, host or random id enters any output; time is a
  recorded argument. A rebuild must be byte-identical, so check that by
  re-hashing.
- **Verbatim and anchored.** Stored text carries BLAKE3 and character offsets,
  and a `verify` command re-slices and re-hashes everything.
- **Pinned.** Scripts are `uv run` PEP 723 scripts with exact versions. Sources
  are pinned by revision and hash in a `MANIFEST.tsv`, and bulk bytes live in a
  gitignored dot-directory (`.eccorpus/`, `.hncorpus/`, ...) that the manifest
  can re-fetch. Where a source cannot be re-fetched byte-identically (Epoch
  bundles, API responses), the saved bytes are the pin.
- **Denominators.** Report a rate against every unit attempted (for example
  `calls.tsv`), and report coverage beside every finding.

## Gotchas

- `scripts/ec_classify_modal.py` must not use `from __future__ import annotations`:
  Modal reads `modal.parameter()` types at runtime.
- Modal methods return only plain Python types: the local side has no torch,
  so a torch object or exception (even `torch.__version__`) fails to unpickle
  after the GPU work is done. Shards are saved as they arrive, so rerunning
  only merges.
- Shards are tagged by model, dtype and backend, so runs on different hardware
  never merge, by design. To combine workers, pass the same `--backend`.
- Without `--out`, the classifier writes to `proposals/earnings-calls/<codebook stem>/`,
  which would overwrite earnings-call results when another corpus reuses a codebook.

  committed script, a pinned source and a hash. A step that only works on one
  machine or with one person's credentials is unfinished.

  byte-identical, `verify` passes. Small commits, one corpus or one result each.

  only your own paths and hunks; never stage `__pycache__/` or `.claude/`.

  review: a draft is marked `DRAFT` until approved.

   pin the source in `corpus/<name>/MANIFEST.tsv` (URL, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3).

   `docs/<name>.md` (method and limits).

   fetched. Private individuals' text is stored as ids and hashes only (see the
   Hacker News corpus).

   commit the deck with the data. `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py check` fails
   if the deck is stale.

  with it. Run `uv run scripts/seal.py check --allow-unsealed`; README "Maintaining the seal".
- **Any model output** (BERT, NLI, embeddings, topics): read
  `docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md` §5 and §9 first. Models are *witnesses* whose
  output is a proposal in `proposals/`, never a verdict. Results are appended to
  that spec's §10 log, never edited into §§1–9.
- **Per-corpus method**: one doc per corpus in `docs/`, linked from `DATASETS.md`.

## Compute

GPU scoring runs on **Modal** in the maintainer's setup (the local `modal`
profile via `uvx`, no BWS secret):

CPU) and can split shards across machines. Measured speeds and costs are in
`docs/earnings-call-ai-corpus.md` §9. For another corpus or codebook, pass
`--units`, `--codebook`, `--id-col` and `--out`. Copy the `ec_classify_modal.py`
pattern for new GPU jobs: shared scoring functions in the local script,
imported by the Modal class.

## Conventions

- **Deterministic.** No clock, host or random id enters any output; time is a
  recorded argument. A rebuild must be byte-identical, so check that by
  re-hashing.
- **Verbatim and anchored.** Stored text carries BLAKE3 and character offsets,
  and a `verify` command re-slices and re-hashes everything.
- **Pinned.** Scripts are `uv run` PEP 723 scripts with exact versions. Sources
  are pinned by revision and hash in a `MANIFEST.tsv`, and bulk bytes live in a
  gitignored dot-directory (`.eccorpus/`, `.hncorpus/`, ...) that the manifest
  can re-fetch. Where a source cannot be re-fetched byte-identically (Epoch
  bundles, API responses), the saved bytes are the pin.
- **Denominators.** Report a rate against every unit attempted (for example
  `calls.tsv`), and report coverage beside every finding.

## Gotchas

- `scripts/ec_classify_modal.py` must not use `from __future__ import annotations`:
  Modal reads `modal.parameter()` types at runtime.
- Modal methods return only plain Python types: the local side has no torch,
  so a torch object or exception (even `torch.__version__`) fails to unpickle
  after the GPU work is done. Shards are saved as they arrive, so rerunning
  only merges.
- Shards are tagged by model, dtype and backend, so runs on different hardware
  never merge, by design. To combine workers, pass the same `--backend`.
- Without `--out`, the classifier writes to `proposals/earnings-calls/<codebook stem>/`,
  which would overwrite earnings-call results when another corpus reuses a codebook.

content.text:
Both are committed as `1acf062`.

**`DATASETS.md`** is at the repo root: a Marp deck with an overview slide, one slide per dataset, and a slide of Epoch's per-dataset update dates. Each dataset slide shows:
- source and license
- pin date and how often the source changes
- what's committed, with folder size
- the manifest's hash
- the method doc and the refresh commands
- the model-scoring runs

A script writes it from one registry file, `corpus/datasets.tsv`, plus each corpus's own manifest. `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py check` fails if the deck is out of date. Adding a dataset means adding one row to the registry and rerunning the script.

It doesn't regenerate on its own yet. A pre-commit hook would do that, but `.githooks/` belongs to another session's uncommitted work, so I left it alone. Tell me if you want the hook added there.

The deck currently lists one v0.2 earnings-call run that is still in progress. I'll regenerate and commit it when the scoring finishes.

**`AGENTS.md`** now opens by saying the repo exists for others to work on: someone new should be able to clone it, rebuild every dataset, check every number and add to it, without access to anything private. It then covers:
- **Start here:** the deck and the roadmap.
- **Collaborating:**
  - keep everything rebuildable by a stranger
  - commit each piece once it's verified
  - stage only your own files
  - change findings by adding to the log, never by rewriting it
  - codebooks change only through human review
  - gold labels come from people, with a second coder working on their own copy
- **Adding a dataset:** a five-step checklist, including respecting source terms and storing private individuals' text as IDs only.
- **Compute:** a way to score without Modal, since Modal runs under my local login.

Still running: the v0.2 scoring and the health-of-democracy agent.

#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["blake3>=1.0"]
# ///
"""Keep the paper, its rendered page, its figures and its hash pins in lockstep.
    uv run scripts/seal.py sync                              # rebuild figures, re-embed paper in index.html
    uv run scripts/seal.py check                             # fail on any drift (CI runs this)
    uv run scripts/seal.py check --allow-unsealed            # same, but a draft whose pins lag only warns
    uv run scripts/seal.py seal --version v0.1 --date 2026-11-04
`seal` = sync, then move every version/hash/date pin from the sealed version
(read from CITATION.cff) to the new one. The date is an argument, never read
from the clock: time is a recorded input (docs/primitives.md).
Zenodo is not touched. With the GitHub-Zenodo integration, publishing a GitHub
release of the sealed commit mints the new version DOI; the script prints the
command and does not run it.
"""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
import blake3
ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
PAPER = ROOT / "docs" / "anthropic-contrapunctus.md"
PAGE = ROOT / "index.html"
FIG_BUILD = ROOT / "docs" / "figures" / "build.py"
CITATION = ROOT / "CITATION.cff"
EMBED_OPEN = '<script type="text/markdown" id="paperSrc">'
EMBED_CLOSE = "</script>"
# Every file that pins the sealed hash. Each holds no other 64-hex token, so
  write via temp+fsync+rename, and treat byte-divergent re-put as
  corruption. Interrupted-write recovery (S5) and directory fsync (S6)
  MUST be decided and tested before any durability claim. `[partial]`
- **PS-2.7 Derivations.** Only allowlisted tools with fixed argument shapes
  MAY produce committed derivations, sandboxed, byte-reproducible; the loop
  MUST re-run them. `[held in part; recipes re-audit per C2]`
- **PS-2.8 Attestation.** Signatures MUST be separations from their subject
  (subject id independent of signer), `did:key` signers, strict Ed25519
  verify, lowercase hex. Whether attestations verify only when listed in a
  snapshot: **[decide — V5]**. Export of a roots bundle (S8): `[open]`.
- **PS-2.9 Loss accounting.** Every translation stage MUST report loss per
  component per circle; implementations MUST NOT report a single aggregate
  fidelity score. Tables/non-text content not yet captured MUST be stated,
  with dependent claims demoted to circle 0. `[held for measured corpus]`

    uvx --with duckdb==2.0.0 --with blake3 modal run scripts/ec_classify_modal.py --model deberta

input.new_string:
**Compute is vendor-agnostic.** The scoring lives in `scripts/ec_classify.py`,
which runs on any machine: CUDA, Apple MPS or CPU. It can split the shards
across several machines (`--workers N --worker i`, then `--merge-only`).

# AGENTS.md

Public research repository: a hash-sealed working paper on Anthropic PBC, plus
public-data corpora that test its method. **It exists to be worked on by
others.** A researcher or agent who has never seen it should be able to clone
it, rebuild every dataset, check every number, and add to it, with no access
to anything private. Every convention below serves that.

Everything here is published, so proprietary Ethical Capital work belongs in
monocloud, never here. Repo content is CC0 except `corpus/*/`, which carries
its own attribution README.

## Start here

- **`DATASETS.md`** is the catalog of every corpus: source, license, pin date,
  how often the source changes, refresh commands, and witness runs. It is a
  Marp deck generated from `corpus/datasets.tsv` and each corpus's
  `MANIFEST.tsv` by `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py`. Never edit it by hand.
- **`docs/corpus-roadmap.md`** lists what is planned and what is open. Pick up
  work there.

## Collaborating

- **Leave the work rebuildable by a stranger.** Every result traces to a
  committed script, a pinned source and a hash. A step that only works on one
  machine or with one person's credentials is unfinished.
- **Commit each piece as soon as it is complete and verified**: rebuild
  byte-identical, `verify` passes. Small commits, one corpus or one result each.
- **Keep to your own files.** Others work in this tree at the same time. Stage
  only your own paths and hunks; never stage `__pycache__/` or `.claude/`.
- **Disagree in the open.** A finding is changed by appending to the spec's
  §10 log, never by rewriting earlier entries. Codebooks change only by human
  review: a draft is marked `DRAFT` until approved.
- **Gold labels come from people.** `scripts/ec_gold.py code --coder NAME`
  records the coder's name on every row. A second coder works on a copy of the
  sample (`--sample PATH`) so that both codings survive and agreement can be
  measured. No LLM labels (spec §9).
- **Write for the next reader.** The method doc for each corpus says what it
  does *not* answer, as plainly as what it does.

## Adding a dataset

1. Choose broad, verifiable, normalisable data, such as Epoch AI datasets, over
   hand-picked sensational sources. Hacker News is the only social forum.
2. Write `scripts/<name>.py` with `pin` (or `fetch`), `build` and `verify`, and
   pin the source in `corpus/<name>/MANIFEST.tsv` (URL, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3).
3. Write `corpus/<name>/README.md` (files and attribution) and
   `docs/<name>.md` (method and limits).
4. Respect source terms. A dataset whose terms bar AI ingestion is not
   fetched. Private individuals' text is stored as ids and hashes only (see the
   Hacker News corpus).
5. Add a row to `corpus/datasets.tsv`, run `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py`, and
   commit the deck with the data. `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py check` fails
   if the deck is stale.

## Where to look

- **Editing the paper** (`docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md`): every hash pin moves
  with it. Run `uv run scripts/seal.py check --allow-unsealed`; README "Maintaining the seal".
- **Any model output** (BERT, NLI, embeddings, topics): read
  `docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md` §5 and §9 first. Models are *witnesses* whose
  output is a proposal in `proposals/`, never a verdict. Results are appended to
  that spec's §10 log, never edited into §§1–9.
- **Per-corpus method**: one doc per corpus in `docs/`, linked from `DATASETS.md`.

## Compute

GPU scoring runs on **Modal** in the maintainer's setup (the local `modal`
profile via `uvx`, no BWS secret):

    uvx --with duckdb==2.0.0 --with blake3 modal run scripts/ec_classify_modal.py --model deberta

Without Modal, `scripts/ec_classify.py` runs the same scoring locally (MPS or
CPU) and can split shards across machines. Measured speeds and costs are in
`docs/earnings-call-ai-corpus.md` §9. For another corpus or codebook, pass
`--units`, `--codebook`, `--id-col` and `--out`. Copy the `ec_classify_modal.py`
pattern for new GPU jobs: shared scoring functions in the local script,
imported by the Modal class.

## Conventions

- **Deterministic.** No clock, host or random id enters any output; time is a
  recorded argument. A rebuild must be byte-identical, so check that by
  re-hashing.
- **Verbatim and anchored.** Stored text carries BLAKE3 and character offsets,
  and a `verify` command re-slices and re-hashes everything.
- **Pinned.** Scripts are `uv run` PEP 723 scripts with exact versions. Sources
  are pinned by revision and hash in a `MANIFEST.tsv`, and bulk bytes live in a
  gitignored dot-directory (`.eccorpus/`, `.hncorpus/`, ...) that the manifest
  can re-fetch. Where a source cannot be re-fetched byte-identically (Epoch
  bundles, API responses), the saved bytes are the pin.
- **Denominators.** Report a rate against every unit attempted (for example
  `calls.tsv`), and report coverage beside every finding.

## Gotchas

- `scripts/ec_classify_modal.py` must not use `from __future__ import annotations`:
  Modal reads `modal.parameter()` types at runtime.
- Modal methods return only plain Python types: the local side has no torch,
  so a torch object or exception (even `torch.__version__`) fails to unpickle
  after the GPU work is done. Shards are saved as they arrive, so rerunning
  only merges.
- Shards are tagged by model, dtype and backend, so runs on different hardware
  never merge, by design. To combine workers, pass the same `--backend`.
- Without `--out`, the classifier writes to `proposals/earnings-calls/<codebook stem>/`,
  which would overwrite earnings-call results when another corpus reuses a codebook.

content.text:
**Vendor-agnostic:** fixed in AGENTS.md (`05c2cf1`). The scoring code lives in `ec_classify.py` and runs on any machine with CUDA, Apple MPS or a plain CPU, and it can split the work across several machines. Modal is now described as one optional wrapper; any other provider gets a thin wrapper of the same shape with its own backend tag. The code was already built this way; only the wording made Modal sound required.

**Signing: no, none of my steps sign anything.** Here's what each layer does:

| Layer | What it does today | Signed? |
|---|---|---|
| Each corpus | BLAKE3/SHA-256 pins in a manifest; `verify`; rebuilds checked byte-identical | No |
| The paper | `seal.py` keeps the paper, its page, its figures and hash pins in lockstep | Hashed, not signed |
| Attestation (`contrapunctus-attest.md`) | Ed25519 SSH signatures in the `contrapunctus` namespace, checked by `verify.sh` | Paper only, and only by outside signers |
| Commits | Signing is off, and git has no signing key configured | No |

The standard itself says signing a release is still open ("no key exists", PS-3.7). So the corpora meet the hashing and reproducibility parts of the white paper, but not the attestation part.

**Proposed fix:**
1. **A signing record for each dataset.** `datasets_md.py` already reads every manifest. I'd extend it to also write one small record per corpus listing the commit and the hash of every output file. That record is what gets signed.
2. **The same mechanism as the paper.** `ssh-keygen -Y sign` with a separate namespace for datasets, so a dataset signature can't be reused as an endorsement of the paper. `verify.sh` would check both kinds. The deck would show each dataset's signers.
3. **Optionally, sign commits** with SSH keys, which is a git setting on your side.

The one decision that's yours is whose key signs. A signature means a specific key holder took a specific step.
- **Your key, or an Ethical Capital dataset key**, means a person vouches for the build. Only you can do that; I'd prepare the record and give you the command.
- **A key for the build process itself** would only prove that this pipeline produced these bytes. That's provenance, a weaker claim, and it would have to say so plainly. I'd recommend this only as an addition to a human signer, not a replacement.

Which do you want: your key, an org dataset key, or both plus a build key?

# Open questions

Decisions and questions waiting on someone. Each has an owner, the context
needed to answer it, and what it blocks. When one is answered, move it to
**Answered** with the answer, who gave it, and the commit that acted on it.
Never delete an entry.

New questions come from the work itself and from `PASTEBIN.md`.

## Open

### Q1 · Who signs the datasets?
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** Every corpus is hash-pinned and rebuilds byte-identical, but
  nothing is signed. The attestation protocol (`docs/contrapunctus-attest.md`:
  SSH Ed25519, `ssh-keygen -Y sign`, `verify.sh`) covers only the paper.
  `docs/praxis-standard.md` PS-3.7 says release signing is open because no key
  exists. Commits are unsigned.
- **Proposal:** each corpus gets a signing record (commit plus the hash of every
  output file), signed in a separate dataset namespace and checked by
  `verify.sh`. `DATASETS.md` shows the signers.
- **Options:** Sloane's key; an Ethical Capital dataset key; either one plus a
  build key. A build key proves only that this pipeline made these bytes; it
  does not mean anyone vouches for them. Separately: whether to sign commits.
- **Blocks:** the attestation part of the white paper's method for the corpora.

### Q2 · Approve the codebook v0.2 wording
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** `corpus/codebooks/codebook-v0.2-draft.tsv` keeps the 16 v0.1
  hypotheses and adds 14, each citing a Wikipedia heading and revision. The
  `democracy` item comes from the health-of-democracy question, not a heading.
  All four sources are scored against the draft so the wording can be judged
  on real output.
- **Blocks:** citing any v0.2 result; the cross-source map of who discusses
  which risks.

### Q3 · Who codes the gold sets?
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** `gold/earnings-calls/` holds two blind samples: 240 windows and
  200 analyst questions. `uv run scripts/ec_gold.py code --coder NAME` codes
  them; a second coder works on a copy (`--sample PATH`). Spec §9 bars LLM
  labels.
- **Blocks:** every rate leaving `proposals/` (spec §7, go criterion a). The
  controls category gets only a handful of positives into the sample; if it
  becomes the headline, it needs a targeted extra sample.

### Q4 · Seal version and date for the paper
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** `uv run scripts/seal.py seal --version vX --date YYYY-MM-DD`
  needs both values.
- **Blocks:** the next sealed version.

### Q5 · Wikipedia corpus scope
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** Category members came in unfiltered: fiction (Skynet, Universal
  Paperclips), some biographies, books and laws. The `via` column records how
  each article entered. The seed "AI-assisted targeting" does not exist;
  "AI-assisted targeting in the Gaza Strip" does and was not substituted.
- **Decide:** filter by article type? Add the Gaza article as a seed?

### Q6 · Hacker News after August 2026
- **Owner:** open
- **Context:** The pinned archive ends in August 2026. September to November
  would come from the HN API by item-id range, pinned as saved bytes.
- **Blocks:** HN numbers for the same 12 months as the earnings calls.

### Q7 · Excluded and local-only Epoch data
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** ChatGPT usage is excluded because YouGov's notice bars AI
  ingestion; access would have to come through YouGov. 67 third-party
  benchmark tables stay local because they keep their own licences.
- **Decide:** pursue YouGov access? Clear the benchmark licences?

### Q8 · Auto-regenerate DATASETS.md on commit
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py check` detects a stale deck. A
  pre-commit hook would run it, but `.githooks/` holds another session's
  uncommitted work.

### Q9 · What would test "Anthropic is good for the health of democracy"?
- **Owner:** open
- **Context:** The proxies being built (GDELT phrase timelines, Rooney
  Institute toplines, the Trust Project and BCG Trust Index notes) measure
  attention and conditions, not Anthropic's effect. A test needs a mechanism
  and a comparison: what Anthropic does that others do not, and an outcome
  that could move.

### Q10 · Point-in-time S&P 500 membership
- **Owner:** open
- **Context:** The earnings-call universe is today's index applied backwards,
  so firms that left are missing (survivorship bias).

### Q11 · Voidly as a source
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** CC BY 4.0 censorship-incident records with ML-assigned classes
  and confidence scores, from one small vendor. It fits the democracy thread as
  one witness among several, not as ground truth (`docs/corpus-roadmap.md`).

## Answered

| # | Question | Answer | By | Commit |
|---|---|---|---|---|

# AGENTS.md

Public research repository: a hash-sealed working paper on Anthropic PBC, plus
public-data corpora that test its method. **It exists to be worked on by
others.** A researcher or agent who has never seen it should be able to clone
it, rebuild every dataset, check every number, and add to it, with no access
to anything private. Every convention below serves that.

Everything here is published, so proprietary Ethical Capital work belongs in
monocloud, never here. Repo content is CC0 except `corpus/*/`, which carries
its own attribution README.

## Start here

- **`DATASETS.md`** is the catalog of every corpus: source, license, pin date,
  how often the source changes, refresh commands, and witness runs. It is a
  Marp deck generated from `corpus/datasets.tsv` and each corpus's
  `MANIFEST.tsv` by `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py`. Never edit it by hand.
- **`docs/corpus-roadmap.md`** lists what is planned and what is open. Pick up
  work there.

## Collaborating

- **Leave the work rebuildable by a stranger.** Every result traces to a
  committed script, a pinned source and a hash. A step that only works on one
  machine or with one person's credentials is unfinished.
- **Commit each piece as soon as it is complete and verified**: rebuild
  byte-identical, `verify` passes. Small commits, one corpus or one result each.
- **Keep to your own files.** Others work in this tree at the same time. Stage
  only your own paths and hunks; never stage `__pycache__/` or `.claude/`.
- **Disagree in the open.** A finding is changed by appending to the spec's
  §10 log, never by rewriting earlier entries. Codebooks change only by human
  review: a draft is marked `DRAFT` until approved.
- **Gold labels come from people.** `scripts/ec_gold.py code --coder NAME`
  records the coder's name on every row. A second coder works on a copy of the
  sample (`--sample PATH`) so that both codings survive and agreement can be
  measured. No LLM labels (spec §9).
- **Write for the next reader.** The method doc for each corpus says what it
  does *not* answer, as plainly as what it does.

## Adding a dataset

1. Choose broad, verifiable, normalisable data, such as Epoch AI datasets, over
   hand-picked sensational sources. Hacker News is the only social forum.
2. Write `scripts/<name>.py` with `pin` (or `fetch`), `build` and `verify`, and
   pin the source in `corpus/<name>/MANIFEST.tsv` (URL, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3).
3. Write `corpus/<name>/README.md` (files and attribution) and
   `docs/<name>.md` (method and limits).
4. Respect source terms. A dataset whose terms bar AI ingestion is not
   fetched. Private individuals' text is stored as ids and hashes only (see the
   Hacker News corpus).
5. Add a row to `corpus/datasets.tsv`, run `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py`, and
   commit the deck with the data. `uv run scripts/datasets_md.py check` fails
   if the deck is stale.

## Where to look

- **Editing the paper** (`docs/anthropic-contrapunctus.md`): every hash pin moves
  with it. Run `uv run scripts/seal.py check --allow-unsealed`; README "Maintaining the seal".
- **Any model output** (BERT, NLI, embeddings, topics): read
  `docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md` §5 and §9 first. Models are *witnesses* whose
  output is a proposal in `proposals/`, never a verdict. Results are appended to
  that spec's §10 log, never edited into §§1–9.
- **Per-corpus method**: one doc per corpus in `docs/`, linked from `DATASETS.md`.

## Compute

**Compute is vendor-agnostic.** The scoring lives in `scripts/ec_classify.py`,
which runs on any machine: CUDA, Apple MPS or CPU. It can split the shards
across several machines (`--workers N --worker i`, then `--merge-only`).
Results are the same wherever they run, up to the documented bfloat16/float32
tolerance. Every run records its device, GPU, library versions and backend
tag, and runs from different hardware never merge silently.

Remote GPU wrappers are conveniences on top of that script, never
requirements. The maintainer uses Modal (`scripts/ec_classify_modal.py`,
through the local `modal` profile via `uvx`):

    uvx --with duckdb==2.0.0 --with blake3 modal run scripts/ec_classify_modal.py --model deberta

A wrapper for another provider (RunPod, a university cluster, k3s) follows the
same pattern. It imports `ec_classify`'s scoring functions, adds no logic of
its own, and tags its shards with its own `--backend`. Measured speeds and
costs are in `docs/earnings-call-ai-corpus.md` §9. To score another corpus or
codebook, pass `--units`, `--codebook`, `--id-col` and `--out`.

## Conventions

- **Deterministic.** No clock, host or random id enters any output; time is a
  recorded argument. A rebuild must be byte-identical, so check that by
  re-hashing.
- **Verbatim and anchored.** Stored text carries BLAKE3 and character offsets,
  and a `verify` command re-slices and re-hashes everything.
- **Pinned.** Scripts are `uv run` PEP 723 scripts with exact versions. Sources
  are pinned by revision and hash in a `MANIFEST.tsv`, and bulk bytes live in a
  gitignored dot-directory (`.eccorpus/`, `.hncorpus/`, ...) that the manifest
  can re-fetch. Where a source cannot be re-fetched byte-identically (Epoch
  bundles, API responses), the saved bytes are the pin.
- **Denominators.** Report a rate against every unit attempted (for example
  `calls.tsv`), and report coverage beside every finding.

## Gotchas

- `scripts/ec_classify_modal.py` must not use `from __future__ import annotations`:
  Modal reads `modal.parameter()` types at runtime.
- Modal methods return only plain Python types: the local side has no torch,
  so a torch object or exception (even `torch.__version__`) fails to unpickle
  after the GPU work is done. Shards are saved as they arrive, so rerunning
  only merges.
- Shards are tagged by model, dtype and backend, so runs on different hardware
  never merge, by design. To combine workers, pass the same `--backend`.
- Without `--out`, the classifier writes to `proposals/earnings-calls/<codebook stem>/`,
  which would overwrite earnings-call results when another corpus reuses a codebook.

#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["blake3==1.0.11"]
# ///
"""Signing records for each dataset, and SSH signatures over them.

The paper has its own attestation protocol (docs/contrapunctus-attest.md). This
is the same mechanism for the corpora: OpenSSH Ed25519 signatures
(`ssh-keygen -Y`), in a separate namespace, `anthropic-pbc-dataset`, so a
dataset signature can never be replayed as an endorsement of the paper.

A record lists, for one dataset in corpus/datasets.tsv:
  - the BLAKE3 of every committed file in its corpus folder;
  - the BLAKE3 of every script its refresh command runs;
  - what a signature over the record attests.
It holds no clock and no commit id, so it is a pure function of the files. When
any file changes, the record changes, and an old signature stops verifying: the
dataset shows as stale until someone re-signs.

    uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py record                 # write attestations/datasets/<id>.txt
    uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py sign --key ~/.ssh/KEY --signer "NAME"   # run by the signer
    uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py verify                 # exit 1 on a bad or stale signature
    uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py status                 # signed / unsigned / stale per dataset

`sign` runs `verify` for each dataset's own build first (`<script> verify`),
when the script has one, and refuses to sign a record that is not current.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import csv
import re
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import blake3

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
REGISTRY = ROOT / "corpus" / "datasets.tsv"
DIR = ROOT / "attestations" / "datasets"
ALLOWED = ROOT / "attestations" / "allowed_signers"
NAMESPACE = "anthropic-pbc-dataset"
STATEMENT = (
    "By signing this record, the signer attests that, when they signed: the files listed\n"
    "had exactly these BLAKE3 hashes; the dataset's own verify step (where it has one)\n"
    "passed; and the files are the output of the listed scripts run on the sources\n"
    "pinned in the dataset's MANIFEST.tsv. It does not attest that any finding drawn\n"
    "from the dataset is true, and it says nothing about model output in proposals/.\n")


def b3(p: Path) -> str:
    return blake3.blake3(p.read_bytes()).hexdigest()


def registry() -> list[dict[str, str]]:
    return [r for r in csv.DictReader(REGISTRY.open(), delimiter="\t") if r["corpus_dir"] != "—"]


def scripts_of(r: dict[str, str]) -> list[str]:
    return sorted(set(re.findall(r"scripts/[\w./-]+\.py", r["refresh"])))


def tracked(folder: str) -> list[str]:
    out = subprocess.run(["git", "ls-files", "-z", "--", folder], cwd=ROOT, capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
    return sorted(p for p in out.decode().split("\0") if p)


def render(r: dict[str, str]) -> str:
    lines = [f"namespace: {NAMESPACE}", f"dataset: {r['id']}", f"title: {r['title']}",
             f"pinned_as_of: {r['pinned_as_of']}", f"registry: corpus/datasets.tsv", "",
             STATEMENT, "files (BLAKE3, path):"]
    for p in tracked(r["corpus_dir"]):
        lines.append(f"{b3(ROOT / p)}  {p}")
    lines += ["", "scripts (BLAKE3, path):"]
    for p in scripts_of(r):
        lines.append(f"{b3(ROOT / p)}  {p}")
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"


def cmd_record(_a) -> int:
    DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for r in registry():
        (DIR / f"{r['id']}.txt").write_text(render(r))
    print(f"wrote {len(registry())} records to {DIR.relative_to(ROOT)}/")
    return 0


def status() -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """(dataset, signed | unsigned | stale | bad-signature)."""
    res = []
    for r in registry():
        rec, sig = DIR / f"{r['id']}.txt", DIR / f"{r['id']}.txt.sig"
        current = rec.exists() and rec.read_text() == render(r)
        if not sig.exists():
            res.append((r["id"], "unsigned" if current else "unsigned, record stale"))
            continue
        if not current:
            res.append((r["id"], "stale (files changed since signing)"))
            continue
        signer = sig.with_suffix(".signer").read_text().strip() if sig.with_suffix(".signer").exists() else ""
        ok = subprocess.run(["ssh-keygen", "-Y", "verify", "-f", str(ALLOWED), "-I", signer, "-n", NAMESPACE,
                             "-s", str(sig)], input=rec.read_bytes(), capture_output=True).returncode == 0
        res.append((r["id"], f"signed by {signer}" if ok else "bad signature"))
    return res


def cmd_status(_a) -> int:
    for d, s in status():
        print(f"{d:20} {s}")
    return 0


def cmd_verify(_a) -> int:
    bad = [(d, s) for d, s in status() if s.startswith(("stale", "bad"))]
    for d, s in bad:
        print(f"FAIL {d}: {s}")
    print("ok" if not bad else f"{len(bad)} dataset(s) failed")
    return 1 if bad else 0


def cmd_sign(a) -> int:
    if "\n" in a.signer or '"' in a.signer:
        sys.exit("signer name must be one line without quotes")
    key = Path(a.key).expanduser()
    pub = key.with_suffix(key.suffix + ".pub") if not key.name.endswith(".pub") else key
    if not pub.exists():
        sys.exit(f"no public key at {pub}")
    ids = [x for x in a.datasets] or [r["id"] for r in registry()]
    for r in registry():
        if r["id"] not in ids:
            continue
        rec = DIR / f"{r['id']}.txt"
        if not rec.exists() or rec.read_text() != render(r):
            sys.exit(f"{r['id']}: record is missing or stale; run `record` and commit it first")
        for s in scripts_of(r):
            src = (ROOT / s).read_text()
            if '"verify"' in src or "'verify'" in src:
                print(f"{r['id']}: {s} verify ...", flush=True)
                if subprocess.run(["uv", "run", s, "verify"], cwd=ROOT).returncode != 0:
                    sys.exit(f"{r['id']}: {s} verify failed; not signing")
        sig = rec.with_suffix(".txt.sig")
        sig.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        # ssh-keygen reads the private key itself (or the agent); no key material passes through here.
        if subprocess.run(["ssh-keygen", "-Y", "sign", "-f", str(key), "-n", NAMESPACE, str(rec)]).returncode != 0:
            sys.exit(f"{r['id']}: ssh-keygen sign failed")
        rec.with_suffix(".txt.signer").write_text(a.signer + "\n")
    # add the signer to allowed_signers once
    line = f'"{a.signer}" namespaces="{NAMESPACE}" ' + " ".join(pub.read_text().split()[:2])
    have = ALLOWED.read_text().splitlines() if ALLOWED.exists() else []
    if line not in have:
        ALLOWED.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        ALLOWED.write_text("\n".join(have + [line]) + "\n")
    return cmd_status(a)


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    sub.add_parser("record")
    sub.add_parser("status")
    sub.add_parser("verify")
    s = sub.add_parser("sign")
    s.add_argument("--key", required=True, help="path to your SSH private key (ssh-keygen reads it; agent keys work)")
    s.add_argument("--signer", required=True, help='name recorded in allowed_signers, e.g. "Sloane Ortel"')
    s.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", help="dataset ids (default: all)")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    return {"record": cmd_record, "status": cmd_status, "verify": cmd_verify, "sign": cmd_sign}[a.cmd](a)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

    for p in scripts_of(r):
        lines.append(f"{b3(ROOT / p)}  {p}")
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"


def cmd_record(_a) -> int:
    DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for r in registry():
        (DIR / f"{r['id']}.txt").write_text(render(r))
    print(f"wrote {len(registry())} records to {DIR.relative_to(ROOT)}/")
    return 0


def status() -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """(dataset, signed | unsigned | stale | bad-signature)."""
    res = []
    for r in registry():
        rec, sig = DIR / f"{r['id']}.txt", DIR / f"{r['id']}.txt.sig"
        current = rec.exists() and rec.read_text() == render(r)
        if not sig.exists():
            res.append((r["id"], "unsigned" if current else "unsigned, record stale"))
            continue
        if not current:
            res.append((r["id"], "stale (files changed since signing)"))
            continue
        signer = sig.with_suffix(".signer").read_text().strip() if sig.with_suffix(".signer").exists() else ""
        ok = subprocess.run(["ssh-keygen", "-Y", "verify", "-f", str(ALLOWED), "-I", signer, "-n", NAMESPACE,
                             "-s", str(sig)], input=rec.read_bytes(), capture_output=True).returncode == 0
        res.append((r["id"], f"signed by {signer}" if ok else "bad signature"))
    return res


def cmd_status(_a) -> int:
    for d, s in status():
        print(f"{d:20} {s}")
    return 0


def cmd_verify(_a) -> int:
    bad = [(d, s) for d, s in status() if s.startswith(("stale", "bad"))]
    for d, s in bad:
        print(f"FAIL {d}: {s}")
    print("ok" if not bad else f"{len(bad)} dataset(s) failed")
    return 1 if bad else 0


def cmd_sign(a) -> int:
    if "\n" in a.signer or '"' in a.signer:
        sys.exit("signer name must be one line without quotes")
    key = Path(a.key).expanduser()
    pub = key.with_suffix(key.suffix + ".pub") if not key.name.endswith(".pub") else key
    if not pub.exists():
        sys.exit(f"no public key at {pub}")
    ids = [x for x in a.datasets] or [r["id"] for r in registry()]
    for r in registry():
        if r["id"] not in ids:
            continue
        rec = DIR / f"{r['id']}.txt"
        if not rec.exists() or rec.read_text() != render(r):
            sys.exit(f"{r['id']}: record is missing or stale; run `record` and commit it first")
        for s in scripts_of(r):
            src = (ROOT / s).read_text()
            if '"verify"' in src or "'verify'" in src:
                print(f"{r['id']}: {s} verify ...", flush=True)
                if subprocess.run(["uv", "run", s, "verify"], cwd=ROOT).returncode != 0:
                    sys.exit(f"{r['id']}: {s} verify failed; not signing")
        sig = rec.with_suffix(".txt.sig")
        sig.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        # ssh-keygen reads the private key itself (or the agent); no key material passes through here.
        if subprocess.run(["ssh-keygen", "-Y", "sign", "-f", str(key), "-n", NAMESPACE, str(rec)]).returncode != 0:
            sys.exit(f"{r['id']}: ssh-keygen sign failed")
        rec.with_suffix(".txt.signer").write_text(a.signer + "\n")
    # add the signer to allowed_signers once
    line = f'"{a.signer}" namespaces="{NAMESPACE}" ' + " ".join(pub.read_text().split()[:2])
    have = ALLOWED.read_text().splitlines() if ALLOWED.exists() else []
    if line not in have:
        ALLOWED.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        ALLOWED.write_text("\n".join(have + [line]) + "\n")
    return cmd_status(a)


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    sub = ap.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    sub.add_parser("record")
    sub.add_parser("status")
    sub.add_parser("verify")
    s = sub.add_parser("sign")
    s.add_argument("--key", required=True, help="path to your SSH private key (ssh-keygen reads it; agent keys work)")
    s.add_argument("--signer", required=True, help='name recorded in allowed_signers, e.g. "Sloane Ortel"')
    s.add_argument("datasets", nargs="*", help="dataset ids (default: all)")
    a = ap.parse_args()
    return {"record": cmd_record, "status": cmd_status, "verify": cmd_verify, "sign": cmd_sign}[a.cmd](a)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Dataset attestations

One signing record per dataset in `datasets/<id>.txt`, written by
`uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py record`. A record lists the BLAKE3 of every
committed file in the dataset's corpus folder and of every script that builds
it, plus what a signature attests. It holds no clock and no commit id, so it
changes exactly when the files do.

Signatures are OpenSSH Ed25519 (`ssh-keygen -Y`), in the namespace
`anthropic-pbc-dataset`, which is separate from the paper's `contrapunctus`
namespace (`docs/contrapunctus-attest.md`). A dataset signature cannot be
replayed as an endorsement of the paper.

## Sign

    uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py record        # then commit the records
    uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py sign --key ~/.ssh/YOUR_KEY --signer "Your Name" [dataset ...]

`sign` refuses a record that is not current. It runs each dataset's own
`verify` first and stops if that fails. `ssh-keygen` reads the key itself, from
the file or from the agent. The signer's public key is added once to
`allowed_signers`. Commit the `.sig`, the `.signer` file and `allowed_signers`.

## Check

    uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py status    # signed / unsigned / stale per dataset
    uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py verify    # exit 1 on a stale or bad signature

A signature goes **stale** when any listed file changes. The dataset is then
unsigned in effect until someone re-signs the new record. `DATASETS.md` shows
each dataset's status.

To bind a key to a person or organization, publish the same public key
somewhere they control, as the paper's protocol asks.
