Signing is set up and committed (`4810456`, plus a one-line help-text fix in `38e337f`). Nothing is signed yet: that step needs your key.

**What the script does:**
- **Records:** `scripts/attest_datasets.py` writes one record per dataset into `attestations/datasets/`: the hash of every committed file and build script, and a short statement of what your signature means. It contains no date and no commit ID, so it changes exactly when the files change.
- **What your signature claims:** the files matched these hashes, the dataset's own `verify` passed, and the files came from the listed scripts run on the pinned sources. It does not vouch for any finding or any model output.
- **How it signs:** the same SSH method as the paper's protocol, but under its own label (`anthropic-pbc-dataset`), so a dataset signature can never pass as an endorsement of the paper.
- **Before signing:** it runs each dataset's `verify` and refuses to sign if that fails or if the record is out of date.
- **After any file change:** the signature shows as stale in `DATASETS.md` until you re-sign.

I tested the whole cycle with a throwaway key: it signed, verified, and flipped to stale after an edit. The test key and its signature are deleted, and nothing signed is committed.

**To sign everything,** run this at the prompt, with the `!` so the passphrase prompt comes to you. I'm assuming `id_ed25519`, but use whichever key you want tied to this; the name is how it will appear publicly.

```
! cd ~/dev/anthropic-pbc && uv run scripts/attest_datasets.py sign --key ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 --signer "YOUR NAME"
```

It runs every dataset's `verify` first, and the earnings-call one takes a few minutes. Afterwards I'll commit the signatures and `attestations/allowed_signers`. To tie the key to you, publish the same public key somewhere you control, for example on ethicic.com.

Still open in `OPENQUESTIONS.md` Q1: which key you use, and whether to sign git commits too. The v0.2 codebook scoring and the health-of-democracy agent are still running.

      "text": "# URI¶

We use Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs) throughout all the ETL to identify files and datasets. The format of a URI varies depending on the ETL step we are dealing with, but in general they follow the following convention:

```
<prefix>://<path>
```

## Prefix¶

Most of the time, the prefix will either be `snapshot` or `data`. The former is used for snapshots of upstream dat files, and the latter for ETL datasets (with different levels of curation).

| Prefix | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `snapshot` | Used for `snapshot` steps. |
| `data` | Used for `meadow`, `garden`, `grapher` and most of the ETL steps where we operate with curated Datasets. |
| `backport` | Used to import datasets from the OWID database that are not present in the ETL. |

## Path¶

The format of the path is different depending on the prefix.

### Path for `snapshot://`¶

```
snapshot://<namespace>/<version>/<filename>.<extension>
```

where

| Prefix | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `namespace` | Used to group files from similar topics or sources. Namespace are typically source names (e.g. `un`) or topic names (e.g. `health`). |
| `version` | Version of the file. Typically, we use the date the file was downloaded in the format `YYYY-mm-dd`. |
| `filename` | Name of the downloaded file. |
| `extension` | Extension of the file. |

Example

```
snapshot://ember/2023-02-20/yearly_electricity.csv
```

### Path for `data://`¶

```
data://<channel>/<namespace>/<version>/<dataset-name>
```

where

| Prefix | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `channel` | Denotes the curation level of the dataset. Possible values include `meadow`, `garden`, `grapher`, `explorers`. |
| `namespace` | Used to group datasets from similar topics or sources. Namespace are typically source names (e.g. `un`) or topic names (e.g. `health`). |
| `version` | Version of the file. Typically, we use the date the file was downloaded in the format `YYYY-mm-dd`. |
| `dataset-name` | Short name of the curated dataset (e.g. `un_wpp`). |

Examples

* **Meadow**: `data://meadow/nasa/2023-03-06/ozone_hole_area`
* **Garden**: `data://garden/nasa/2023-03-06/ozone_hole_area`
* **Grapher**: `data://grapher/nasa/2023-03-06/ozone_hole_area`
* **Explorers**: `data://explorers/faostat/2023-02-22/food_explorer`

      "text": "# ETL steps¶

We have designed an ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) system that allows us to manage the entire lifecycle of data, from ingestion to publication.

There are four main types of ETL steps: snapshots (ingest data from source), data steps (process and curate data), viz steps (produce visualizations: charts, explorers, static images) and export steps (make data available to other parts of the system). We elaborate on these below.

## Five stages¶

The ETL project provides an opinionated data management workflow, which separates a data manager's work into five stages:

```
graph LR

snapshot --> format --> harmonize/process --> import --> publish
```

The design of the ETL involves steps that mirror the stages above, which help us to meet several design goals of the project:

1. Snapshot step: Take a **snapshot** of the upstream data product and store it.
2. Meadow step: Bring the data into a **common format**.
3. Garden step: **Harmonise** the names of countries, genders and any other columns we may want to join on. Also do the necessary **data processing** to make the dataset usable for our needs.
4. Grapher step: **Adapt** the data to our internal MySQL database.
5. Export step: **Publish** the data to other parts of the system, such as data explorers or multi-dimensional indicators.

A data manager must implement all these steps to make something chartable on the Our World in Data site.

Info

When all steps (1 to 4) are implemented, the data is available for publication on our site. The publication step can involve creating new charts or updating existing ones with the new data.

Note that there are other steps, which are used only in specific cases.

## Snapshot¶

The initial step consists in **transferring an external file from an upstream producer into our platform**. This ensures, that the source data is always accessible. This is because the upstream producer might remove the file at any time, or change it.

Snapshot steps are executed with command `etls`

The accompanying diagram illustrates the process of importing various versions of the same dataset into our snapshot catalog, depicted over time. Imagine that the vertical axis represents time.

```
flowchart LR

    upstream1((   )):::node -.->|copy| snapshot1((v1)):::node_ss
    upstream2((   )):::node -.->|copy| snapshot2((v2)):::node_ss

    subgraph id0 [Upstream]
    upstream1
    upstream2
    end

    subgraph id [Snapshot]
    snapshot1
    snapshot2
    end

    classDef node fill:#002147,color:#002147
    classDef node_ss fill:#002147,color:#fff
```

The snapshot step typically consists of a DVC file and a script that downloads the upstream data and saves it to our snapshot catalog. Snapshot files are located in the  `snapshots/` directory of the project.

Note that we need a DVC file per upstream data file; hence, in some instances, if the source publishes a dataset using multiple files, we need multiple DVC files.

### Snapshot metadata¶

A Snapshot is a picture of a data product (e.g. a data CSV file) provided by an upstream data producer at a particular point in time. It is the entrypoint to ETL and where we define metadata attributes of that picture. This is fundamental to ensure that the data is properly documented and that the metadata is propagated to the rest of the system.

The metadata in Snapshot consists mainly of one object: `meta.origin`.

Learn more in our metadata reference.

This metadata is captured in a DVC file (similar to a YAML file), which contains all the snapshot metadata fields as key-value pairs.

This file specifies all the upstream source file details (including link to download it, metadata fields, etc.). Filling the fields of this file requires some manual work, as we are "translating" all the information that the source provides into our snaphsot metadata format.

snapshots/animal\_welfare/2024-12-17/fur\_laws.csv.dvc

```
meta:
    origin:
        title: Fur banning
        description: |-
        Legal status of fur farming around the world.
        producer: Fur Free Alliance
        citation_full: Overview national fur legislation, Fur Free Alliance (2024).
        url_main: https://www.furfreealliance.com/fur-bans/
        date_published: 2024-12-17
        date_accessed: 2024-12-17
        license:
        name: CC BY 4.0
        url: https://www.furfreealliance.com/fur-bans/
    outs:
    - md5: 6b46a8a465453c383e6ffda96deb1d2f
        size: 44197
        path: fur_laws.csv
```

## Data steps¶

There are different kinds of data steps, depending on the stage of data curation: `meadow`, `garden` and `grapher`.

Data steps are executed with command `etlr`

### Meadow¶

The meadow step is the first Transform step of our ETL. In it, we load a `Snapshot` and adapt it to be in a convenient format. A convenient format means creating an instance of a `Dataset`, with the appropriate data as a `Table` (or tables).

In this step, you can add and define metadata, but we rarely do this. Instead, we propagate the metadata defined in the Snapshot step and leave it to the Garden step to enhance the metadata.

Meadow steps should only have `snapshot` dependencies and ー by definition ー should not depend on `garden` or any other steps.

### Garden¶

The Garden step is where most of the work falls in. This is where the data manager needs to carefully look at the data, filter outliers, harmonize labels (e.g. country names), improve the dataset metadata, etc.

Garden steps typically depend on meadow steps. For instance, the Garden step `data://garden/un/2024-07-12/un_wpp`, which generates the dataset *World Population Prospects (UN, 2024)*, depends on this same process but in Meadow (i.e. `data://meadow/un/2024-07-12/un_wpp`). After some pre-liminary work (mostly re-formating tables, and some minor cleaning), we can now focus on more complex processing steps in Garden.

A typical flow up to the Garden step could look like:

```
flowchart LR

    upstream1((   )):::node -.->|copy| snapshot1((   )):::node
    snapshot1((   )):::node -->|format| meadow1((   )):::node
    meadow1((   )):::node -->|process| garden1((   )):::node

    subgraph id0 [Upstream]
    upstream1
    end

    subgraph id1 [Snapshot]
    snapshot1
    end

    subgraph id2 [Meadow]
    meadow1
    end

    subgraph id3 [Garden]
    garden1
    end

    subgraph id [ETL]
    id1
    id2
    id3
    end

    classDef node fill:#002147,color:#002147
    classDef node_ss fill:#002147,color:#fff
```

However, Garden steps could also depend on other garden steps. This is often the case for datasets containing *long-run indicators*, or just in general when different `garden` datasets are combined.

Long-run indicators

A long-run indicator is an indicator that has datapoints spanning over a broad period of time and that typically relies on multiple sources.

For instance, we have a  population indicator that combines data from the UN and other sources that goes back to 10,000 BCE. In particular, it uses data from the UN, Gapminder and HYDE.

This is how the dependency graph our population indicator looks like:

```
  data://garden/demography/2023-03-31/population:
   - data://garden/hyde/2017/baseline
   - data://garden/gapminder/2023-03-31/population
   - data://garden/un/2022-07-11/un_wpp
   - data://open_numbers/open_numbers/latest/gapminder__systema_globalis
```

An important processing step in Garden is to standardize (or harmonize) the country names. You can learn more about this in our country harmonization guide.

#### Garden metadata¶

After adapting and processing the origin's data, we have a curated dataset. This dataset, contains indicators (maybe not present in the origin) that we need to properly document.

The metadata in Garden consists mainly of two objects: `Dataset` and a list of `Table`, which contains various `Indicator` columns. The metadata comes as a YAML file next to the processing scripts.

### Grapher¶

In the Grapher step the work should be minimal. Here, we create a `Grapher` view by adapting our Garden dataset to adhere to the Grapher requirements.

Grapher views are still normal datasets, but they adapt the data to the way it must look when being inserted into MySQL. For each grapher view, there is a corresponding matching `grapher://` step automatically generated which does the actual insert to MySQL, if MySQL credentials have been configured.

A typical flow up to the Grapher step could look like:

```
flowchart LR

    upstream1((   )):::node -.->|copy| snapshot1((   )):::node
    snapshot1((   )):::node -->|format| meadow1((   )):::node
    meadow1((   )):::node -->|harmonize| garden1((   )):::node
    garden1((   )):::node -->|format| grapher1((   )):::node
    grapher1((   )):::node -->|load| grapher2((   )):::node

    subgraph id0 [Upstream]
    upstream1
    end

    subgraph id1 [Snapshot]
    snapshot1
    end

    subgraph id2 [Meadow]
    meadow1
    end

    subgraph id3 [Garden]
    garden1
    end

    subgraph id4 [Grapher]
    grapher1
    end

    subgraph id5 [Grapher]
    grapher2
    end

    subgraph id [ETL]
    id1
    id2
    id3
    id4
    end

    classDef node fill:#002147,color:#002147
    classDef node_ss fill:#002147,color:#fff
```

In principle, a Grapher step only loads a single garden step.

Note that the diagram shows a final step outside of the ETL. This is when the `grapher://` step is executed, and takes data from the ETL (from the etl `garden` step) and imports it to our database.

## Viz and export steps¶

Sometimes we want to perform an action instead of creating a dataset. For instance, we might want to create the config of a chart or a multi-dimensional indicator, create an explorer, render a static image, or commit a CSV to a GitHub repository. This is where the `viz://` and `export://` steps come in.

A step's type says what it produces. Viz steps produce visualizations, and their channel says which kind:

* **Charts and multi-dimensional indicators** (`viz://chart/`): Create the configuration of a chart or an MDIM and upsert it to the grapher DB.
* **Explorers** (`viz://explorer/`): Create a data explorer and upsert it to the grapher DB.
* **Static images** (`viz://static/`): Render a PNG/SVG with matplotlib next to the recipe.
* **Bespoke visualizations** (`viz://bespoke/`): Produce the data feed of a bespoke interactive visualization. The step writes JSON files into its output folder and the framework syncs them to R2, under the path of the environment being built.

Viz steps publish with `--grapher`. Named by their URI they also run without it, in which case they only build locally (the chart config, the data feed) and skip the DB upsert or upload; a pattern such as `energy` selects them only with the flag.

Export steps ship files to an external destination, e.g. **Export to GitHub** (`export://github/`) commits a dataset to a GitHub repository, and `export://s3/` uploads files to R2. Run with `--export`.

Both kinds of steps should be used after the data has been processed and is ready to be used (post-Garden).

Learn more about viz and export steps

### MDIMs and explorers¶

This space is very new and in development

MDIMs (`viz://chart/`) and explorers (`viz://explorer/`) are Grapher charts expanded with additional functionalities to facilitate exploration, such as dynamic entity filters or customizable menus. They are usually powered by indicators from OWID's Grapher database.

In ETL, both are defined as a `Chart` config: the dimensions a reader can select, and the views (indicator selections) each combination points to. The step upserts that config to the database. Having chart and explorer steps in the DAG lets us track their dependencies and keep them up to date.

These steps must depend only on `data://grapher` steps, since they require indicators to be in the Database. This is because explorers and multidims on the site access indicators in the database.

Learn more about creating Data explorers on  Notion.

Legacy explorers

In the past Explorers were manually defined from our Admin. Data was sourced by CSV files generated by ETL  served from S3, or on GitHub.

We have slowly transitioned into a new system where explorers are generated from the ETL pipeline. This is a more scalable and maintainable solution.",

```

```

## Prefix¶

Most of the time, the prefix will either be `snapshot` or `data`. The former is used for snapshots of upstream dat files, and the latter for ETL datasets (with different levels of curation).

| Prefix | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `snapshot` | Used for `snapshot` steps. |
| `data` | Used for `meadow`, `garden`, `grapher` and most of the ETL steps where we operate with curated Datasets. |
| `backport` | Used to import datasets from the OWID database that are not present in the ETL. |

### Path for `snapshot://`¶


| --- | --- |

| `version` | Version of the file. Typically, we use the date the file was downloaded in the format `YYYY-mm-dd`. |
| `filename` | Name of the downloaded file. |
| `extension` | Extension of the file. |

```

```

      "text": "# ETL steps¶

We have designed an ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) system that allows us to manage the entire lifecycle of data, from ingestion to publication.

There are four main types of ETL steps: snapshots (ingest data from source), data steps (process and curate data), viz steps (produce visualizations: charts, explorers, static images) and export steps (make data available to other parts of the system). We elaborate on these below.

## Five stages¶

The ETL project provides an opinionated data management workflow, which separates a data manager's work into five stages:

```
graph LR

snapshot --> format --> harmonize/process --> import --> publish
```

The design of the ETL involves steps that mirror the stages above, which help us to meet several design goals of the project:

1. Snapshot step: Take a **snapshot** of the upstream data product and store it.
2. Meadow step: Bring the data into a **common format**.
3. Garden step: **Harmonise** the names of countries, genders and any other columns we may want to join on. Also do the necessary **data processing** to make the dataset usable for our needs.
4. Grapher step: **Adapt** the data to our internal MySQL database.
5. Export step: **Publish** the data to other parts of the system, such as data explorers or multi-dimensional indicators.

A data manager must implement all these steps to make something chartable on the Our World in Data site.

Info

When all steps (1 to 4) are implemented, the data is available for publication on our site. The publication step can involve creating new charts or updating existing ones with the new data.

Note that there are other steps, which are used only in specific cases.

## Snapshot¶

The initial step consists in **transferring an external file from an upstream producer into our platform**. This ensures, that the source data is always accessible. This is because the upstream producer might remove the file at any time, or change it.

Snapshot steps are executed with command `etls`

The accompanying diagram illustrates the process of importing various versions of the same dataset into our snapshot catalog, depicted over time. Imagine that the vertical axis represents time.

```
flowchart LR

    upstream1((   )):::node -.->|copy| snapshot1((v1)):::node_ss
    upstream2((   )):::node -.->|copy| snapshot2((v2)):::node_ss

    subgraph id0 [Upstream]
    upstream1
    upstream2
    end

    subgraph id [Snapshot]
    snapshot1
    snapshot2
    end

    classDef node fill:#002147,color:#002147
    classDef node_ss fill:#002147,color:#fff
```

The snapshot step typically consists of a DVC file and a script that downloads the upstream data and saves it to our snapshot catalog. Snapshot files are located in the  `snapshots/` directory of the project.

Note that we need a DVC file per upstream data file; hence, in some instances, if the source publishes a dataset using multiple files, we need multiple DVC files.

### Snapshot metadata¶

A Snapshot is a picture of a data product (e.g. a data CSV file) provided by an upstream data producer at a particular point in time. It is the entrypoint to ETL and where we define metadata attributes of that picture. This is fundamental to ensure that the data is properly documented and that the metadata is propagated to the rest of the system.

The metadata in Snapshot consists mainly of one object: `meta.origin`.

Learn more in our metadata reference.

This metadata is captured in a DVC file (similar to a YAML file), which contains all the snapshot metadata fields as key-value pairs.

This file specifies all the upstream source file details (including link to download it, metadata fields, etc.). Filling the fields of this file requires some manual work, as we are "translating" all the information that the source provides into our snaphsot metadata format.

```
    origin:
        title: Fur banning
        description: |-
        Legal status of fur farming around the world.
        producer: Fur Free Alliance
        citation_full: Overview national fur legislation, Fur Free Alliance (2024).

```

## Data steps¶

There are different kinds of data steps, depending on the stage of data curation: `meadow`, `garden` and `grapher`.

Data steps are executed with command `etlr`

### Meadow¶

The meadow step is the first Transform step of our ETL. In it, we load a `Snapshot` and adapt it to be in a convenient format. A convenient format means creating an instance of a `Dataset`, with the appropriate data as a `Table` (or tables).

In this step, you can add and define metadata, but we rarely do this. Instead, we propagate the metadata defined in the Snapshot step and leave it to the Garden step to enhance the metadata.

Meadow steps should only have `snapshot` dependencies and ー by definition ー should not depend on `garden` or any other steps.

### Garden¶

The Garden step is where most of the work falls in. This is where the data manager needs to carefully look at the data, filter outliers, harmonize labels (e.g. country names), improve the dataset metadata, etc.

Garden steps typically depend on meadow steps. For instance, the Garden step `data://garden/un/2024-07-12/un_wpp`, which generates the dataset *World Population Prospects (UN, 2024)*, depends on this same process but in Meadow (i.e. `data://meadow/un/2024-07-12/un_wpp`). After some pre-liminary work (mostly re-formating tables, and some minor cleaning), we can now focus on more complex processing steps in Garden.

A typical flow up to the Garden step could look like:

```

    upstream1((   )):::node -.->|copy| snapshot1((   )):::node

    id2
    id3
    end

    classDef node_ss fill:#002147,color:#fff
```

However, Garden steps could also depend on other garden steps. This is often the case for datasets containing *long-run indicators*, or just in general when different `garden` datasets are combined.

Long-run indicators

A long-run indicator is an indicator that has datapoints spanning over a broad period of time and that typically relies on multiple sources.

For instance, we have a  population indicator that combines data from the UN and other sources that goes back to 10,000 BCE. In particular, it uses data from the UN, Gapminder and HYDE.

This is how the dependency graph our population indicator looks like:

```
  data://garden/demography/2023-03-31/population:
   - data://garden/hyde/2017/baseline

   - data://garden/un/2022-07-11/un_wpp

```

An important processing step in Garden is to standardize (or harmonize) the country names. You can learn more about this in our country harmonization guide.

#### Garden metadata¶

After adapting and processing the origin's data, we have a curated dataset. This dataset, contains indicators (maybe not present in the origin) that we need to properly document.

The metadata in Garden consists mainly of two objects: `Dataset` and a list of `Table`, which contains various `Indicator` columns. The metadata comes as a YAML file next to the processing scripts.

### Grapher¶

In the Grapher step the work should be minimal. Here, we create a `Grapher` view by adapting our Garden dataset to adhere to the Grapher requirements.

Grapher views are still normal datasets, but they adapt the data to the way it must look when being inserted into MySQL. For each grapher view, there is a corresponding matching `grapher://` step automatically generated which does the actual insert to MySQL, if MySQL credentials have been configured.

A typical flow up to the Grapher step could look like:

```

    upstream1((   )):::node -.->|copy| snapshot1((   )):::node
    snapshot1((   )):::node -->|format| meadow1((   )):::node
    meadow1((   )):::node -->|harmonize| garden1((   )):::node

    garden1
```

In principle, a Grapher step only loads a single garden step.

Note that the diagram shows a final step outside of the ETL. This is when the `grapher://` step is executed, and takes data from the ETL (from the etl `garden` step) and imports it to our database.

## Viz and export steps¶

Sometimes we want to perform an action instead of creating a dataset. For instance, we might want to create the config of a chart or a multi-dimensional indicator, create an explorer, render a static image, or commit a CSV to a GitHub repository. This is where the `viz://` and `export://` steps come in.

A step's type says what it produces. Viz steps produce visualizations, and their channel says which kind:

* **Charts and multi-dimensional indicators** (`viz://chart/`): Create the configuration of a chart or an MDIM and upsert it to the grapher DB.
* **Explorers** (`viz://explorer/`): Create a data explorer and upsert it to the grapher DB.
* **Static images** (`viz://static/`): Render a PNG/SVG with matplotlib next to the recipe.
* **Bespoke visualizations** (`viz://bespoke/`): Produce the data feed of a bespoke interactive visualization. The step writes JSON files into its output folder and the framework syncs them to R2, under the path of the environment being built.

Viz steps publish with `--grapher`. Named by their URI they also run without it, in which case they only build locally (the chart config, the data feed) and skip the DB upsert or upload; a pattern such as `energy` selects them only with the flag.

Export steps ship files to an external destination, e.g. **Export to GitHub** (`export://github/`) commits a dataset to a GitHub repository, and `export://s3/` uploads files to R2. Run with `--export`.

Both kinds of steps should be used after the data has been processed and is ready to be used (post-Garden).

Learn more about viz and export steps

### MDIMs and explorers¶

This space is very new and in development

MDIMs (`viz://chart/`) and explorers (`viz://explorer/`) are Grapher charts expanded with additional functionalities to facilitate exploration, such as dynamic entity filters or customizable menus. They are usually powered by indicators from OWID's Grapher database.

These steps must depend only on `data://grapher` steps, since they require indicators to be in the Database. This is because explorers and multidims on the site access indicators in the database.

Learn more about creating Data explorers on  Notion.

Legacy explorers

In the past Explorers were manually defined from our Admin. Data was sourced by CSV files generated by ETL  served from S3, or on GitHub.

# Compute graph of every dataset step in this repository.
#
# Modelled on Our World in Data's ETL
# (https://docs.owid.io/projects/etl/architecture/design/compute-graph/): each
# step is a node named by a URI, and an edge means "depends on". When a node
# changes, every node downstream of it is stale. `uv run scripts/dag.py status`
# computes that from content hashes; nothing here reads a clock.
#
# URIs follow OWID's convention:
#   snapshot://<namespace>/<version>/<name>          an upstream copy, pinned in a MANIFEST
#   data://<channel>/<namespace>/<version>/<name>    a dataset built from other steps
#   viz://static/<namespace>/<version>/<name>        a chart
# version is the pin date (YYYY-MM-DD), or the codebook version for hand-written codebooks.
#
# Channels:
#   meadow   OWID's: the source in a common format. Here, the verbatim, byte-anchored
#            extraction (windows, questions, ids, inventories).
#   garden   OWID's: processed and harmonised. Here, counts and joins built
#            deterministically from meadow (no model).
#   witness  OUR EXTENSION, not in OWID: model output (NLI scores, topics). A
#            proposal under docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md §5, never a finding. Steps that
#            read witness output stay proposals too.
#
# Paths are unchanged from before the graph existed; the URI names a step and
# `outputs` says where it writes. `cmd` documents how to rebuild; any compute
# backend may run witness steps (see AGENTS.md "Compute").

steps:
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------- snapshots
  snapshot://defeatbeta/2026-11-04/stock_earning_call_transcripts:
    cmd: uv run scripts/ec_extract.py fetch
    outputs: [corpus/earnings-calls/MANIFEST.tsv]
  snapshot://wikipedia/2026-10-27/sp500_constituents:
    cmd: uv run scripts/ec_extract.py constituents
    deps: [snapshot://defeatbeta/2026-11-04/stock_earning_call_transcripts]   # shares MANIFEST.tsv
    outputs: [corpus/earnings-calls/sp500-constituents.tsv]
  snapshot://open_index/2026-08-31/hacker_news:
    cmd: uv run scripts/hn_extract.py pin && uv run scripts/hn_extract.py fetch
    outputs: [corpus/hacker-news/MANIFEST.tsv]

# Compute graph of every dataset step in this repository.
#
# Modelled on Our World in Data's ETL
# (https://docs.owid.io/projects/etl/architecture/design/compute-graph/): each
# step is a node named by a URI, and an edge means "depends on". When a node
# changes, every node downstream of it is stale. `uv run scripts/dag.py status`
# computes that from content hashes; nothing here reads a clock.
#
# URIs follow OWID's convention:
#   snapshot://<namespace>/<version>/<name>          an upstream copy, pinned in a MANIFEST
#   data://<channel>/<namespace>/<version>/<name>    a dataset built from other steps
#   viz://static/<namespace>/<version>/<name>        a chart
# version is the pin date (YYYY-MM-DD), or the codebook version for hand-written codebooks.
#
# Channels:
#   meadow   OWID's: the source in a common format. Here, the verbatim, byte-anchored
#            extraction (windows, questions, ids, inventories).
#   garden   OWID's: processed and harmonised. Here, counts and joins built
#            deterministically from meadow (no model).
#   witness  OUR EXTENSION, not in OWID: model output (NLI scores, topics). A
#            proposal under docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md §5, never a finding. Steps that
#            read witness output stay proposals too.
#
# Paths are unchanged from before the graph existed; the URI names a step and
# `outputs` says where it writes. `cmd` documents how to rebuild; any compute
# backend may run witness steps (see AGENTS.md "Compute").

# step is a node named by a URI, and an edge means "depends on". When a node
# changes, every node downstream of it is stale. `uv run scripts/dag.py status`
# computes that from content hashes; nothing here reads a clock.
#
# URIs follow OWID's convention:
#   snapshot://<namespace>/<version>/<name>          an upstream copy, pinned in a MANIFEST
#   data://<channel>/<namespace>/<version>/<name>    a dataset built from other steps
#   viz://static/<namespace>/<version>/<name>        a chart
# version is the pin date (YYYY-MM-DD), or the codebook version for hand-written codebooks.
#
# Channels:
#   meadow   OWID's: the source in a common format. Here, the verbatim, byte-anchored
#            extraction (windows, questions, ids, inventories).
#   garden   OWID's: processed and harmonised. Here, counts and joins built
#            deterministically from meadow (no model).
#   witness  OUR EXTENSION, not in OWID: model output (NLI scores, topics). A
#            proposal under docs/bert-enrichment-spec.md §5, never a finding. Steps that
#            read witness output stay proposals too.

the whole graph's status.

EOF

The repo now follows OWID's compute-graph design. It's committed as `e83412f`, and every file stays where it was.

**What lines up with OWID:**
- **Step names.** Every dataset step has an OWID-style address: `snapshot://namespace/version/name` for upstream copies, and `data://channel/namespace/version/name` for built data. For example:
  - `snapshot://open_index/2026-08-31/hacker_news`
  - `data://meadow/earnings_calls/2026-11-04/ai_questions`
- **Channels.** Meadow is the verbatim extraction, and garden is deterministic counts and joins. I added one channel OWID doesn't have, `witness`, for model output. That builds the "a model's output is a proposal, not a finding" rule into the graph itself: anything reading witness output is visibly downstream of a model.
- **The graph.** `dag.yml` lists 26 steps, each with its build command, dependencies and outputs. It covers the earnings calls, Hacker News, Wikipedia, CVE, Epoch and the codebooks.
- **What needs rebuilding.** As in OWID, a change anywhere marks everything downstream as stale. Here it's detected from file contents, not timestamps. `scripts/dag.py` does four things:
  - `check`: confirms the graph has no cycles and every script and output exists
  - `lock`: records the current state in `dag.lock.tsv`
  - `status`: shows what's out of date
  - `plan`: prints the rebuild commands in order
- **Tested.** I edited the HN extraction script as a test. That flagged the HN snapshot and extraction steps as needing a rebuild, and the scoring and report steps below them as stale. I then reverted the edit and everything was back to ok.
- **In the deck.** `DATASETS.md` shows each dataset's steps and their status, plus a slide for the whole graph. AGENTS.md tells contributors to add steps to the graph and to cite data by step address in the docs.

**What doesn't line up yet:**
- **No files moved.** OWID organizes folders by step. Ours keep their old paths, which the hash pins and other sessions' work reference; the step address names the step and lists where it writes.
- **Source metadata.** OWID records producer, full citation, main URL, date published and date accessed for every snapshot. We have most of that spread across the MANIFESTs and the registry, but not in its fields. I can adopt those fields next, starting from Epoch's citations, which are already captured.
- **Codebooks.** They're written in this repo, so I modelled them as snapshots with an author but no upstream source. That's a slight stretch of OWID's terms.
- **Pending steps.** The v0.2 codebook scoring and the health-of-democracy work will get their own steps when they land.

The signing command is ready whenever you want to run it. Signing runs each dataset's own `verify` first, and the graph's status is also in the deck.

# Plan: regroup by the compute graph, with strict metadata

Status: PLAN · 2026-11-04. Requested by Sloane: regroup the repository along
OWID's ETL design (https://docs.owid.io/projects/etl/architecture/design/compute-graph/)
and be "ultra, ultra rigorous" about metadata.

## Goal

1. Every step in `dag.yml` lives at a path derived from its URI.
2. Every step carries complete metadata, and a missing field fails the build.

A reader holding any file can tell, from the file alone, what it is, where it
came from, how it was made, what each column means, and under what license.

## 1. Layout

OWID derives paths from URIs. We do the same:

| URI | Committed path | Bulk bytes (gitignored) |
|---|---|---|
| `snapshot://ns/version/name` | `snapshots/ns/version/name.meta.yml` and the MANIFEST | `.snapshots/ns/version/name/` |
| `data://meadow/ns/version/name` | `data/meadow/ns/version/name/` | `.data/meadow/...` for local-only text |
| `data://garden/ns/version/name` | `data/garden/ns/version/name/` | |
| `data://witness/ns/version/name` | `data/witness/ns/version/name/` (was `proposals/`) | shards |
| `data://gold/ns/version/name` | `data/gold/ns/version/name/` (was `gold/`) | |

`gold` is a new channel: human labels. It is never written by a model.

What changes:
- `corpus/`, `proposals/` and `gold/` are replaced.
- The dot-directories (`.eccorpus/`, `.hncorpus/`, ...) collapse into
  `.snapshots/` and `.data/`.

What stays:
- Scripts stay in `scripts/` and are named by `cmd` in each step. Splitting
  them per step, as OWID's `etl/steps/` does, can come later; it buys little
  while one script builds several steps.
- `docs/` stays as it is.
- The paper, `index.html`, and the seal and its hash pins are untouched; none
  of them reference these paths.

A compatibility note in each old folder's README points to the new path for
one release.

## 2. Metadata: required fields, enforced

The schema follows OWID's metadata reference (origin → dataset → table →
indicator) and adds fields this repository needs: hashes, witness status, and
what a dataset does not answer.

**Snapshot origin** (`<name>.meta.yml`). Every field is required, or `null`
with a `reason:`.
- `producer`, `title`, `description`
- `citation_full`, `attribution_short`
- `url_main`, `url_download`
- `date_published`, `date_accessed`, `version_producer`
- `license: {name, url}`, `terms_notes`: for example, YouGov's no-AI-ingestion
  notice, or third-party benchmark tables that keep their own licences
- `files`: path, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3. This absorbs the MANIFEST.
- `refetch`: `exact` | `saved_bytes_are_pin`, with the reason
- `personal_data`: `none` | `ids_only` | `verbatim_public_figures` | ...

**Dataset** (`<name>.meta.yml` beside the outputs):
- `title`, `description`, `channel`, `uri`
- `origins`: the snapshot URIs, resolved transitively
- `processing`: what the step does, in plain sentences, and what it drops
- `unit_of_analysis`, `denominator`: which file holds it
- `coverage`: dates, universe, known gaps
- `does_not_answer`: required; it may not be empty
- `license`: derived from the origins, the most restrictive wins
- `status`: held | witness | gold
- for `witness`: `model`, `revision`, `codebook`, and `proposal_only: true`

**Table** (one entry per output file):
- `title`, `description`, `primary_key`, `rows`
- `columns`, one entry for **every** column:
  - `title`, `description`, `type`, `unit`
  - for verbatim text: `verbatim: true`
  - for a hash column: `hash_of`
  - for a code column: `values`

**Enforcement** (`uv run scripts/dag.py check`). It fails when:
- a required field is missing or empty;
- a column in the file is not documented, or a documented column is not in the
  file;
- a hash in the metadata does not match the file;
- a `witness` dataset lacks `proposal_only: true`, or a non-witness step depends
  on a witness step without being marked a proposal;
- a license is weaker than an origin's.

Row counts and hashes are written by the build, never by hand. Descriptions
are written by hand and reviewed like code.

`DATASETS.md` renders all of this, so the deck becomes the human view of the
metadata.

## 3. Phases (one commit each, each verified)

1. **Schema and validator.** Write `schema/metadata.schema.yml`. Add checks to
   `dag.py check` that report missing metadata without failing yet, so we can
   see the gap.
2. **Metadata backfill.** One dataset per commit, starting with CVE and Epoch
   (smallest), then Wikipedia, Hacker News and the earnings calls. Columns are
   introspected from the files; descriptions are written and checked against
   the method docs.
3. **Regroup.** Wait until the v0.2 scoring and the democracy work have landed.
   Then `git mv` everything to the URI paths, in one commit per dataset:
   - update script constants and the graph's outputs;
   - rebuild, check byte-identical, `verify`, `dag.py lock`, re-record the
     attestations.
4. **Strict.** Flip `check` to fail on any gap, and add it to the
   collaboration rules in AGENTS.md.
5. **Signing.** Sloane signs once the layout is final. Signatures taken before
   the regroup would go stale on the move.

## Open decisions (also in OPENQUESTIONS.md)

- Whether `snapshots/` keeps a TSV MANIFEST beside the YAML for grep-ability
  (proposed: yes, generated from the YAML).
- Whether scripts split into per-step files now or later (proposed: later).

input.content:
# Plan: regroup by the compute graph, with strict metadata

Status: PLAN · 2026-11-04. Requested by Sloane: regroup the repository along
OWID's ETL design (https://docs.owid.io/projects/etl/architecture/design/compute-graph/)
and be "ultra, ultra rigorous" about metadata.

## Goal

1. Every step in `dag.yml` lives at a path derived from its URI.
2. Every step carries complete metadata, and a missing field fails the build.

A reader holding any file can tell, from the file alone, what it is, where it
came from, how it was made, what each column means, and under what license.

## 1. Layout

OWID derives paths from URIs. We do the same:

| URI | Committed path | Bulk bytes (gitignored) |
|---|---|---|
| `snapshot://ns/version/name` | `snapshots/ns/version/name.meta.yml` and the MANIFEST | `.snapshots/ns/version/name/` |
| `data://meadow/ns/version/name` | `data/meadow/ns/version/name/` | `.data/meadow/...` for local-only text |
| `data://garden/ns/version/name` | `data/garden/ns/version/name/` | |
| `data://witness/ns/version/name` | `data/witness/ns/version/name/` (was `proposals/`) | shards |
| `data://gold/ns/version/name` | `data/gold/ns/version/name/` (was `gold/`) | |

`gold` is a new channel: human labels. It is never written by a model.

What changes:
- `corpus/`, `proposals/` and `gold/` are replaced.
- The dot-directories (`.eccorpus/`, `.hncorpus/`, ...) collapse into
  `.snapshots/` and `.data/`.

What stays:
- Scripts stay in `scripts/` and are named by `cmd` in each step. Splitting
  them per step, as OWID's `etl/steps/` does, can come later; it buys little
  while one script builds several steps.
- `docs/` stays as it is.
- The paper, `index.html`, and the seal and its hash pins are untouched; none
  of them reference these paths.

A compatibility note in each old folder's README points to the new path for
one release.

## 2. Metadata: required fields, enforced

The schema follows OWID's metadata reference (origin → dataset → table →
indicator) and adds fields this repository needs: hashes, witness status, and
what a dataset does not answer.

**Snapshot origin** (`<name>.meta.yml`). Every field is required, or `null`
with a `reason:`.
- `producer`, `title`, `description`
- `citation_full`, `attribution_short`
- `url_main`, `url_download`
- `date_published`, `date_accessed`, `version_producer`
- `license: {name, url}`, `terms_notes`: for example, YouGov's no-AI-ingestion
  notice, or third-party benchmark tables that keep their own licences
- `files`: path, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3. This absorbs the MANIFEST.
- `refetch`: `exact` | `saved_bytes_are_pin`, with the reason
- `personal_data`: `none` | `ids_only` | `verbatim_public_figures` | ...

**Dataset** (`<name>.meta.yml` beside the outputs):
- `title`, `description`, `channel`, `uri`
- `origins`: the snapshot URIs, resolved transitively
- `processing`: what the step does, in plain sentences, and what it drops
- `unit_of_analysis`, `denominator`: which file holds it
- `coverage`: dates, universe, known gaps
- `does_not_answer`: required; it may not be empty
- `license`: derived from the origins, the most restrictive wins
- `status`: held | witness | gold
- for `witness`: `model`, `revision`, `codebook`, and `proposal_only: true`

**Table** (one entry per output file):
- `title`, `description`, `primary_key`, `rows`
- `columns`, one entry for **every** column:
  - `title`, `description`, `type`, `unit`
  - for verbatim text: `verbatim: true`
  - for a hash column: `hash_of`
  - for a code column: `values`

**Enforcement** (`uv run scripts/dag.py check`). It fails when:
- a required field is missing or empty;
- a column in the file is not documented, or a documented column is not in the
  file;
- a hash in the metadata does not match the file;
- a `witness` dataset lacks `proposal_only: true`, or a non-witness step depends
  on a witness step without being marked a proposal;
- a license is weaker than an origin's.

Row counts and hashes are written by the build, never by hand. Descriptions
are written by hand and reviewed like code.

`DATASETS.md` renders all of this, so the deck becomes the human view of the
metadata.

## 3. Phases (one commit each, each verified)

1. **Schema and validator.** Write `schema/metadata.schema.yml`. Add checks to
   `dag.py check` that report missing metadata without failing yet, so we can
   see the gap.
2. **Metadata backfill.** One dataset per commit, starting with CVE and Epoch
   (smallest), then Wikipedia, Hacker News and the earnings calls. Columns are
   introspected from the files; descriptions are written and checked against
   the method docs.
3. **Regroup.** Wait until the v0.2 scoring and the democracy work have landed.
   Then `git mv` everything to the URI paths, in one commit per dataset:
   - update script constants and the graph's outputs;
   - rebuild, check byte-identical, `verify`, `dag.py lock`, re-record the
     attestations.
4. **Strict.** Flip `check` to fail on any gap, and add it to the
   collaboration rules in AGENTS.md.
5. **Signing.** Sloane signs once the layout is final. Signatures taken before
   the regroup would go stale on the move.

## Open decisions (also in OPENQUESTIONS.md)

- Whether `snapshots/` keeps a TSV MANIFEST beside the YAML for grep-ability
  (proposed: yes, generated from the YAML).
- Whether scripts split into per-step files now or later (proposed: later).

# CVE records: monthly series and AI-related records

Monthly counts of published CVE records since January 2020, by severity and by
CNA, plus the CVE ids that concern AI software or credit an AI system or AI lab.
The universe, dating and severity rules reproduce Epoch AI's CVE explorer.
Method and limits: [`docs/cve-series.md`](../../docs/cve-series.md).

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MANIFEST.tsv` | Pins: the cvelistV5 daily baseline release asset (URL, release tag, tag commit, bytes, SHA-256, BLAKE3) and its single inner archive `cves.zip`. |
| `monthly.tsv` | One row per month, 2020-01 to 2026-10: `n_published` (the universe), severity buckets (`critical` … `unknown`), `n_notable_cna`, `n_linux_cna`, `n_excl_linux`, and `n_published_any_id_year` (the same count without the id-year rule). |
| `monthly-by-cna.tsv` | Month × Epoch's 21 notable CNAs + `Other`. Rows sum to `n_published`. |
| `ai-related.tsv` | One row per AI-related CVE: id, publication date, CNA short name, severity, the product/description rules that matched (`field:family`), the credited AI systems, and `system:credit-type` pairs. No descriptions or credit text. |
| `monthly-ai.tsv` | Per month: `n_published`, `n_ai_product` (affected product or description matched), `n_ai_product_affected` (affected-product fields only), `n_ai_credited`, `n_ai_credited_discovery` (excluding remediation-only credits), and one `n_credit_<system>` column per credited system. |

Rebuild and check from scratch:

    uv run scripts/cve_series.py fetch     # ~650 MB release asset + ~720 MB inner zip into .cvecorpus/, checked against MANIFEST
    uv run scripts/cve_series.py build     # byte-identical outputs on rerun
    uv run scripts/cve_series.py verify    # re-check pins, rebuild in memory, compare BLAKE3
    uv run scripts/cve_series.py pin --as-of YYYY-MM-DD   # only to move the snapshot

GitHub keeps the hourly cvelistV5 releases for a limited period (about six
weeks were listed at pin time). If the asset URL stops resolving, the tag commit
in `MANIFEST.tsv` identifies the same tree in the repository's history; a zip
built from it will not be byte-identical to the release asset, so re-pin.

content.content:
# CVE series: method
Data: [`corpus/cve/`](../corpus/cve/README.md). Code: `scripts/cve_series.py`.
## What it measures
The number of CVE records published each month since January 2020, how severe
their CNAs and ADPs scored them, which CNAs published them, and which ones
concern AI software or credit an AI system or AI lab. It rebuilds Epoch AI's CVE
explorer (https://epoch.ai/data/cve, CC BY 4.0) from the primary source, so the
same counts carry a pin, a hash and a rebuild command.
## Source and pin
`CVEProject/cvelistV5`, daily baseline release asset
`2026-11-04_all_CVEs_at_midnight.zip.zip` (every record as of 2026-11-04T00:00Z),
taken from release `cve_2026-11-04_0100Z`, the first release that carries it
(tag commit `dc7ec785f05ef024090048b6468bc7eddf06bc95`). Bytes, SHA-256 (equal to
GitHub's asset digest) and BLAKE3 are in `corpus/cve/MANIFEST.tsv`, as is the
inner `cves.zip` the build reads. The snapshot holds 418,964 records: 400,091
PUBLISHED, 18,873 REJECTED.
## Rules
| Step | Rule |
|---|---|
| State | `cveMetadata.state == "PUBLISHED"`. REJECTED records are dropped. |
| Universe | CVE id year ≥ 2020. This is what Epoch's "every published record 2020+" means in practice: its monthly totals equal ours only under the id-year rule. A CVE-2019-* id published in 2023 is outside. `n_published_any_id_year` shows the excluded mass (6,836 records in the window). |
| Month | `cveMetadata.datePublished[:7]`, UTC. Publication date, not discovery or reservation. 2020-01 through 2026-10, the last full month before the snapshot. |
| Severity | First CVSS base score found: CNA container first, then each ADP container in record order (in practice CISA's). Within a container, v4.0, then v3.1, then v3.0; v2 is ignored. Bucket by score: none 0, low 0.1–3.9, medium 4–6.9, high 7–8.9, critical 9–10; no score → unknown. |
| CNA | `cveMetadata.assignerShortName`, grouped into Epoch's 21 notable CNAs (mapping in `NOTABLE` in the script) or Other. Google = Chrome, ChromeOS, Google, GoogleCloud, Google_Devices, google_android. Samsung = Samsung Mobile, SamsungMobile, samsung.tv_appliance. GitHub = GitHub_P (own products), not GitHub_M (maintainer advisories, ~22,000 records). Red Hat excludes redhat-cnalr; VMware excludes brocade. |
| AI product (a) | `ANY_RE` from `scripts/ec_extract.py` (families ai, ai_phrase, ml, llm, vendor, agentic), plus the AI-software families in `AI_PRODUCT`: LangChain, LlamaIndex, Ollama, vLLM, MCP / Model Context Protocol, Hugging Face, PyTorch/TorchServe, TensorFlow/Keras, ONNX Runtime, llama.cpp/GGUF, chat front ends (Open WebUI, text-generation-webui, LibreChat, LobeChat, AnythingLLM, LoLLMs, LocalAI), ComfyUI/Stable Diffusion, Gradio, MLflow/Kubeflow/BentoML, LiteLLM, agent builders (Langflow, Flowise, Dify, AutoGPT, CrewAI, AutoGen, Semantic Kernel), NVIDIA AI (Triton Inference Server, TensorRT, DeepSpeed, NeMo), AI IDEs (Codeium, Windsurf, Anysphere). Searched in the CNA container's affected `vendor`, `product`, `packageName`, `repo` (field `product`) and English `descriptions` (field `description`). A bare `mcp` token counts in product fields only. |
| AI credit (b) | The CNA container's `credits[].value` only, never the description. Named systems in `AI_CREDIT`: Claude, Mythos, Anthropic, OpenAI, GPT/ChatGPT, Codex, Aardvark, Big Sleep/Naptime, DeepMind/CodeMender, Gemini, XBOW, Copilot, AIxCC/Team Atlanta, ZeroPath, Vulnhuntr. A credit naming none of them but carrying a generic AI term (ec_extract families ai, ai_phrase, ml, llm, agentic) is `ai_term`. "Claude" followed by a capitalised word counts only when that word is Code, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, Fable, Mythos, AI, Agent(s) or Security, so people named Claude are excluded. Each match keeps the credit's `type` (finder, reporter, tool, analyst, remediation developer, …; missing → `unspecified`). |
`n_ai_credited` counts records with any AI credit. `n_ai_credited_discovery`
drops records whose only AI credits are remediation types (remediation
developer, reviewer or verifier): a model that wrote the fix did not find the
bug. Per-system columns count records, so one record can count under Claude and
Anthropic both.
## Cross-check against Epoch
Epoch's page bundle (`https://epoch.ai/_astro/CveExplorerViz.D0wyPE-d.js`,
SHA-256 `ed04092a3ea8a7e06fedfd82e4db53c568fbd3a0ba4733c1e4c69a94f7553609`,
fetched 2026-11-04) embeds its monthly table as CSV (`month, cna, severity,
count`). Compared with `monthly.tsv` and `monthly-by-cna.tsv` for all 82 months
2020-01 to 2026-10:
- Monthly totals: 82 of 82 equal.
- Month × CNA (22 groups): every cell equal.
- Severity: critical, high, medium and unknown equal in every month. Epoch has
  no "none" bucket; its low equals our low + none. 112 records score 0.0.
- Epoch's partial 2026-11 count (1,356) equals the count of records in this
  snapshot published 2026-11-01..03, so Epoch's build used the same or an
  equivalent snapshot.
The AI columns have no Epoch counterpart.
## Selected values
| Month | Published | Linux CNA | Excl. Linux | AI product | AI credited | of which Claude | Anthropic | OpenAI | Codex |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2025-10 | 4,235 | 651 | 3,584 | 76 | 15 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| 2026-04 | 5,650 | 377 | 5,273 | 280 | 29 | 14 | 17 | 1 | 1 |
| 2026-10 | 17,013 | 1,051 | 15,962 | 595 | 258 | 134 | 49 | 58 | 36 |
## What it does not answer
- **A CVE count measures reporting, not risk.** It counts records that a CNA
  chose to publish. It says nothing about exploitation, exposure, or harm.
- **The count moves when the reporting system moves.** CNA onboarding raises
  counts with no change in software: the Linux kernel became a CNA in February
  2024 and publishes thousands of fix-level records a year, which is why
  `n_excl_linux` exists. New CNAs, CNA backlogs and policy changes do the same.
- **AI-assisted discovery raises counts too.** The 2026 rise coincides with AI
  vulnerability-finding programmes (Epoch marks the Claude Mythos Preview
  announcement on 2026-04-07). This series can show the coincidence; it cannot
  separate more bugs found from more bugs reported, or AI's share from other
  causes.
- **AI credit is self-reported by CNAs and incomplete.** Credits are optional
  free text; many CNAs omit them, and an AI tool used by a human finder is often
  not named. A named lab (`anthropic`, `openai`) can mean a person employed
  there, not a model. `ai_term` is a loose residual that includes company names
  containing "AI" and the occasional personal name.
- **The product rule is a regex.** `description:vendor` and `description:ai`
  catch some non-AI records (a person named Claude in a kernel changelog, a
  product called Gemini that is not Google's). `n_ai_product_affected`, which
  ignores descriptions, is the stricter count. Every match records its rule, so
  any family can be dropped.

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
import csv
systems = {"claude":"Claude (Claude Code, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, Fable, Mythos, AI, Agent, Security; not people named Claude)",
 "mythos":"Mythos","anthropic":"Anthropic","openai":"OpenAI","gpt":"GPT or ChatGPT","codex":"Codex","aardvark":"Aardvark",
 "big_sleep":"Big Sleep or Naptime","deepmind":"DeepMind or CodeMender","gemini":"Gemini","xbow":"XBOW","copilot":"Copilot",
 "aixcc":"AIxCC or Team Atlanta","zeropath":"ZeroPath","vulnhuntr":"Vulnhuntr",
 "ai_term":"no named system but a generic AI term (ec_extract families ai, ai_phrase, ml, llm, agentic); loose residual"}
def q(s): return '"' + s.replace('"','\\"') + '"'
L = []
A = L.append
A("# Metadata for data://garden/cve/2026-11-04/monthly_series (schema/metadata.schema.yml)")
A("title: Monthly CVE series with AI-related flags, 2020-01 to 2026-10")
A("description: >-\n  Monthly counts of published CVE records by severity and by reporting\n  organization (CNA), rebuilt from the CVE Program's records with Epoch AI's\n  rules, plus the CVE ids that concern AI software or credit an AI system or\n  AI lab as finder.")
A("processing: >-\n  Keep records with state PUBLISHED and CVE id year >= 2020; date each by\n  cveMetadata.datePublished (UTC month). Severity is the first CVSS base score\n  found (CNA container, then ADP containers in record order; v4.0, then v3.1,\n  then v3.0; v2 ignored), bucketed none 0 / low 0.1-3.9 / medium 4-6.9 /\n  high 7-8.9 / critical 9-10, else unknown. CNA short names are grouped into\n  Epoch's 21 notable CNAs or Other. AI product flags are regex matches on the\n  CNA container's affected-product fields and English descriptions; AI credit\n  flags are regex matches on credits[].value only. Drops REJECTED records,\n  pre-2020 ids, the partial month 2026-11, all description and credit text.\n  Rules in docs/cve-series.md.")
A("unit_of_analysis: one published CVE record")
A("denominator: corpus/cve/monthly.tsv (n_published, every record in the universe per month)")
A("coverage: >-\n  Records published 2020-01-01 to 2026-10-31 with CVE id year >= 2020;\n  6,836 records published in the window carry pre-2020 ids and are outside\n  (n_published_any_id_year shows them). Snapshot as of 2026-11-04T00:00Z.")
A("does_not_answer:")
for x in ["Whether a vulnerability was exploited, how exposed anyone was, or what harm followed: a CVE count measures reporting, not risk.",
          "Why counts move: CNA onboarding (Linux from February 2024), backlogs, policy changes and AI-assisted discovery all raise counts, and the series cannot separate them.",
          "How much discovery AI did: credits are optional, self-reported and incomplete, and a named lab can mean a person employed there."]:
    A(f"  - {q(x)}")
A("license:\n  name: CVE Program Terms of Use (records); method credit Epoch AI, CC BY 4.0\n  url: https://www.cve.org/Legal/TermsOfUse")
A("status: held")
A("tables:")
def table(path, title, desc, pk, cols):
    A(f"  {path}:"); A(f"    title: {q(title)}"); A(f"    description: {q(desc)}"); A(f"    primary_key: [{', '.join(pk)}]"); A("    columns:")
    for c,(t,u,d) in cols.items():
        A(f"      {q(c)}:"); A(f"        type: {t}")
        if u: A(f"        unit: {u}")
        A(f"        description: {q(d)}")
month = {"month": ("string","YYYY-MM","Publication month, UTC.")}
sev = {k:("integer","records",f"Records whose severity bucket is {k}.") for k in ["critical","high","medium","low","none","unknown"]}
sev["none"] = ("integer","records","Records with CVSS base score 0.0 (Epoch files these under low).")
sev["unknown"] = ("integer","records","Records with no CVSS v4.0, v3.1 or v3.0 score in any container.")
table("corpus/cve/monthly.tsv","Published CVE records per month","One row per month: totals, severity buckets, notable-CNA and Linux counts.",["month"],
  {**month, "n_published":("integer","records","Published records with id year >= 2020 (the universe)."), **sev,
   "n_notable_cna":("integer","records","Records from Epoch's 21 notable CNAs."),
   "n_linux_cna":("integer","records","Records published by the Linux kernel CNA."),
   "n_excl_linux":("integer","records","n_published minus n_linux_cna."),
   "n_published_any_id_year":("integer","records","Published records in the month regardless of id year (shows the id-year rule's exclusions).")})
hdr = next(l for l in open("corpus/cve/monthly-by-cna.tsv") if not l.startswith("#")).rstrip("\n").split("\t")
table("corpus/cve/monthly-by-cna.tsv","Published CVE records per month by CNA","Month by Epoch's notable CNAs plus Other; each row sums to n_published.",["month"],
  {**month, **{c:("integer","records", "Records from all CNAs outside the notable list." if c=="Other" else f"Records whose CNA maps to {c} (mapping in NOTABLE in scripts/cve_series.py).") for c in hdr[1:]}})
table("corpus/cve/ai-related.tsv","AI-related CVE records","One row per published CVE in the universe that matched an AI product rule or an AI credit rule. Ids and rule labels only.",["cve_id"],
  {"cve_id":("string","","CVE identifier."),
   "date_published":("date","YYYY-MM-DD","cveMetadata.datePublished, UTC date."),
   "cna":("string","","cveMetadata.assignerShortName (raw short name, not grouped)."),
   "severity":("string","","Severity bucket: critical, high, medium, low, none or unknown."),
   "ai_product_rules":("string","","Semicolon-separated field:family matches, field in {product, description}; empty if none."),
   "ai_credit_systems":("string","","Semicolon-separated credited AI systems (see monthly-ai.tsv n_credit_* columns); empty if none."),
   "ai_credit_system_types":("string","","Semicolon-separated system:credit-type pairs (finder, reporter, tool, remediation developer, ...; unspecified if missing).")})
hdr = next(l for l in open("corpus/cve/monthly-ai.tsv") if not l.startswith("#")).rstrip("\n").split("\t")
cols = {**month, "n_published":("integer","records","Published records in the universe (same as monthly.tsv)."),
  "n_ai_product":("integer","records","Records matching an AI product rule in product fields or descriptions."),
  "n_ai_product_affected":("integer","records","Records matching an AI product rule in affected-product fields only (stricter)."),
  "n_ai_credited":("integer","records","Records with any AI credit."),
  "n_ai_credited_discovery":("integer","records","Records with an AI credit other than remediation types (remediation developer, reviewer, verifier).")}
for c in hdr:
    if c.startswith("n_credit_"):
        cols[c] = ("integer","records",f"Records crediting {systems[c[len('n_credit_'):]]}.")
table("corpus/cve/monthly-ai.tsv","AI-related CVE records per month","Per month: AI product and AI credit counts, and records per credited system (one record can count under several).",["month"], cols)
open("corpus/cve/monthly_series.meta.yml","w").write("\n".join(L)+"\n")
EOF
python3 - <<'EOF'
p='/Users/srvo/dev/anthropic-pbc/dag.yml'; s=open(p).read()
s=s.replace("""    outputs: [corpus/cve/MANIFEST.tsv]
""","""    meta: corpus/cve/snapshot.meta.yml
    outputs: [corpus/cve/MANIFEST.tsv]
""")
s=s.replace("""    inputs: [scripts/ec_extract.py]   # reuses its AI term regex
""","""    inputs: [scripts/ec_extract.py]   # reuses its AI term regex
    meta: corpus/cve/monthly_series.meta.yml
""")
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF
uv run scripts/dag.py meta | grep -A8 cve; uv run scripts/dag.py meta | tail -1

content.text:
Yes, it's the right time to regroup, before more data lands on the current layout. The plan, the schema and a working validator are in, and the first dataset passes it.

**The plan** is in `docs/plan-owid-regroup.md` (`2b8c78e`):
- **New layout:** every step moves to a folder named after its step address (`snapshots/…`, `data/meadow/…`, `data/garden/…`, `data/witness/…`), replacing `corpus/`, `proposals/` and `gold/`. Human labels become a new `data/gold` channel that a model never writes to.
- **Metadata:** we adopt OWID's four levels (where the data came from, the dataset, each table, each column) and add what we need on top:
  - hashes
  - whether something is model output
  - what each dataset does *not* answer, which can't be left empty
  - the terms of use, and whether a source contains personal data
- **Strictness:** a new check fails the build when a required field is missing or empty, when a file has a column the metadata doesn't describe (or the metadata describes one the file lacks), when a hash doesn't match, or when something downstream of model output isn't marked as a proposal.
- **Order of work:**
  1. schema and validator
  2. fill in the metadata, one dataset per commit
  3. move the files (after the current scoring and democracy jobs finish)
  4. make the check strict
  5. sign

  Signing comes last, because signatures taken before the move would go stale.

**Done so far:**
- **Schema:** `schema/metadata.schema.yml`.
- **Validator:** `uv run scripts/dag.py meta` reads the real columns from each file and lists every gap. For now it reports without failing.
- **First dataset:** CVE is complete, every column of its four tables described (`ef04fa8`).
- **"Unknown" stays visible:** a field can be marked unknown only with a stated reason, and those fields are counted and shown, never treated as done (`edda31f`).

Coverage is 2 of 26 steps.

**In progress:** three agents are filling in metadata in parallel, for the earnings calls (13 steps), HN plus Wikipedia (9) and Epoch (2 steps, 68 tables). Each has the same rule: every description must trace to the code, a method doc or the source's own documentation, and anything that can't be established gets marked unknown with a reason, never guessed. They'll also report anywhere the code contradicts the docs. The v0.2 scoring and the democracy agent are still running too.

Two small decisions are logged as Q12 in `OPENQUESTIONS.md`:
- keep a plain-table manifest next to each metadata file so it's easy to grep (I'd say yes)
- split scripts into one file per step now or later (I'd say later)

#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["duckdb==2.0.0"]
# ///
"""The dialogue space under codebook-v0.2-draft: which sources discuss which AI risks.

For each source, the share of its AI-risk units (both witnesses >= 0.5 on
`ai_risk`) that also carry each risk type (both witnesses >= 0.5). Sources:
  executives   earnings-call windows not spoken by an analyst or the operator, 12 months to 2026-11-04
  analysts     analyst questions on calls, 12 months to 2026-11-04
  hn_anthropic Hacker News Anthropic/Claude windows, 2025-09..2026-08
  hn_security  Hacker News AI-security windows, 2025-09..2026-08
  wikipedia    Wikipedia AI-risk article windows, revisions as of 2026-11-04
DRAFT codebook, witness proposals, no gold set. Writes
proposals/cross-source/codebook-v0.2-draft/report/.

    uv run scripts/v02_map.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import sys
from html import escape
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CB = ROOT / "corpus" / "codebooks" / "codebook-v0.2-draft.tsv"
OUT = ROOT / "proposals" / "cross-source" / "codebook-v0.2-draft" / "report"
EC, HN, WP = ROOT / "corpus" / "earnings-calls", ROOT / "corpus" / "hacker-news", ROOT / "corpus" / "wikipedia-ai-risk"
P = ROOT / "proposals"
SOURCES = [  # (key, label, scores dir, id col, unit filter SQL over table u)
    ("executives", "Executives (calls)", P / "earnings-calls/codebook-v0.2-draft", "window_id",
     f"SELECT window_id AS id FROM '{EC / 'ai-windows.parquet'}' WHERE role NOT IN ('analyst_heuristic', 'operator') "
     "AND report_date::DATE > DATE '2025-11-04' AND report_date::DATE <= DATE '2026-11-04'"),
    ("analysts", "Analyst questions", P / "earnings-calls/codebook-v0.2-draft-questions", "question_id",
     f"SELECT question_id AS id FROM '{EC / 'ai-questions.parquet'}' "
     "WHERE report_date::DATE > DATE '2025-11-04' AND report_date::DATE <= DATE '2026-11-04'"),
    ("hn_anthropic", "HN: Anthropic", P / "hacker-news/anthropic-v0.2-draft", "window_id",
     f"""SELECT window_id AS id FROM '{HN / 'windows.parquet'}' WHERE "set" = 'anthropic' AND day BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-31'"""),
    ("hn_security", "HN: AI security", P / "hacker-news/ai_security-v0.2-draft", "window_id",
     f"""SELECT window_id AS id FROM '{HN / 'windows.parquet'}' WHERE "set" = 'ai_security' AND day BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-31'"""),
    ("wikipedia", "Wikipedia", P / "wikipedia-ai-risk/codebook-v0.2-draft", "window_id",
     f"SELECT window_id AS id FROM '{WP / 'windows.parquet'}'"),
]


def main() -> int:
    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cb = list(csv.DictReader(CB.open(), delimiter="\t"))
    types = [r for r in cb if r["group"] == "risk_type"]
    con = duckdb.connect()
    shares: dict[str, dict[str, tuple[int, int]]] = {}
    for key, _, d, idc, units in SOURCES:
        con.execute(f"""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE f AS
            SELECT x.{idc} AS id, x.hypothesis_id AS h, x.p_entail >= .5 AND y.p_entail >= .5 AS b
            FROM '{d / 'deberta.parquet'}' x JOIN '{d / 'modernbert.parquet'}' y USING ({idc}, hypothesis_id)
            WHERE x.{idc} IN ({units})""")
        risk = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM f WHERE h = 'ai_risk' AND b").fetchone()[0]
        shares[key] = {}
        for t in types:
            n = con.execute(f"""SELECT count(*) FROM f a JOIN f r USING (id)
                WHERE a.h = '{t['id']}' AND a.b AND r.h = 'ai_risk' AND r.b""").fetchone()[0]
            shares[key][t["id"]] = (n, risk)
    new = {r["id"] for r in cb if r["status"].startswith("v0.2")}
    rows = sorted(types, key=lambda t: -max(shares[k][t["id"]][0] / max(shares[k][t["id"]][1], 1) for k, *_ in SOURCES))
    with (OUT / "dialogue-space.tsv").open("w") as f:
        f.write("# Share (%) of each source's AI-risk units naming each risk type; both witnesses >= 0.5. "
                "codebook-v0.2-draft (DRAFT wording), witness proposals, no gold set.\n")
        f.write("risk_type\tnew_in_v0.2\t" + "\t".join(f"{k}_pct\t{k}_n" for k, *_ in SOURCES) + "\n")
        f.write("ai_risk_units\t\t" + "\t".join(f"\t{shares[k][types[0]['id']][1]}" for k, *_ in SOURCES) + "\n")
        for t in rows:
            cells = []
            for k, *_ in SOURCES:
                n, base = shares[k][t["id"]]
                cells += [f"{100 * n / base:.1f}" if base else "", str(n)]
            f.write(f"{t['id']}\t{'yes' if t['id'] in new else ''}\t" + "\t".join(cells) + "\n")
    plot(rows, shares, new)
    print(f"wrote {OUT.relative_to(ROOT)}/dialogue-space.tsv and .svg")
    return 0


def plot(rows, shares, new) -> None:
    """Heatmap: risk types x sources, cell = share; one sequential hue, value printed."""
    cw, rh, left, top = 128, 24, 210, 96
    W, H = left + cw * len(SOURCES) + 24, top + rh * len(rows) + 64
    def fill(v: float) -> str:  # light -> dark blue, sequential
        t = min(v / 50.0, 1.0)
        lo, hi = (236, 243, 249), (16, 70, 120)
        return "#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(round(a + (b - a) * t) for a, b in zip(lo, hi))
    o = [f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 {W} {H}" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,sans-serif" role="img">',
         '<style>text{fill:#1b1b1b}.m{fill:#5f6368}</style>', f'<rect width="{W}" height="{H}" fill="#fcfcfb"/>',
         '<text x="16" y="30" font-size="18" font-weight="600">Who talks about which AI risks</text>',
         '<text x="16" y="52" font-size="12" class="m">Share of each source\'s AI-risk passages naming each type. '
         'Codebook v0.2 DRAFT; * = new in v0.2.</text>']
    for j, (_, label, *_r) in enumerate(SOURCES):
        o.append(f'<text x="{left + j * cw + cw / 2}" y="{top - 10}" font-size="12" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">{escape(label)}</text>')
    for i, t in enumerate(rows):
        y = top + i * rh
        o.append(f'<text x="{left - 8}" y="{y + rh / 2 + 4}" font-size="12" text-anchor="end">{escape(t["id"])}{" *" if t["id"] in new else ""}</text>')
        for j, (k, label, *_r) in enumerate(SOURCES):
            n, base = shares[k][t["id"]]
            v = 100 * n / base if base else 0.0
            ink = "#ffffff" if v >= 25 else "#1b1b1b"
            o.append(f'<g><title>{escape(label)}: {escape(t["id"])} {v:.1f}% ({n} of {base})</title>'
                     f'<rect x="{left + j * cw + 1}" y="{y + 1}" width="{cw - 2}" height="{rh - 2}" rx="2" fill="{fill(v)}"/>'
                     f'<text x="{left + j * cw + cw / 2}" y="{y + rh / 2 + 4}" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:{ink}">{v:.0f}</text></g>')
    o.append(f'<text x="16" y="{H - 16}" font-size="11" class="m">Both NLI witnesses ≥ 0.5 on ai_risk and on the type; a unit can name several. '
             'Calls and questions: 12 months to 2026-11-04; HN: 2025-09..2026-08; Wikipedia: revisions as of 2026-11-04.</text>')
    o.append("</svg>")
    (OUT / "dialogue-space.svg").write_text("\n".join(o) + "\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

#!/usr/bin/env -S uv run --script
# /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.10"
# dependencies = ["duckdb==2.0.0"]
# ///
"""The dialogue space under codebook-v0.2-draft: which sources discuss which AI risks.

For each source, the share of its AI-risk units (both witnesses >= 0.5 on
`ai_risk`) that also carry each risk type (both witnesses >= 0.5). Sources:
  executives   earnings-call windows not spoken by an analyst or the operator, 12 months to 2026-11-04
  analysts     analyst questions on calls, 12 months to 2026-11-04
  hn_anthropic Hacker News Anthropic/Claude windows, 2025-09..2026-08
  hn_security  Hacker News AI-security windows, 2025-09..2026-08
  wikipedia    Wikipedia AI-risk article windows, revisions as of 2026-11-04
DRAFT codebook, witness proposals, no gold set. Writes
proposals/cross-source/codebook-v0.2-draft/report/.

    uv run scripts/v02_map.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import csv
import sys
from html import escape
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
CB = ROOT / "corpus" / "codebooks" / "codebook-v0.2-draft.tsv"
OUT = ROOT / "proposals" / "cross-source" / "codebook-v0.2-draft" / "report"
EC, HN, WP = ROOT / "corpus" / "earnings-calls", ROOT / "corpus" / "hacker-news", ROOT / "corpus" / "wikipedia-ai-risk"
P = ROOT / "proposals"
SOURCES = [  # (key, label, scores dir, id col, unit filter SQL over table u)
    ("executives", "Executives (calls)", P / "earnings-calls/codebook-v0.2-draft", "window_id",
     f"SELECT window_id AS id FROM '{EC / 'ai-windows.parquet'}' WHERE role NOT IN ('analyst_heuristic', 'operator') "
     "AND report_date::DATE > DATE '2025-11-04' AND report_date::DATE <= DATE '2026-11-04'"),
    ("analysts", "Analyst questions", P / "earnings-calls/codebook-v0.2-draft-questions", "question_id",
     f"SELECT question_id AS id FROM '{EC / 'ai-questions.parquet'}' "
     "WHERE report_date::DATE > DATE '2025-11-04' AND report_date::DATE <= DATE '2026-11-04'"),
    ("hn_anthropic", "HN: Anthropic", P / "hacker-news/anthropic-v0.2-draft", "window_id",
     f"""SELECT window_id AS id FROM '{HN / 'windows.parquet'}' WHERE "set" = 'anthropic' AND day BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-31'"""),
    ("hn_security", "HN: AI security", P / "hacker-news/ai_security-v0.2-draft", "window_id",
     f"""SELECT window_id AS id FROM '{HN / 'windows.parquet'}' WHERE "set" = 'ai_security' AND day BETWEEN '2025-09-01' AND '2026-08-31'"""),
    ("wikipedia", "Wikipedia", P / "wikipedia-ai-risk/codebook-v0.2-draft", "window_id",
     f"SELECT window_id AS id FROM '{WP / 'windows.parquet'}'"),
]


def main() -> int:
    OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    cb = list(csv.DictReader(CB.open(), delimiter="\t"))
    types = [r for r in cb if r["group"] == "risk_type"]
    con = duckdb.connect()
    shares: dict[str, dict[str, tuple[int, int]]] = {}
    for key, _, d, idc, units in SOURCES:
        con.execute(f"""CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE f AS
            SELECT x.{idc} AS id, x.hypothesis_id AS h, x.p_entail >= .5 AND y.p_entail >= .5 AS b
            FROM '{d / 'deberta.parquet'}' x JOIN '{d / 'modernbert.parquet'}' y USING ({idc}, hypothesis_id)
            WHERE x.{idc} IN ({units})""")
        risk = con.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM f WHERE h = 'ai_risk' AND b").fetchone()[0]
        shares[key] = {}
        for t in types:
            n = con.execute(f"""SELECT count(*) FROM f a JOIN f r USING (id)
                WHERE a.h = '{t['id']}' AND a.b AND r.h = 'ai_risk' AND r.b""").fetchone()[0]
            shares[key][t["id"]] = (n, risk)
    new = {r["id"] for r in cb if r["status"].startswith("v0.2")}
    rows = sorted(types, key=lambda t: -max(shares[k][t["id"]][0] / max(shares[k][t["id"]][1], 1) for k, *_ in SOURCES))
    with (OUT / "dialogue-space.tsv").open("w") as f:
        f.write("# Share (%) of each source's AI-risk units naming each risk type; both witnesses >= 0.5. "
                "codebook-v0.2-draft (DRAFT wording), witness proposals, no gold set.\n")
        f.write("risk_type\tnew_in_v0.2\t" + "\t".join(f"{k}_pct\t{k}_n" for k, *_ in SOURCES) + "\n")
        f.write("ai_risk_units\t\t" + "\t".join(f"\t{shares[k][types[0]['id']][1]}" for k, *_ in SOURCES) + "\n")
        for t in rows:
            cells = []
            for k, *_ in SOURCES:
                n, base = shares[k][t["id"]]
                cells += [f"{100 * n / base:.1f}" if base else "", str(n)]
            f.write(f"{t['id']}\t{'yes' if t['id'] in new else ''}\t" + "\t".join(cells) + "\n")
    plot(rows, shares, new)
    print(f"wrote {OUT.relative_to(ROOT)}/dialogue-space.tsv and .svg")
    return 0


def plot(rows, shares, new) -> None:
    """Heatmap: risk types x sources, cell = share; one sequential hue, value printed."""
    cw, rh, left, top = 128, 24, 210, 96
    W, H = left + cw * len(SOURCES) + 24, top + rh * len(rows) + 64
    def fill(v: float) -> str:  # light -> dark blue, sequential
        t = min(v / 50.0, 1.0)
        lo, hi = (236, 243, 249), (16, 70, 120)
        return "#%02x%02x%02x" % tuple(round(a + (b - a) * t) for a, b in zip(lo, hi))
    o = [f'<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 {W} {H}" font-family="system-ui,-apple-system,sans-serif" role="img">',
         '<style>text{fill:#1b1b1b}.m{fill:#5f6368}</style>', f'<rect width="{W}" height="{H}" fill="#fcfcfb"/>',
         '<text x="16" y="30" font-size="18" font-weight="600">Who talks about which AI risks</text>',
         '<text x="16" y="52" font-size="12" class="m">Share of each source\'s AI-risk passages naming each type. '
         'Codebook v0.2 DRAFT; * = new in v0.2.</text>']
    for j, (_, label, *_r) in enumerate(SOURCES):
        o.append(f'<text x="{left + j * cw + cw / 2}" y="{top - 10}" font-size="12" font-weight="600" text-anchor="middle">{escape(label)}</text>')
    for i, t in enumerate(rows):
        y = top + i * rh
        o.append(f'<text x="{left - 8}" y="{y + rh / 2 + 4}" font-size="12" text-anchor="end">{escape(t["id"])}{" *" if t["id"] in new else ""}</text>')
        for j, (k, label, *_r) in enumerate(SOURCES):
            n, base = shares[k][t["id"]]
            v = 100 * n / base if base else 0.0
            ink = "#ffffff" if v >= 25 else "#1b1b1b"
            o.append(f'<g><title>{escape(label)}: {escape(t["id"])} {v:.1f}% ({n} of {base})</title>'
                     f'<rect x="{left + j * cw + 1}" y="{y + 1}" width="{cw - 2}" height="{rh - 2}" rx="2" fill="{fill(v)}"/>'
                     f'<text x="{left + j * cw + cw / 2}" y="{y + rh / 2 + 4}" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:{ink}">{v:.0f}</text></g>')
    o.append(f'<text x="16" y="{H - 16}" font-size="11" class="m">Both NLI witnesses ≥ 0.5 on ai_risk and on the type; a unit can name several. '
             'Calls and questions: 12 months to 2026-11-04; HN: 2025-09..2026-08; Wikipedia: revisions as of 2026-11-04.</text>')
    o.append("</svg>")
    (OUT / "dialogue-space.svg").write_text("\n".join(o) + "\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
