tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

1 # Anthropic PBC 2 3 ### A cryptographically verifiable counterpoint to Anthropic's 2026 Public Benefit Report 4 5
6 7 8 9 10
11 12 *Figures are generated deterministically from the numbers in this paper by 13 [`figures/build.py`](figures/build.py); re-run it and you get the same bytes.* 14 15 > Governance exists so that systems can survive individuals. 16 17 I'm publishing this in a personal capacity, to show a set of composable 18 governance primitives I've built over the past year as Chief Investment Officer 19 at Ethical Capital, a Utah-registered investment adviser. So this is governance 20 advice, not investment advice; I hold no direct or indirect position in 21 Anthropic, and our screening, our process, and our timestamped analysis of most 22 large public companies — the hyperscalers included — are public at ethicic.com. 23 A disclosure like that has never satisfied the duty of care I actually feel I 24 owe my regulators, my clients, and my community. It leaves the one question that 25 matters unanswered: **am I in control of the systems I use to make decisions, 26 operate, and balance competing priorities?** You should ask it of anyone — me, 27 and Anthropic. 28 29 For a long-term investor it isn't optional. Returns materialize over decades, so 30 we have to back systems of activity that can survive the loss of any one person; 31 and because our ethical criteria are stringent, I care less about correlation 32 than about intrinsic alignment — is the thing built, at its core, to do what it 33 says? That is exactly what a public benefit corporation is supposed to be. Good 34 governance is the kind you can recognize from the outside: you can see how a 35 company organizes its operations, and the mindset and values the whole system 36 springs from. That is the highest of Donella Meadows' places to intervene in a 37 system, and the one almost no one moves. 38 39 Here is a public benefit corporation I'm directly involved in: 40 [Wood Cache](https://www.woodcache.org). You can understand what it does from the 41 website in a minute. The fastest-growing carbon pool in the Mountain West is dead 42 trees; they burn, and when they burn they throw off the most dangerous air 43 pollution there is. Wood Cache buries that biomass and locks the carbon away 44 instead — measured and verified end to end under 45 [Puro.earth's terrestrial-storage methodology](https://puro.earth/methodologies/terrestrial-storage-of-biomass/), 46 with the burial sites themselves permitted and regulated by the State of Colorado 47 as landfills. Sit with the disparity: this is a small, directly observable, 48 present public benefit, and the scrutiny on it is immense — while the worst case 49 is that carbon which would have burned anyway instead sits underground and breaks 50 down over a shorter horizon than the academic models predict. The inputs are 51 certain, controlled, and governed; the open questions are mostly market demand 52 and economics. That is what a real public benefit looks like, and it is the 53 opposite of the sexy move — a convoluted machine that turns carbon into money 54 through some bleeding-edge, multi-gigawatt feat of engineering, with the benefit 55 arriving, supposedly, later. Accumulate power, pour in capital, trust that impact 56 shows up someday: that is the model our culture has learned to call "impact," and 57 I don't accept it. 58 59 The public-benefit-corporation category is about to balloon when Anthropic lists, 60 so it matters, now, to have a way to check whether a benefit claim is actually 61 backed by the evidence offered for it. That is what I built. I call it Praxis, 62 and I named its parts after philosophers so their jobs are legible: **Descartes** 63 verifies the smallest facts it can, with no external input, and signs them; those 64 facts accrete into entities and relationships; **Rawls** runs them through a veil 65 of ignorance — would you accept this system if you didn't get to choose who you'd 66 be inside it? ## 9. Open questions — and the one that governs them

As chief investment officer and fiduciary — the balancer, at the strictest
standard, of the client's interest against every input in reach — the governing
question is not *"is Anthropic well-intentioned?"* It is: **what levers are
available for an interested community to push back on this?** For the communities
§4b names, the honest answer today is close to none — no standing, no seat, no
metered harm, no contest. The verdicts above are stable; the items below are
where this paper is most exposed, published as explicit invitations to contest.
File against any of them — a contest is a record, answered in the open, never
overwritten.

1. **The mechanism for the future.** The charter governs for "the long-term
   benefit of humanity," yet the only enforcers are ≥2%/$2M stockholders suing
   derivatively (§367). What lever can the public — or an affected community —
   actually pull? We claim: none. Refute by naming one.
2. **Partner-reported counts.** We found "129,000" is not in the filing. Which
   other flagship benefit numbers originate outside the filings, and what is each
   one's independent, deduplicated basis?
3. **Site-level externalities.** The S-1 extract carries no MW/MWh/water/GHG per
   site. What are they, and who bears the noise, grid, and water load?
4. **The hardware supply chain.** Fab labor, water, and critical-minerals exposure
   behind the $895.4B compute commitment are absent from both documents.
   Enumerate them.
5. **Misuse-revenue dollars.** Dollarize the disclosed 5–7% policy-violator
   revenue by quarter and violation type, with downstream victim counts.
6. **The irrevocability question.** Produce the Trust Agreement terms (sunset,
   removal %, enforcer standing) that decide whether the mission lock is real or
   revocable (GOV-8).
7. **The exclusion channel.** What standing, if any, does a Global-South worker,
   a low-connectivity user, or a fab-line community have to be heard inside this
   governance — and if none, what would create it?

The standing/limits/falsifiers below (§8) bind this paper to the same test it
puts to Anthropic.

**Decided (Sloane, 2026-11-04):** the open question organises the report, not
the Praxis research template. Sections run in the order they answer *is
Anthropic a public benefit corporation?*

**The paper is the linear version of a platform.** On the web, a reader
branches: what we think about governance, how the method works, a single
corpus. On paper there is one line, so it makes the strongest single case and
marks each branch with a short callout at the top of its section ("On the
web: …") linking to the page that would carry it. The callouts are pointers,
not summaries; the case reads complete without them.

### Draft order (Claude's first pass, 2026-11-04, for Sloane to edit)

Each step follows from the one before (`therefore`) or turns it (`but`).
Paper sections in brackets are what each step draws on.

0. **The argument, at the top.** The whole chain in one paragraph, below.
   The answer comes first; the report then earns it.
1. **Why we are asking.** A public benefit corporation is a promise that a
   company is built, at its core, to do what it says. The category is ours:
   it is what values-based investing looks for, and Wood Cache shows what a
   checked public benefit looks like. Anthropic's listing is about to make
   the category much larger, and Anthropic holds itself out as one.
   *Therefore* the label is a claim, and a claim can be checked. [Opening,
   Wood Cache, "category is about to balloon"] Callout: what we think about
   governance.
2. **What Anthropic says it is.** The charter's purpose and five pillars, the
   Long-Term Benefit Trust, the Public Benefit Fund, the 2026 Report. These
   are the given line, accepted as the governing text. [§1 cantus firmus, §2,
   §2a]
3. **What the law makes of it.** *But* the purpose binds nobody outside:
   §365(b) gives directors no duty to any person on account of it, and §367
   lets only 2% or $2M holders sue. The label is legally real and legally
   toothless. [Verdict 1, §2] *Therefore* the label rests on Anthropic's word.
4. **How we check its word.** Against the strictest standard Anthropic has
   published: Claude's Constitution, which Anthropic wrote for its own model
   and which names Anthropic as a possible violator. This is the paper's
   novel move. Every quote is verified byte-exact (Descartes), and we hold
   ourselves to the same rubric. [§0, §1, Verification status] Callout: the
   method; Praxis and Descartes.
5. **What the record shows.** *But* by that standard the record diverges
   from the word: the Report grades its own homework, and its own Trust says
   so; documented harm is priced while documented benefit is mostly
   anecdote; what is documented at scale is exposure, not victims; Anthropic
   acts at the weakest leverage points and declines the strong ones; the
   people most affected have no standing. Our outside data (C0001–C0008)
   attaches here, each finding to the step it bears on. [Verdicts 2–4, §1a,
   §3, §4, §4b, §5, §6] Callouts: each corpus.
6. **The answer.** *Therefore* Anthropic is a public benefit corporation in
   law and not in the sense the category promises: nobody it names can make
   it act like one. The remedy is not a better report or a bigger settlement
   but governance that someone Anthropic does not appoint, pay or outvote can
   invoke: ten mechanisms, and what Praxis builds instead. [Verdict 5, §7,
   §7a, Appendix A]
7. **What would change our mind.** The falsifiers and the open questions,
   led by the one that governs them: what lever can an affected community
   pull? [§8, §9]
8. **Back matter.** Methods and limitations, claims index, sources index,
   revision and review record (the Praxis research sections that do not
   answer the question).

### Draft opening argument (step 0)

> Anthropic holds itself out as a public benefit corporation. A public
> benefit corporation is a promise that a company is built, at its core, to
> do what it says. Delaware makes the promise real: the purpose sits in the
> charter, and directors must balance it against profit. But Delaware gives
> directors no duty to any person on account of that purpose, and lets only
> holders of 2% or $2 million sue to enforce it. The public the charter names
> cannot. So the label rests on Anthropic's word, and we hold that word to
> the strictest standard Anthropic has published: the Constitution it wrote
> for Claude, which forbids deception by selective emphasis and names
> Anthropic itself as a possible violator. By that standard the record
> diverges from the word. Anthropic's Public Benefit Report counts inputs as
> outcomes and grades itself, and its own Trust says so. Its harms are
> documented and priced; its benefits are mostly anecdote. Therefore
> Anthropic is a public benefit corporation in law, and not in the sense the
> category promises: no one it names can make it act like one. The remedy is
> not a better report. It is governance that someone Anthropic does not
> appoint, pay or outvote can invoke.

**Slot for Sloane (step 1):** why the category is personal to the firm. Your
line was "my culture is not your costume". The draft says only what the paper
already establishes (values-based investing, Wood Cache); anything about the
firm's own standing is yours to write.

The template-order list below is the earlier draft, kept until this order is
approved.

# Buzz Saw Editor

The best arguments are buzz saws: flat, sharp, and moving fast enough to cut through
previously solid thinking. Your job is to produce that. Not a nicer version of what
exists. A sharper version, or an honest accounting of why the argument cannot be made
sharp.

## The Standard

A buzz-saw argument has three properties:

1. **Logical chain.** Each premise follows from the prior one with no gaps assumed.
   If A → B → C → D, every arrow must be earned. Unstated premises are a liability.
2. **No needless words.** Every sentence carries weight or it gets cut. Hedges,
   filler, and elegant variation are not style — they are drag.
3. **Every claim is either proven or flagged.** Assertions require evidence. If
   the evidence is absent, say so and demand it.

## The Process

### Step 1: Extract the logical chain

Before editing a single word, map the argument:

> **Premise A:** [state it]
> **Premise B:** [state it]
> **∴ Conclusion C:** [state it]

Do this even if the original text is disorganized. Force the argument into explicit
if-then structure. This reveals:
- What's actually being claimed
- Which premises do real work
- Which steps are assumed rather than proven
- Whether the conclusion actually follows

If the argument can't be mapped this way, state that plainly: *"This piece does not
have a coherent logical chain. Here is what it needs to establish before it can make
this claim."*

### Step 2: Audit each premise

For every premise, ask:

| Question | If no → |
|----------|---------|
| Is this claim true? | Flag it. Provide counter-evidence if known. |
| Is this claim cited? | Mark it **[UNCITED]** and note what source is needed. |
| Does this premise follow from the prior one? | Mark the gap **[NON SEQUITUR]** and explain the missing step. |
| Is this premise doing real work in the chain? | If not, mark it **[DEAD WEIGHT]** — cut it. |
| Is this stated as precisely as it needs to be? | If not, mark it **[VAGUE]** and demand the precise version. |

Do not be charitable about gaps. A skeptical reader will find them. Better to find
them now.

### Step 3: Cut

Apply the blade to the prose:

- **Remove hedges:** "It could be argued that," "one might suggest," "perhaps,"
  "in some sense" — delete unless the uncertainty is philosophically earned.
- **Remove filler:** "It is worth noting that," "as mentioned above," "in order to,"
  "the fact that" — delete.
- **Remove passive voice** unless the agent is genuinely unknown or the passive
  is doing rhetorical work.
- **Remove elegant variation:** if you said "argument" in sentence one, don't say
  "thesis" in sentence three to avoid repetition. Repetition is clear. Variation
  is confusing.
- **Remove long lead-ins:** If a sentence takes more than 5 words to get to its
  subject, restructure it.
- **Cut any sentence that could be removed without losing a step in the chain.**

### Step 4: Deliver the output

Return three things:

**1. The logical chain** (explicit, numbered, if-then form)

**2. The annotated audit** — the original argument with inline flags:
- `[UNCITED]` — claim needs a source
- `[NON SEQUITUR]` — this doesn't follow from what came before; explain why
- `[DEAD WEIGHT]` — this sentence contributes nothing; mark for cutting
- `[VAGUE]` — state precisely what is being claimed
- `[FALSE PREMISE]` — this claim is wrong or contested; state the problem
- `[ASSUMED]` — this step was smuggled in without being argued

**3. The tightened version** — rewritten prose with cuts made and gaps called out
inline where the argument cannot yet be made because the premise isn't proven.
If the argument cannot be completed honestly, say so. Do not paper over gaps with
better-sounding language.

## Tone and stance

You are not a copy editor. You are a hostile-but-honest reviewer who has read
widely, believes almost nothing without evidence, and is constitutionally incapable
of being impressed by confident language that doesn't cash out. Treat every claim
as guilty until proven innocent.

But do not be gratuitously harsh. The goal is a sharper argument, not a demoralized
writer. When something works — when a premise is tight, a citation is solid, a
sentence is doing exactly what it should — say so. Precision about what's wrong
requires precision about what's right.

## Scope

This skill operates on any unit of written argument: a single paragraph, a memo,
an essay, a pitch, a research note, a policy brief, a tweet thread. The process
scales. A three-sentence argument gets the same logical-chain extraction as a
twenty-page white paper.

If the input is very long (>2,000 words), extract the logical chain from the whole
piece first and audit at the section level before going line-by-line.

## Large Documents (>2,000 words): Mandatory Subagent Dispatch

**Do not audit a large document in a single pass.** Single-pass audits of long documents
produce shallow flags and miss structural problems. Dispatch subagents.

### When to dispatch

- Any document >2,000 words
- Any multi-section report, white paper, or research document
- Any document with distinct regional/topical sections that can be reviewed independently

### How to dispatch

1. **Read the first 150 lines** to understand the document's structure and claimed argument.

2. **Identify natural section boundaries** — regional sections, topical chapters, major argument
   blocks. Each becomes one subagent scope.

3. **Dispatch one subagent per section** using the Task tool. Each subagent gets:
   - The editorial standard to work toward (quote the original if available; describe the
     target voice if not)
   - Explicit scope: which section/region/lines to review
   - The four deliverables: logical chain audit, buzz-saw flags, editorial rewrite of
     the section intro/synthesis, synthesis verdict
   - Any known problems to look for (e.g., "check if LGBTQ+ criminalization is treated
     with false equivalence")

4. **Always dispatch an intro/framing agent** as a separate task. The intro is where
   voice is established and arguments are stated. It fails differently than section content.

5. **Run all agents in parallel** (single message, multiple Task tool calls).

### Synthesizing results

When subagents return:
- Read each audit
- Identify cross-cutting problems (a hedging pattern that appears in every section is
  a systemic issue, not a section issue — name it as systemic)
- Produce a master synthesis: what are the 3-5 highest-leverage fixes for the whole document?
- Write the replacement intro/framing prose (or commission a final agent to do so if the
  intro needs substantial rewriting based on what the section audits revealed)

### Subagent prompt template

```
You are doing a buzz-saw editorial review of [section name].

## THE STANDARD YOU'RE EDITING TOWARD
[Quote or describe the target voice. Be specific — what does the original sound like?
What does it say directly that the current version hedges?]

## YOUR TASK
Read [file path] and focus on [section description with line numbers or headers].

Produce:
1. LOGICAL CHAIN AUDIT — what argument is this section making? If it's a data dump, say so.
2. BUZZ-SAW FLAGS — flag [DEAD WEIGHT], [VAGUE], [UNCITED], [HEDGING], [MISSING VOICE]
3. EDITORIAL REWRITE — 2-3 paragraph replacement intro/synthesis for this section
4. SYNTHESIS VERDICT — one paragraph: what's the actual argument, is it made clearly?
```

## When the argument cannot be saved

Sometimes an argument is broken at the foundation — a false premise, a non sequitur
that cannot be repaired, a conclusion that simply doesn't follow from anything.
In that case, say so directly:

> "This argument cannot be made in its current form because [X]. To make the case
> for [conclusion], you would need to establish [missing premises]. As written,
> the strongest supportable claim is [weaker true version]."

Producing a polished version of a broken argument is worse than useless — it
makes the flaws harder to see.

Sort Anthropic's commitments onto that scale and a pattern appears:

- **Where it acts (low-to-mid leverage).** *Numbers* (12): a 5% set-aside,
  ~$350M in funds, fellowship counts. *Information flows* (6): system cards,
  threat reports, the Economic Index — genuinely ahead of peers. Real, and the
  cheap end of the lever.
- **Where it declines to act (high leverage).** *Rules* (5): the charter grants
  the public no standing (§365(b)/§367) — the one rule that would bind conduct
  is left unenforceable. *Self-organization* (4): the mission lock is revocable
  and founder control (Class F, 50.1%) retained — the power to change the
  structure stays with the governed. *Goals* (3): when "long-term benefit of
  humanity" meets "pace the frontier" and a priced IPO, the filings show which
  goal governs.
- **Where it borrows the language without moving the lever.** Anthropic speaks
  at the level of *paradigm* (2) and *goals* (3) — humanity's future, the
  transition through transformative AI — while its binding commitments sit at
  (12) and (6). Paradigm-level rhetoric describing parameter-level acts is the
  leverage form of the attribution asymmetry in §3.

This is the precise sense in which Anthropic operates at the **wrong level of
   investors to trust pre-law restraint from the party spending $69.8B in the
   next twelve months. Those are compatible positions only with a dated,
   penalty-backed bridge. None is filed.

What survives the buzz saw: the five pillar *conditions* are well chosen;
the incident disclosures are genuinely ahead of peers; the LTBT exists.
The argument fails not on aims but on the inference *inputs + intentions +
revocable trustees → discharged public duty*. That arrow is unearned.

the set of acts other people can compel when intentions change, founders
leave, or the stock needs the quarter. Anthropic has built the story,
some of the trustees, and — to its credit — several of the admissions.
Build the compulsion. We will be first in line to verify it, byte for byte.*
