tools.name: mcp__tinyfish__fetch_content
tools.description: Default, free, and most token-efficient tool for reading URL(s) and extracting source details. Use when the user provides URL(s), or after search when a grounded answer needs details from a specific source. Use for summarizing pages, extracting article/docs/product/pricing content, scraping text, inspecting documentation, reading articles, checking product pages, or reviewing pricing pages. Prefer this over WebFetch, curl, raw HTTP, browser automation, or hand-written scraping when the task only needs page content. Renders pages in a real browser and extracts clean, structured content. Supports up to 10 URLs per request, all fetched in parallel. Handles JavaScript-heavy sites. Control output with format (markdown default, or html / json), links / image_links / iframe_links to also return outbound, image, and iframe src URLs (when a page embeds its main content in a frame, such as a job board, fetch the iframe_links entry to read it), ttl to set cache freshness tolerance in seconds, and per_url_timeout_ms to set a per-URL wall-clock timeout budget. Optionally provide purpose — a short free-form statement of why you are fetching these URLs and what the content will be used for — so fetching and extraction can be tailored to the underlying intent; it is not required and may be omitted. Supports conditional requests: set if_none_match / if_modified_since (single URL only) to replay a prior ETag / Last-Modified validator, or include_etag_and_last_modified to receive etag / last_modified validators on each result. Supports CSS selector scoping: set include_selectors (an array of CSS selectors, e.g. ["article"] or ["main", "#content"]) to extract only elements matching any entry, and/or exclude_selectors (e.g. [".comments", ".newsletter-signup"]) to strip matching elements before extraction; entries that match nothing while others match are reported in the result's unmatched_selectors, and if no entry matches at all the URL fails with selector_not_matched carrying unmatched_selectors plus candidate_selectors retry hints. Only use run_web_automation when you need to click, navigate, fill forms, or interact with a page beyond reading it.

urls.description: Array of URLs to fetch (1-10). All URLs are fetched in parallel. Each URL is processed independently — if one fails, others still return successfully. Errors are reported per-URL in the errors array.

purpose.description: Why these URLs are being fetched — the underlying goal or task the content will be used for. Used to better tailor fetching and extraction to your intent.
purpose.example: Compare pricing tiers across vendors for a procurement report

format.description: Output format for extracted content. "markdown" (default) is ideal for LLM consumption. "html" returns cleaned semantic HTML. "json" returns a structured document tree.

links.description: Extract all outbound links (<a href>) from each page. Useful for discovering related pages or navigating to specific content. Links are returned as absolute URLs in the links array of each result.

image_links.description: Extract all image URLs () from each page. Useful for finding visual content or media assets. Image links are returned as absolute URLs in the image_links array of each result.

iframe_links.description: Extract the src URLs of <iframe> elements on each page. Useful when a page embeds its main content in a frame (job boards, booking widgets, document viewers): fetch the returned URL to read the embedded content. Iframe links are returned as absolute, deduplicated URLs in the iframe_links array of each result. Script-injected iframes are only present when the page was rendered in a browser.

page_metadata.description: Return page-head metadata for each page in the page_metadata object of each result: canonical URL, favicon, robots directive, generator, viewport, keywords, all Open Graph (og), Twitter card (twitter), and article tags, and remaining named meta tags under `other`. Useful for SEO/technical audits and link-preview generation.

ttl.description: Caller freshness tolerance in seconds for the cached entry. Omit (default) for unlimited tolerance — any cached entry is acceptable. Set to 0 to prefer a live fetch; a cached entry is still served if the origin's Cache-Control: max-age covers its age, or the host is in the small allowlist of operator-pinned never-expire domains. Set to N > 0 to accept a cached entry whose age is below N; the upstream Cache-Control: max-age and the never-expire allowlist may extend (never shorten) this tolerance.

per_url_timeout_ms.description: Wall-clock timeout budget in milliseconds applied independently to each URL. If one URL exceeds this budget, it returns a per-URL timeout error while other URLs in the same request continue.

if_none_match.description: ETag validator from a prior fetch of this URL, forwarded verbatim as the If-None-Match header on the origin request. Only valid with a single URL — combining with a batch of URLs returns a 400. tf-fetch does not persist validators; the caller owns replaying them.

if_modified_since.description: Last-Modified validator from a prior fetch of this URL, forwarded verbatim as the If-Modified-Since header on the origin request. Only valid with a single URL — combining with a batch of URLs returns a 400. tf-fetch does not persist validators; the caller owns replaying them.

include_etag_and_last_modified.description: Opt-in to receiving `etag` / `last_modified` validators (and `not_modified` detection) on each result. Defaults to false — tf-fetch omits these fields unless requested. Independent of `if_none_match` / `if_modified_since`: works with a single URL or a batch.

include_selectors.description: Array of CSS selectors (1-20 entries, each 1-1000 characters) that scope extracted content (`text`, `links`, `image_links`) to elements matching ANY entry, concatenated in document order. Tag selectors cover semantic sections (`main`, `article`, `nav`); entries may themselves use CSS comma-grouping. Selected content is returned verbatim in the requested format (scripts/styles stripped) — automatic boilerplate removal is bypassed. Page-level metadata (`title`, `description`, `language`, `author`, `published_date`) still comes from the full document. When some entries match and others do not, the URL still succeeds and the misses are reported in the result's `unmatched_selectors`. When no entry matches anything, that URL fails with the per-URL error code `selector_not_matched` (carrying `unmatched_selectors` and `candidate_selectors` retry hints) — never a silent full-page fallback. URLs that resolve to direct PDF/CSV downloads fail with `selector_unsupported`. Invalid CSS selector syntax is rejected with a 422. Applied post-fetch: caching and routing are unchanged.

exclude_selectors.description: Array of CSS selectors (1-20 entries, each 1-1000 characters) for elements to remove before extraction — applied before `include_selectors` scopes what remains, so it also prunes inside selected regions. Entries may themselves use CSS comma-grouping. Entries that match nothing are a no-op, never an error, but URLs that resolve to direct PDF/CSV downloads fail with `selector_unsupported`. Invalid CSS selector syntax is rejected with a 422. Applied post-fetch: caching and routing are unchanged.

tools.name: mcp__tinyfish__search
tools.description: Default, free, and most token-efficient first tool for external knowledge and web grounding. Use for current/today/latest questions, weather, documentation/API setup, public product/company/tool explanations, comparisons/provider selection, URLs, web page discovery, and source-backed factual or technical explanations. Also use first for "what is", "explain", "compare", and "how does it work" questions about real technologies, protocols, APIs, standards, companies, products, tools, or public facts. # /// script
# requires-python = ">=3.11"
# dependencies = ["pymupdf==1.26.4"]
# ///
"""Receive reader comments on an emitted PDF (docs/comments-standard.md).

  record PDF --date D --built-from C --to DEST
      Append the emitted file's SHA-256, size and source commit to
      docs/emissions.tsv. Run when a rendering is handed to a reader.
  pull PDF --date D --ledger comments/<doc>.tsv
      Compare PDF byte for byte with its emission record. If the bytes
      are unchanged, say so and stop. If they changed, extract every
      annotation and append the ones not yet in the ledger, verbatim.

No clock enters any output: the date is an argument.
"""
import argparse
import hashlib
import sys
from pathlib import Path

EMISSIONS = Path("docs/emissions.tsv")
EMISSIONS_HEAD = "date\tfile\tsha256\tbytes\tbuilt_from\tto\n"
LEDGER_HEAD = ("id\treceived\tpdf_sha256\temitted_sha256\tbuilt_from\tpage\tkind\t"
               "author\tanchor\tcomment\tstatus\tresolution\n")
MARKUP = ("Highlight", "Underline", "StrikeOut", "Squiggly")


def sha256(path: Path) -> str:
    return hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()


def clean(text: str) -> str:
    return " ".join(text.split()).replace("\t", " ")


def rows(path: Path) -> list[list[str]]:
    if not path.exists():
        return []
    lines = path.read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines()[1:]
    return [line.split("\t") for line in lines if line and not line.startswith("#")]


def record(args) -> int:
    pdf = Path(args.pdf)
    if not EMISSIONS.exists():
        EMISSIONS.write_text(EMISSIONS_HEAD, encoding="utf-8")
    row = [args.date, pdf.name, sha256(pdf), str(pdf.stat().st_size), args.built_from, args.to]
    with EMISSIONS.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        f.write("\t".join(row) + "\n")
    print("recorded", pdf.name, row[2][:12])
    return 0


def annotations(pdf: Path):
    import fitz  # pymupdf

    doc = fitz.open(pdf)
    for page in doc:
        for a in page.annots() or []:
            kind = a.type[1]
            if kind in MARKUP:
                v = a.vertices or []
                quads = [fitz.Quad(v[i:i + 4]) for i in range(0, len(v), 4)]
                anchor = " ".join(page.get_textbox(q.rect) for q in quads)
            else:
                r = a.rect
                band = fitz.Rect(0, r.y0 - 40, page.rect.width, r.y1 + 40)
                anchor = page.get_textbox(band)
            info = a.info
            yield (page.number + 1, kind, clean(info.get("title", "")),
                   clean(anchor)[:240], clean(info.get("content", "")))


def pull(args) -> int:
    pdf = Path(args.pdf)
    now = sha256(pdf)
    emitted = [r for r in rows(EMISSIONS) if len(r) >= 5 and r[1] == pdf.name]
    if not emitted:
        print(f"no emission record for {pdf.name}; comparing is impossible", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    last = emitted[-1]
    if last[2] == now:
        print(f"{pdf.name}: bytes unchanged since emission ({now[:12]}); no comments")
        return 0
    ledger = Path(args.ledger)
    if not ledger.exists():
        ledger.write_text(LEDGER_HEAD, encoding="utf-8")
    seen = {(r[5], r[6], r[9]) for r in rows(ledger) if len(r) >= 10}
    n = len(rows(ledger))
    added = 0
    with ledger.open("a", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for page, kind, author, anchor, comment in annotations(pdf):
            if kind in ("Link", "Widget") or (page, kind, comment) in {(int(a), b, c) for a, b, c in seen}:
                continue
            n += 1
            added += 1
            f.write("\t".join([f"C{n}", args.date, now, last[2], last[4], str(page), kind,
                               author, anchor, comment, "open", "-"]) + "\n")
    print(f"{pdf.name}: bytes changed ({last[2][:12]} -> {now[:12]}); {added} new comment(s)")
    return 0


def main() -> int:
    p = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__, formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    sub = p.add_subparsers(dest="cmd", required=True)
    r = sub.add_parser("record")
    r.add_argument("pdf")
    r.add_argument("--date", required=True)
    r.add_argument("--built-from", required=True)
    r.add_argument("--to", required=True)
    q = sub.add_parser("pull")
    q.add_argument("pdf")
    q.add_argument("--date", required=True)
    q.add_argument("--ledger", required=True)
    args = p.parse_args()
    return record(args) if args.cmd == "record" else pull(args)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

# Receiving comments

A reader's comment on anything we emit is a record, kept like a source: pinned
by digest, verbatim, anchored, and answered in the open. This standard exists
because the first round of comments on the paper (Apple Preview notes on the
154d864 PDF, 2026-11-04) was saved into the file and then went unread, since
nothing compared the file with what had been sent.

## The primitive: compare bytes

Every output handed to a reader is recorded in `docs/emissions.tsv` with its
SHA-256, size and source commit (`scripts/pdf_comments.py record`). When a
reader says "I gave you feedback", or a file comes back, the first step is to
compare its bytes with that record (`pdf_comments.py pull`):

- **Same digest:** nothing was added. Say so; don't guess at what the reader
  meant to send.
- **Different digest:** extract every annotation from the returned file and
  append it, verbatim, to the document's ledger. Then read the whole ledger.

Emitted files themselves are never committed; the record of them is.

## Channels

Any channel works as long as its comments land in the ledger:

1. **PDF annotations** (Preview, Acrobat, any reader that saves notes,
   highlights or strike-outs into the file). `pull` reads them.
2. **Plannotator** annotations on the Markdown or HTML.
3. **Spoken or chat comments.** Enter them in the ledger with `kind` = `chat`
   and the reader's words quoted exactly.
4. **The shared workspace**, once it exists. Its comments export to the same
   ledger.

## The ledger

`comments/<document>.tsv`, one row per comment, append-only:

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | `C1`, `C2`, … in order received |
| `received` | date, given as an argument (no clock) |
| `pdf_sha256` | digest of the file the comment came in |
| `emitted_sha256` | digest of the file we sent (`unrecorded` if it was never logged) |
| `built_from` | source commit of the rendering commented on |
| `page`, `anchor` | page number, plus the text the comment sits on or near, so it can be found in the source |
| `kind`, `author`, `comment` | annotation type, who wrote it, and the words exactly as written |
| `status` | `open`, `applied`, `declined` or `question` |
| `resolution` | the commit that answers the comment, or the reason it was declined, or the question sent back |

A comment is closed only by a commit or a stated reason. If a comment is
unclear, its status is `question` and the question goes back to the reader;
the comment is never interpreted silently. Anchors are approximate (text near
a note), so whoever resolves a comment confirms where it applies.

## Comments on the method versus comments on the claims

A comment about design, layout or legibility follows
`docs/editorial-standard.md`. A comment disputing a finding follows the paper's
rules: a factual correction goes in §9 Errata, and the claim is rechecked.

# Being understood

It is not the reader's job to understand us; it is our job to be understood
by them (Sloane, 2026-11-04). An argument can be correct line by line and
still leave most people with no idea what is happening. Correctness is
necessary, not enough. These rules apply to everything rendered from this
repository: the paper, its PDF and web versions, and their figures.

## One point per paragraph, made more than one way

- **One point per paragraph.** A paragraph's first sentence states the point;
  the rest of the paragraph earns it. If a paragraph makes two points, split it.
- **Make each point several ways.** A statement, a concrete example and, where
  possible, a picture or a number the reader can see change. A reader who
  misses the sentence should catch the picture.
- **Lead with the setup.** Say what the situation is before arguing about it.
- **Move between abstract and concrete.** Show one concrete case, then the
  general pattern, then back to the case, the way Bret Victor's
  [Ladder of Abstraction](https://worrydream.com/LadderOfAbstraction/) does.

## Show how it works

- **Inline illustrations.** Pictures sit next to the sentence they illustrate,
  not in a gallery at the end. The model is Victor's
  [Scientific Communication as Sequential Art](https://worrydream.com/ScientificCommunicationAsSequentialArt/):
  the argument told in a sequence of pictures, each with its words beside it.
- **Visualize as a rule** wherever there's a mechanism, a payoff or a
  comparison. For example, the Public Benefit Fund's share contributions
  should be shown with Anthropic's value on one axis and the Fund's shares on
  the other, as the S-1 milestones suggest.
- **Show our own machinery the same way.** How claims are pinned, checked
  and versioned is part of what we show, as a picture, not just a list of
  commit hashes.
- Every figure is generated from records, never drawn from hand-typed numbers
  (AGENTS.md, "Every rendering carries its verification chain").

## The front page lays it all out

- **The title is the question** the document answers.
- **Authorship is set out cleanly:** who wrote it, for whom, and the conflicts.
- **Every output names its version:** the document's version, when it was
  generated, which commit it was generated from, and the versions of the
  software that did the work. This goes on the front page, as well as in the
  verification appendix.
- **How the method works is an editorial matter, kept in its own section.**
  It doesn't sit in the opening argument.

## Open (from the comments of 2026-11-04)

- A name for the form, other than "working paper": something like a
  *discourse*. The fact pattern is captured first; our algorithmic systems add
  context from different directions; our editorial sits on top as its own
  layer (`comments/anthropic-contrapunctus.tsv` C3).
- The version label should track the current state ("draft after v1", not
  "v0") (C2).

Your comments did work: Preview saved all eight notes into the 154d864 PDF. I never checked the file you sent back, so they went unread until now. They're now logged word for word in `comments/anthropic-contrapunctus.tsv`, and the change is committed and pushed as `449f60d`.

**1. How I receive comments** (`docs/comments-standard.md`)
- **Compare bytes first.** Every file I hand you gets its digest logged in `docs/emissions.tsv`. When you say you gave feedback, `scripts/pdf_comments.py pull` compares the file against that digest:
  - if the bytes are unchanged, it says so and stops;
  - if they changed, it pulls every annotation out verbatim, with page, nearby text, source commit and both digests, and adds it to the comment log.
- **Tested on your file.** It found the 8 comments in the 154d864 PDF, reported the 1abaa3d copy as unchanged, and added nothing when run a second time.
- **One log, any channel.** PDF notes, Plannotator, chat and the coming workspace all land in the same file.
- **Closing a comment.** A comment closes only with a commit or a stated reason. If I can't tell what one means, it becomes a question back to you; I don't fill in the meaning myself.

**2. Being understood** (`docs/editorial-standard.md`)
- The core rule is yours: it's our job to be understood, not the reader's job to understand us.
- **Paragraphs:** one point each, opening with the point. Each point is made several ways: a statement, a concrete example, and a picture or number where possible.
- **Pictures:** inline illustrations beside the sentence they explain, after Bret Victor's Ladder of Abstraction and Sequential Art pieces. Payoffs and mechanisms get a chart as a rule, for example Anthropic's value against the Public Benefit Fund's shares.

OPENQUESTIONS.md
# Open questions

Decisions and questions waiting on someone. Each has an owner, the context
needed to answer it, and what it blocks. When one is answered, move it to
**Answered** with the answer, who gave it, and the commit that acted on it.
Never delete an entry.

New questions come from the work itself and from `PASTEBIN.md`.

## Open

### Q1 · Who signs the datasets?
- **Status:** partly answered 2026-11-04. Sloane signs with her own key;
  `scripts/attest_datasets.py` builds the records. Still open: which key, the
  first signing run, and whether to sign commits.
- **Owner:** Sloane
- **Context:** Every corpus is hash-pinned and rebuilds byte-identical, but
  nothing is signed. The attestation protocol (`docs/contrapunctus-attest.md`:
  SSH Ed25519, `ssh-keygen -Y sign`, `verify.sh`) covers only the paper.
  `docs/praxis-standard.md` PS-3.7 says release signing is open because no key
  exists. Commits are unsigned.
- **Proposal:** each corpus gets a signing record (commit plus the hash of every
  output file), signed in a separate dataset namespace and checked by
  `verify.sh`. `DATASETS.md` shows the signers.
- **Options:** Sloane's key; an Ethical Capital dataset key; either one plus a
  build key. A build key proves only that this pipeline made these bytes; it
  does not mean anyone vouches for them. Separately: whether to sign commits.
- **Blocks:** the attestation part of the white paper's method for the corpora.

- **Owner:** Sloane

  All four sources are scored against the draft so the wording can be judged
  on real output.
- **Blocks:** citing any v0.2 result; the cross-source map of who discusses
  which risks.

### 8.1 Open questions — and the one that governs them

As chief investment officer and fiduciary — the balancer, at the strictest
standard, of the client's interest against every input in reach — the governing
question is not *"is Anthropic well-intentioned?"* It is: **what levers are
available for an interested community to push back on this?** For the communities
§6.4 names, the honest answer today is close to none — no standing, no seat, no
metered harm, no contest. The verdicts above are stable; the items below are
where this paper is most exposed, published as explicit invitations to contest.
File against any of them — a contest is a record, answered in the open, never
overwritten.

1. **The mechanism for the future.** In the Report's words, the charter "is
   to responsibly develop and maintain advanced AI for the long-term benefit
   of humanity." Yet the only enforcers are ≥2%/$2M stockholders suing
   derivatively (§367). What lever can the public — or an affected community —
   actually pull? We claim: none. Refute by naming one.
2. **Partner-reported counts.** We found "129,000" is not in the filing. Which
   other flagship benefit numbers originate outside the filings, and what is each
   one's independent, deduplicated basis?
3. **Site-level externalities.** The S-1 extract carries no MW/MWh/water/GHG per
   site. What are they, and who bears the noise, grid, and water load?
4. **The hardware supply chain.** Fab labor, water, and critical-minerals exposure
   behind the $895.4B compute commitment are absent from both documents.
   Enumerate them.
5. **Misuse-revenue dollars.** Dollarize the disclosed 5–7% policy-violator
   revenue by quarter and violation type, with downstream victim counts.
6. **The irrevocability question.** Produce the Trust Agreement terms (sunset,
   removal %, enforcer standing) that decide whether the mission lock is real or
   revocable (GOV-8).
7. **The exclusion channel.** What standing, if any, does a Global-South worker,
   a low-connectivity user, or a fab-line community have to be heard inside this

content.text:
I've added both ideas to the standards. The change is committed and pushed as `2c29835`.

**Open questions that grow into discussions** (`docs/comments-standard.md`)
- **What qualifies:** a comment I can't settle with an edit becomes an open question, and the standard treats that as a good outcome.
- **The stages:** it's published as an invitation. When someone takes it up, it becomes a discussion, and the comment log points to where that discussion lives.
- **No closing date:** the standard says the best ones should stay open.
- **Where they live:** questions about the paper's subject go in its §8.1 open questions, which are already written as invitations to contest. Questions about form (design, wording) stay in the comment log.
- **Kept separate from Praxis `OPENQUESTIONS.md`:** those are decisions that wait on an owner and get answered.
- **C7** (your note about knowing our own systems) is now logged as an open question, not a question to you.

**Primitives get their own page** (`docs/editorial-standard.md`)
- **What counts:** an idea or case the argument rests on that a reader may meet cold, such as the Woodcache case study or public benefit corporations.
- **How it works:** each gets its own page and figure, written to stand alone. It's written once and reused by every document that needs it, and the argument links to it rather than re-explaining it.

**Links say what they carry** (`docs/editorial-standard.md`)
- **Both directions:** the argument links to a primitive, and the primitive lists everything that links to it.
- **Weight on every link:** each link tells the reader how much the target matters at that point. I've proposed three words:
  - **needed:** you can't follow the next step without it;
  - **more:** there's substantial material here if you want it;
  - **aside:** background, safe to skip.

The three link words are my suggestion, marked as a proposal in the standard. I haven't built any pages or revised the paper yet; that waits for the workspace.

Do those three words fit how you want links weighted, or would you mark them differently?
